In the kitchen with Henny: Sweetness in every course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:58:09 UTC
18:58:09 KST

Rosh Hashanah marks a new beginning for all of us, but for me, it also marks the start of my career as a kitchen coach.
Back in 2020, after months of quarantine, my daughter finally started first grade. That first day she went back to school, I sat down at my computer to plan our Rosh Hashanah menus and thought, maybe I can share these ideas and recipes with others.
The name “In the Kitchen with Henny” popped into my head; I put together a simple PDF for friends and family, and a new chapter began.
Ever since then, Rosh Hashanah has felt even more special to me. It reminds me how something small can turn into something you never expected, which somehow feels very fitting for the start of a new year.
I love that we can incorporate the simanim into the meal itself, using these traditional symbolic foods throughout. So I worked them into simple, festive dishes, using honey, silan, pomegranate, apples, and other familiar Rosh Hashanah flavors. Nothing complicated, just food that feels special and lets you enjoy the sweetness of the simanim from the first bite to the last spoonful.
Honey-orange salmon bites
By the time we fill our plates with sweet challah, apples, and honey, dates, pomegranate, and all the other simanim, there is already a lot going on. I love the idea of adding fish in a way that doesn’t turn it into a whole extra course.
These bite-sized salmon pieces make it easy for everyone to have a taste, while the honey-orange glaze keeps them festive and right at home on the Rosh Hashanah table.
Yields 6-8 servings, as a starter or siman
600 gr. skinless salmon fillet, cut into 5-6 cm. cubes
2 Tbsp. honey
3 Tbsp. fresh orange juice
1 Tbsp. grated orange zest
2 Tbsp. olive oil
2 garlic cloves, crushed
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. black pepper
Pomegranate seeds, fresh parsley, and orange slices for garnish 
In a bowl, whisk together the honey, orange juice, olive oil, garlic, salt, pepper, and orange zest. Add the salmon cubes and gently toss until well coated. Let marinate in the refrigerator for 20-30 minutes.
Arrange the salmon in a single layer on a baking-paper-lined pan and pour any remaining marinade over the top. Bake at 200°C / 400°F for 10-12 minutes, or until the salmon is just cooked through and lightly glazed. Transfer to a serving platter and garnish with pomegranate seeds, chopped parsley, and a few orange slices. Chill until serving.
Silan-roasted carrots & squash
By now, you’ve probably noticed how much I love cooking with – and eating – zucchini. So when I came across a version of this dish made with just carrots and butternut squash, which honestly is delicious enough on its own, I had to try adding zucchini.
I love the extra flavor, and especially the pop of green it brings to the platter. Best of all, the oven and silan do all the work, caramelizing the vegetables beautifully without you having to stand over a pan to sauté them. Serve them as is, or spoon them over warm brown rice for a more substantial side.
Yields 6 servings
4 large carrots, peeled and cut into thick diagonal slices
1 small butternut squash, peeled and cut into 3-4 cm. cubes
2 medium zucchini, cut into thick half-moons
8-10 garlic cloves, peeled
3 Tbsp. olive oil
2 Tbsp. silan
1 Tbsp. lemon juice
½ tsp. salt
¼ tsp. black pepper
2 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, for garnish
6 Medjool dates, pitted and chopped, for garnish 
Preheat the oven to 200°C / 400°F. In a small bowl, whisk together the olive oil, silan, lemon juice, salt, and pepper. Place the carrots, butternut squash, and garlic in a large baking pan. Pour about two-thirds of the marinade over the vegetables and toss well to coat. Roast for 25 minutes.
Meanwhile, toss the zucchini with the remaining marinade. Add the zucchini to the pan and gently mix with the other vegetables. Return to the oven and roast for another 15 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender and caramelized. Transfer to a serving platter and scatter the chopped dates and parsley over the top. Serve warm or at room temperature.
Sweet & shallot chicken
I like to have two different mains available when we’re hosting a large crowd, which is usually the case for the first night of Rosh Hashanah. So I was on the lookout for a chicken dish that looked and tasted a little different.
I love the idea of roasting lots of whole shallots alongside the chicken. They become soft and caramelized, and add a rich flavor that balances the sweet and tart glaze.
Although this recipe is written for chicken, the marinade would also work beautifully with brisket or short ribs, just allowing for a longer, slower cooking time.
Yields 6-8 servings
8-10 bone-in chicken thighs or a mix of thighs and drumsticks
10-12 small shallots, peeled and left whole
3 Tbsp. pomegranate molasses
2 Tbsp. honey
3 Tbsp. olive oil
3 garlic cloves, crushed
1 tsp. salt
½ tsp. black pepper
½ tsp. paprika
Pomegranate seeds and chopped parsley, for garnish 
Preheat the oven to 160°C / 325°F. Line a baking pan with baking paper. Arrange the chicken in the pan, pour the marinade over the top, and tuck the whole shallots around the chicken. Place a sheet of wet baking paper directly over the chicken, then cover the pan tightly with foil to seal. Bake for 1½ hours.
Raise the oven to 175°C / 350°F, remove the foil and baking paper, and bake uncovered for another 30 minutes, until the chicken is browned and the sauce is glossy and caramelized. Transfer to a serving platter and garnish with pomegranate seeds and parsley.
Apple-honey upside-down layer cake
A few years back, I shared my Bubby’s delicious honey cake recipe. It’s a no-fail, perfectly delicious honey cake, and one I come back to every year.
When I saw the idea of an upside-down apple-honey cake, I knew her recipe would be perfect for it. Since the apples add more volume to the pan than usual, I scaled the recipe down to about two-thirds so it bakes nicely in a 9-inch round springform pan.
And while Rosh Hashanah is not usually the holiday when we like to turn things upside down, maybe there is something fitting about it as we start a new year. We all have things in our lives we would love to see turn around for the better, and there is something especially sweet about watching that apple-honey layer on the bottom become the beautiful top of the cake.
Yields 1 - 9” round springform pan
3 medium apples, peeled, cored, and thinly sliced
3 Tbsp. honey
2 Tbsp. brown sugar
½ tsp. cinnamon
Cake batter:
3 eggs
½ cup sugar
²⁄³ cup oil
1 cup honey
2 cups flour
2 tsp. baking powder
½ tsp. baking soda
²⁄³  cup cold strong coffee
½ tsp. cinnamon
¼ tsp. nutmeg
Preheat the oven to 190°C / 375°F. Line the bottom of a deep 9-inch round springform pan with baking paper, then grease the baking paper and the sides of the pan well. Drizzle the honey over the bottom of the pan, then sprinkle with the brown sugar and cinnamon. Arrange the apple slices on top in a circular pattern, slightly overlapping. Bake for 8–10 minutes, until the apples begin to soften and caramelize.
In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs and sugar until combined. Add the remaining ingredients, alternating between the dry and wet ingredients, and mix until smooth. Gently pour the batter over the apples.
While the apples are baking, prepare the cake batter. In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs and sugar until combined. Add the remaining ingredients, alternating between the dry and wet ingredients, and mix until smooth.
Remove the caramelized apple layer from the oven and carefully pour the cake batter over the apples. Return the pan to the oven and bake at 190°C / 375°F for 35–45 minutes, or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean.
Let the cake cool in the pan for 15–20 minutes. Run a knife around the sides, release the springform, then carefully invert the cake onto a serving plate and remove the baking paper.
Enjoying simanim throughout the meal
FROM THE first bite to the last spoonful, these recipes let us enjoy the simanim throughout the meal, not just at the beginning. And maybe that is something we can carry beyond the table, too.
As we begin a new year, may all the sweetness we eat inspire us to bring a little more sweetness into our homes, our families, and our communities. May we be kinder to one another, more united, and more aware of how much we need each other.
And especially here in Israel, may this be a year of peace, healing, and good news, with our soldiers safely home with their families, and a year in which we have so much more to celebrate together.
Shana tova u’metuka! ■
The writer is a kitchen coach who teaches women how to meal plan and cook, so they get dinner on the table and prepare for Shabbat and chag on time. Learn more about one-on-one coaching and food workshops: www.inthekitchenwithhenny.com

Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:56:53 UTC
18:56:53 KST

Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
As oil tanker struck off Kharg island, Trump threatens one of the remaining parts of Iran’s nuclear complex.
United States President Donald Trump says Washington may strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very soon”, in just the latest in a series of threats he has made against the heavily fortified underground site located next to the bombed-out Natanz enrichment complex.
Just hours after he made that threat, an Iranian oil tanker off Kharg Island was struck by four US missiles, according to Iranian news outlet Khabar Fouri. Kharg Island is the main hub for Iran’s oil exports, handling about 90 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 2 of 4South Korea mulls ‘contributions’ in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 4 of 4US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
Trump made the threat against Pickaxe Mountain as he was speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, saying the US knows “everybody that’s moving at Pickaxe” and across Iran.
His remarks echoed a similar threat he made back in mid-July, when he stated on the Hugh Hewitt Show: “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready … We’ll probably give Pickaxe a shot relatively soon.”
The latest threat comes more than six months into the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28, amid mixed messages about the war from the Trump administration.
On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”, while a day earlier, at a White House news briefing, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US strike on a wedding in southern Iran with “sometimes things happen“.
At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict with Iran that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and claimed there was “no active shooting right now”.
But the US and Iran have exchanged attacks this week, including a US hit close to Iran’s oil infrastructure on Kharg Island.
Meanwhile, talks related to Iran’s nuclear programme have remained in limbo since a 60-day negotiating window expired in mid-August without a deal.
Iran says it is not undertaking any work at the Natanz nuclear site.
Its Khatam al-Anbiya central military headquarters has warned that bombing the nearby mountain would amount to a renewal of war across the region, at a time when the Trump administration would prefer to keep the war contained before pivotal mid-term elections.
So why has Pickaxe Mountain become the latest focus of Trump’s threats – again?
What is Pickaxe Mountain?
Known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, the site sits roughly 220km (140 miles) south of the capital Tehran, in Isfahan province, and just 2km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz enrichment plant.
US intelligence reports indicate that the facility has been excavated deep inside the mountain, beneath hundreds of metres of solid granite rock, to protect it from powerful bombs designed to penetrate bunkers.
The main chambers are thought to lie at least 100 metres (330ft) underground.
Some Western analysts have speculated that the mountain was intended to house an undeclared enrichment plant, a hedge against attacks on Iran’s known facilities.
The Institute for Science and International Security, which tracks the site by satellite, has assessed that it is still under construction and not yet operational.
However, Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only, and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.
Why does Pickaxe Mountain matter?
Because it is intact.
Pickaxe Mountain was left alone during the US’s June 2025 strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at the end of the 12-day Israel war on Iran, and has escaped the current war almost entirely; the Institute for Science and International Security has recorded only the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile.
With Iran’s centrifuge manufacturing base and enrichment halls at other sites damaged in the war, analysts see the tunnels as the most obvious place for Tehran to rebuild: For component production, assembly or enrichment of uranium.
The Wall Street Journal reported in July that Israel had passed Washington intelligence suggesting thousands of centrifuges had been moved inside the facility late last year, a claim the US has not confirmed.
Trump has been less alarmist than Israel.
Centrifuges only matter if there is uranium to put through them; the machines concentrate uranium gas, and without a supply of it they cannot produce anything.
How much damage has been done to Iran’s nuclear sites?
According to most estimates, a considerable amount.
The European Council on Foreign Relations estimates that the 2025 strikes likely destroyed many of the roughly 18,000 centrifuges then operating at Iran’s Natanz and Fordow facilities, along with several centrifuge production sites and Ardakan, Iran’s only yellowcake milling plant. Yellowcake is powdered uranium concentrate obtained from milled uranium ore.
Nearly 4,000 additional centrifuges were installed but idle at the time; however, they may have survived the strikes.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed further damage to the entrance buildings of Natanz’s underground enrichment plant in March 2026, although it detected no additional impact on the plant itself.
The Institute for Science and International Security reported in June that tunnel entrances at all three main sites remain sealed, that there is no evidence of any enrichment taking place, and that the centrifuge programme still appears to have been destroyed.
Didn’t Trump say Iran’s nuclear sites had already been destroyed?
Yes. After the June 2025 attacks, Trump said the three sites had been “completely and totally obliterated”.
However, just days later, a leaked preliminary US Defence Intelligence Agency assessment concluded that the sites had been significantly damaged but not destroyed, estimating that the strikes had set Iran’s nuclear programme back by less than six months.
The situation today remains unclear.
“No one really knows what the state of Iran’s nuclear programme is at this moment; there’s a lot of uncertainty and ambiguity about how much damage Iran has suffered as a result of these last two wars,” Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera.
Iran is currently believed to be holding about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent.
But having the material is only part of the equation, Hashemi said.
In order for Iran to produce a nuclear weapon, it would have to enrich that uranium up to 90 percent.
That would require access to its centrifuges, “of which we don’t know to what extent they may have been damaged”, he said.
No inspector has entered the bombed sites, and Trump’s framing has shifted from “obliteration” to a promise to hit any site where Iran is “even thinking about nuclear”.
What do we know about Iran’s nuclear programme?
Less than at any point in two decades.
Just before the US-Israel attacks on Iran in June 2025, the IAEA verified about 10 tonnes of enriched uranium in total, including the 440kg stockpile enriched to 60 percent.
In theory, this amount of enriched uranium – should it be enriched to 90 percent – is enough to produce more than 10 nuclear warheads, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told Al Jazeera in early March. It is unclear where this stock may be, however.
Iran suspended cooperation with the agency after the strikes, and the IAEA now says it has no way to report on the size, location or composition of that stockpile, though it believes much of the 60-percent material is bottled up in tunnels at Isfahan.
On Friday, Trump claimed again that the US had prevented Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, arguing that Washington’s intervention had protected Israel and the wider Middle East.
Tehran insists the programme is peaceful, and has dismissed Washington’s focus on Pickaxe Mountain as a manufactured pretext for attacking it.

Second this month: another Metinvest steel plant halts production after Russian strike – photos

Second this month: another Metinvest steel plant halts production after Russian strike – photos
The Kametstal steel plant in the city of Kamianske has halted all production following a nighttime Russian ballistic missile strike, while the company says it is unable to estimate when operations can resume.
Source: Metinvest Group, the largest steel producer in Ukraine, that owns the plant
Details: The blast furnace and sinter production facilities, as well as the plant's energy and transport infrastructure, were damaged. Emergency repair and restoration work is currently underway, while a full assessment of the equipment will only be possible once the rubble has been cleared.
Five people were killed: four plant employees and one employee of a contractor. Another four plant employees were injured. Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, initially reported four fatalities and five injuries, with three people taken to hospital. The death toll later rose to five.
The strike occurred at around 01:50. Metinvest says only a few minutes passed between an air-raid warning being issued and the strike, which was not enough time for all employees to reach shelters.
"There were no military targets, military equipment or military production facilities at Kametstal. Only civilians worked there, producing iron and steel exclusively for civilian needs," said Oleksandr Myronenko, Chief Operating Officer of the Metinvest Group.
This is the second steel plant in the group to halt production because of Russian strikes in less than a month. Myronenko said Metinvest is going through "the most difficult period in its 20-year history".
Background: Russia struck Zaporizhstal (ZaporizhzhiaSteelworks) twice on 11 and 27 August. The plant also completely halted production. Metinvest compared the damage to the destruction seen during the Second World War. Seven employees were killed and 21 injured in the first strike.

Police to keep assisting fallen seniors outside working hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Police to keep assisting fallen seniors outside working hours
The Ministry of the Interior has changed its initial decision, under which police officers would no longer have to go help elderly people who have fallen at home, leaving this to ambulance crews and social workers, and has now announced that it will temporarily continue providing this assistance outside working hours.
The Ministry of the Interior's decision to stop providing this service came as a surprise to local governments and the Ministry of Social Affairs.
Starting 1 September, elderly people who have fallen at home must be helped by ambulance crews and social workers from local governments. Both the Ministry of Social Affairs and local governments say they are unable to fulfill the obligation set by the Ministry of the Interior.
Excessive workload and lack of resources are among the reasons why such a decision was made, said Tuuli Räim, deputy secretary general of the Ministry of the Interior.
"Police resources are limited. If the police deal with responding to calls for social assistance, it may happen that somewhere else, where they definitely need to be, it becomes harder for them to reach. There are two issues. One is the competence to assess a person's health condition. The other is that we do not consider it appropriate that an armed police patrol is by default the first responding resource. That is why we have made these decisions," the deputy secretary general said.
Räim emphasized that a solution must be found to the problem. She added that since this concerns the social field, the primary responsibility lies with the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Ministry of Regional Affairs in cooperation with the Association of Cities and Municipalities. The Ministry of the Interior sees itself rather as a partner, Räim noted.
The fact remains, however, that local governments are not yet able to take on the entire workload. According to Veikko Luhalaid, head of the Association of Estonian Cities and Municipalities, concerns include the protection of personal and health data, the inability to keep social workers on call around the clock in all municipalities, and their lack of authority to break open a home's door.
The role of local governments would primarily be to prevent falls. The analysis showed that nearly 40 percent of falls were repeat cases — meaning police had gone several times to the same home to help the same person up.
The Ministry of the Interior is now offering temporary relief: "During working hours — Monday to Friday from nine to five — assistance is organized by the local government. Outside working hours, national emergency resources will continue responding for now, whether ambulance, police or rescue services," Räim said.

World grasped out nuclear club was nothing more than a lie
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:55:00 UTC
18:55:00 KST

Speaking at the 2nd Alavi Empowerment and Entrepreneurship Festival, with a focus on the incidents imposed by enemies against the Iranian nation over the past years, he stressed that the world realized that the nuclear club is nothing more than a lie.

UK sends aircraft carrier to strengthen NATO defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:54:07 UTC
18:54:07 KST

- HMS Queen Elizabeth departs Portsmouth on September 5 for a three-month deployment, serving as NATO's afloat command platform for the Allied Reaction Force.
- The Royal Navy took command of the alliance's high-readiness maritime force from Spain in July, and Queen Elizabeth will return to UK high-readiness carrier duty from HMS Prince of Wales in 2027.
HMS Queen Elizabeth is due to leave Portsmouth Naval Base at 6:20 p.m. on Saturday, September 5, carrying more than 800 sailors on a three-month deployment around British and northern European waters, according to UK Defence Journal.
The deployment is the first extended sea period for the 65,000-tonne carrier since it took on a new NATO role in July: serving as the alliance’s afloat command platform for the Allied Reaction Force (Maritime), NATO’s high-readiness naval crisis-response formation. It’s the first time either of the UK’s two Queen Elizabeth-class carriers has held that specific command role. The UK Royal Navy assumed leadership of the force on July 1, taking over from the Spanish Navy, with Rear Admiral Mark Anderson and his Portsmouth-based staff now running it for a 12-month rotation. If activated, the force is designed to assemble warships, naval aircraft and support vessels within ten days to respond to a crisis anywhere in NATO’s area of responsibility.
Over the coming three months, Queen Elizabeth will train alongside allied forces to build up the crew’s ability to run high-end naval operations and command a multinational force under pressure, according to the Royal Navy. The ship will also work through advanced training under the Royal Navy’s Fleet Operational Standards and Training organization, covering the full spectrum of modern naval warfare.
“We’ve returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training,” said Captain Claire Thompson, commanding officer of HMS Queen Elizabeth. “Sailing this autumn is a key milestone for both our NATO commitment, as the Afloat Command Platform and also on our journey back to the Royal Navy’s ‘very high readiness’ aircraft carrier, a duty we will resume from our sister ship HMS Prince of Wales in 2027. Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of NATO should it be required.”
The autumn deployment is doing double duty. Alongside its NATO command responsibilities, Queen Elizabeth is working through the training cycle that will eventually return it to the role of UK principal carrier at very high readiness, a status HMS Prince of Wales currently holds. That handover, along with participation in major NATO exercises, is scheduled to continue through 2027, when Queen Elizabeth is due to take over from Prince of Wales as the UK’s flagship and high-readiness strike carrier.
This is not the first time a Queen Elizabeth-class carrier has worn a NATO hat. Prince of Wales served as NATO’s afloat command platform for the alliance’s rapid response force in 2022, and Queen Elizabeth itself briefly came under NATO operational control during the Neptune Strike exercise in 2023. What’s changed since is the underlying force structure: NATO replaced its old Response Force with the current three-tiered model, including the Allied Reaction Force, following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine and the alliance’s 2023 Vilnius summit, and this deployment marks the first time either British carrier has held the maritime command role under that newer structure.
The Royal Navy said the deployment sits within a broader pattern of British contributions to NATO deterrence. More than 1,000 UK personnel currently serve in NATO command posts, and Britain leads the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps from its headquarters in Gloucestershire. Separately, the UK maintains an 800-strong battlegroup in Estonia, has RAF Typhoon fighters defending NATO airspace over Romania, and operates P-8 Poseidon and RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft around the Baltic Sea.
Britain also assigns its nuclear deterrent to NATO’s defense and, under its Defence Investment Plan, intends to join the alliance’s Dual Capable Aircraft nuclear mission using F-35A fighters, a step that would put the UK in the group of NATO members that can carry nuclear weapons on aircraft rather than only via its submarine-based deterrent.

KATHMANDU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Nepali rescuers on Saturday rescued a Chinese national from a hydropower plant hit by the deadly mudslide in Nepal, according to the Chinese Embassy in Nepal.
The Chinese national was rescued by the Nepali Army in coordination with a disaster expert team from South Korea, 11 days after a devastating mudslide struck the area.
The survivor was taken for further medical assessment and care.
The rescue is part of an intensified effort to locate and evacuate people believed to be trapped inside hydropower project tunnels following a mudslide that swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.

Before the rescue of the Chinese national, the Nepali Army said in a social media post that a joint rescue team comprising 20 Nepali Army personnel and project representatives had been conducting search operations.
The Nepali Army has been conducting search and rescue operations in coordination with foreign technical teams, including experts from China, India and South Korea, to reach people stranded inside structures at several hydropower projects. ■

Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attends the Asia-Pacific Media Forum and delivers a keynote speech in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Sept. 5, 2026. SHENZHEN, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Asia-Pacific Media Forum opened on Saturday in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, with the theme of "Building a Path to Shared Prosperity for the Asia-Pacific Community: Media Consensus and Action."
Li Shulei, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Central Committee, attended the forum and delivered a keynote speech. Huang Kunming, a member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and secretary of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee, attended the forum and delivered a speech.

AU welcomes UN's adoption of maps that show accurate size of Africa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
17:52:18 CST
18:52:18 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The Chairperson of the African Union (AU) Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has welcomed the United Nations General Assembly resolution that encourages the use of the Equal Earth cartographic projection in maps worldwide to replace the Mercator projection widely used so far, which distorts the sizes of continental landmasses.
In a statement issued on Friday, Youssouf commended the leadership of the Republic of Togo, which championed this initiative on behalf of Africa and helped mobilize broad support within the international community. He also congratulated members of the AU for their unity and collective mobilization in support of this initiative.
The AU said the adoption of this resolution marks an important step forward. Designed in the 16th century primarily for navigation, the Mercator projection does not accurately reflect the relative surface areas of different regions of the world and significantly understates the true size of the African continent.
Beyond cartography, this initiative underscores the importance of representing Africa on the basis of objective and scientifically established realities. In this regard, the chairperson encourages international institutions, educational systems, publishers and digital platforms to progressively promote the use of cartographic representations that more accurately reflect actual land areas, according to the statement.
The AU Commission will continue to work with Togo, member states and relevant partners to support efforts towards the implementation of this initiative. Africa must be represented as it truly is, in its true dimensions and in its rightful place in the world, the statement added.
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to adopt a non-binding resolution that encourages the use of the Equal Earth cartographic projection in maps worldwide to replace the Mercator projection.
The 'Correct the Map' resolution, aimed at rebalancing global cartographic representation and promoting equitable representation of the world's regions, particularly Africa, was adopted with 164 votes in favor, 1 against, and 6 abstentions.
It recognizes that the Mercator projection, widely used around the world, distorts continental masses located far from the equator, resulting in a proportional shrinkage of Africa and other regions. ■

The total length of the railway will exceed 500 kilometers, including 304.84 kilometers in Kyrgyzstan. ■

The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:49:30 UTC
18:49:30 KST

The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Many Lives of Anne Frank is a biography, of the German Jewish teenager herself, of her famous diary and, also, of her legacy. Ruth Franklin’s innovative approach to the most famous work of the Holocaust is fascinating, thought-provoking and well worth the read.
The Diary of Anne Frank has been assigned to thousands of students and has sold millions of copies. The annex where the teenager hid with her family during the Second World War is visited by a million tourists a year, whose queue snakes along the canal in Amsterdam for blocks.
Published in 2025, the first half of the book is a classic biography. We follow the Frank family from Germany to exile in the Netherlands and then to further banishment above a warehouse on the Prinsengracht. Franklin brings the story to life, with minute details (it was raining on the evening the Franks walked across the Dutch capital to their hiding place) and wider context (the ongoing round-up of Jews by the occupying Nazis.)
The biography does not end, as most biographies do, with the subject’s death. The young girl died somewhere in March or April of 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, possibly just weeks before it was liberated by the British army.
Her legacy lives on, in her diary published, following edits from her father, shortly after the war. Anne herself also edited the work, inspired by a 1944 appeal from the Dutch minister for education diaries and letters documenting the German occupation. The teen aspired to get her thoughts and feelings into print.
The second half of the book follows the legacy of the diary, how it came into being and how it became a phenomenon, vaulting Anne Frank to an epic level of fame.
Franklin delves into the details of the book’s publication journey, raising questions about what it means for something to be “authentic.”
Anne’s father Otto sends a translated (and edited) version to relatives in Switzerland, who encourage him to publish the work. A composite of Anne’s two versions, plus her father’s edits is submitted to a publisher, who suggests certain cuts as to not offend more conservative readers. A longer, critical edition was published in 1986 and, based on that, the English-language version was published in 1989.
The first German-language version edits a passage Anne wrote taking a dig at the country. She writes “Only civilized languages are permitted [in the Annex], therefore no German,” which is changed to “all civilised languages may be spoken.” The occupants made an effort to speak to one another in Dutch, rather than in their native German, as a form of resistance.
The chapters are all titled with descriptors of the various versions of Anne. The final one is called “Pawn” and addresses her legacy. Otto intended for the diary to “promote peace and tolerance,” Franklin writes, but he couldn’t control his daughter’s celebrity.
The adaptation of the diary in a play in the United States is complicated by differing artistic versions of the work, the iconic image of Anne is used by those protesting South African apartheid and later, Israel’s war on Gaza. Franklin’s chronicle leaves the reader with many questions about how to contextualise the diary of a teenage girl.
A prize-winning literary critic, Franklin is a former editor at The New Republic. Her first biography, Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life, won multiple awards. The Many Lives of Anne Frank was a finalist for the 2025 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.
The Many Lives of Anne Frank is deeply researched, well-written and stimulating.
You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

Qatar removed from Fitch’s negative watch list as risks to LNG sites ease
The global ratings agency has also maintained the country’s sovereign rating at AA.
Fitch Ratings has removed Qatar from “Rating Watch Negative” while maintaining its sovereign rating at AA amid the US-Israel war on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz blockade.
The global ratings agency announced the decision on Friday, citing reduced risks to the country’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities since March.

The agency, however, kept a negative outlook on the rating, citing ongoing risks surrounding the movement of gas exports through the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

Qatar, one of the world’s largest gas exporters, continues to face export disruptions and shortages caused by damaged energy facilities during the war on Iran, which began six months ago.
Earlier this year, credit agencies S&P and Moody’s also affirmed Qatar’s ratings, noting that the country’s sizeable financial cushion helps protect it from the economic impact of the war.

IFA 2026: Looking beyond the smart home with Haier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:47:52 UTC
18:47:52 KST

From AI-powered appliances to humanoid robots, Haier is using IFA 2026 to showcase its vision of the "intelligent home". Euronews spoke to Haier Europe CEO Neil Tunstall about what comes after the smart home — and how soon some of these ideas could become reality.
"The Future is Now" is the motto of this year's IFA. Chinese home appliance and consumer electronics group Haier has brought its own take on that theme to Berlin, under the slogan "Home of Intelligent Possibilities".
The company is using IFA 2026 to lay out its vision of intelligent living — a home where connected appliances and AI do not just assist, but anticipate.
Euronews spoke to Haier Europe CEO Neil Tunstall about what comes after the smart home, and how soon some of these ideas could become reality.
Beyond the smart home
The idea is to go one step beyond the smart home towards what Haier calls the intelligent home, a system built around people rather than products.
Instead of putting individual devices at the centre, the company says it wants to build connected systems around the people using them and their everyday needs.
A large part of that vision is about making technology more intuitive and reducing the amount of thought people have to put into everyday household tasks.
"I think in the area of the cooking, the possibility for the product to see what's inside, to make sure it's done to the right way, to take out the variation of people not being so confident in putting something in the oven and hoping it's cooked," Tunstall said.
"The product now will do that for you. And that hopefully means then that we can actually enjoy eating much more at home."
Sustainability in the intelligent home
But making everyday life easier is not the only reason Haier is investing in smarter and more connected appliances. Sustainability is also a key consideration, according to Tunstall.
"If you think about the whole cycle, so from the manufacturing, from the logistics, the lorries moving around, the biggest one for our industry is actually use, because we are electrical products, so we use a lot of electricity and water," he said.
For Tunstall, reducing the environmental impact of appliances also means looking at how they are used once they are in people's homes, with smart technology helping manage energy consumption more efficiently.
Haier's "end-to-end innovation"
Sustainability is also being considered at the production stage. Haier describes its approach as "end-to-end innovation," with AI and data being used across different stages of developing, manufacturing and delivering its products.
"We have mass of big data where we can understand how do people use products, which programmes do they use? How do they load the washing machine? What do they do? All this data comes together to allow us then to create new use cases and new things," Tunstall said.
According to Tunstall, the aim is to use that information not only to develop products but also to make the way they are manufactured and delivered more efficient.
To continue developing these technologies, Haier is also planning significant investment in the coming years.
"Our next five years is spending 13 billion on AI, on robotics, on R&D, advanced engineering, and all of those things," Tunstall said.
Tunstall says the investment is intended to speed up the development and rollout of new technologies across Haier's product range.
"We want to innovate to bring better value to consumers and to our trade partners. And that 13 billion will be accelerating how fast we can bring innovation to market. Across all our product categories, we can create new ideas, new use cases faster as a result of this investment."
'We do not want to replace the human'
Tunstall has a clear vision of where these developments could lead. Looking further into the future, connected devices could eventually be joined by humanoid robots. For him, the key is ensuring that the human element does not get lost along the way, avoiding a "science fiction" scenario in which robots simply take over.
"We're not trying to replace the human," Tunstall said.
"But there are basic tasks that robotics can do. Already robot vacuum cleaners, robots cutting the grass. And some of the basic things that we need to do ourselves, the robots will be able to do it for us together with AI."
And when it comes to the timeframe, Tunstall believes this future may not be as far away as it seems.
"I think you will see our industry creating this innovation very rapidly. Things move faster than we think."
The technology may not be fully there yet, but Tunstall is optimistic that it will not take long to reach consumers, not just overseas, but also here in Europe.
"We have to commercialise them and bring them to market, so they're not here right now, but they are going to be here pretty soon in this industry."
From innovation to the market
But bringing new technology to market also means adapting it to very different consumers. For Tunstall, Haier's global scale allows the company to develop technologies and components across markets while adapting the products built around them to local habits and needs.
"The Chinese consumer cooks something completely different to the British consumer, as you can imagine," he told Euronews.
And those differences do not only exist between continents. Tunstall says there is no single European consumer either.
"The French consumer is different to the European, the English consumer very different Italians, so even within Europe we don't have one consumer, we have many different cases and we need to make sure then that we are ... truly listening to the individual consumer and giving them the product they want."
For now, some of Haier's ideas remain concepts. But Tunstall suggests visitors may not have to wait too long to see which of them make the transition from the exhibition floor to the market.
"We'll be here next year as well, perhaps launching some of those things that we're just showing as concept today."

Hundreds attend memorial march for Swiss rave shooting victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Hundreds attend memorial march for Swiss rave shooting victims
An estimated 300 people took part in a memorial march at the Schachen in Aarau, northern Switzerland, on Friday evening to remember victims of the shooting rampage at a rave last weekend. The event, arranged by the rave organisers, included a minute’s silence.
According to the organisers, the event – which had been authorised by the City of Aarau – was intended to create “a dignified space for mourning, compassion and solidarity”. They also wanted to take a stand against all forms of hatred and violence. The organisers had issued an invitation to the memorial march via social media.
The march began in a car park near the swimming pool on the Schachen site in Aarau. Most participants held a candle in their hands; some also carried a white rose, whilst others carried whole bouquets of flowers. Quite a few people were dressed in black.
More
The march ended at the entrance to the Aarau racecourse. There, the participants laid candles and flowers at a makeshift memorial and stood in silence for a few minutes before leaving. Among those taking part in the march was Dieter Egli, a member of the Aargau cantonal government and head of the police.
Early on Sunday morning, a 43-year-old Swiss man from the canton of Jura in western Switzerland had fired over 40 shots indiscriminately using two guns at a rave party in Schachen. A 22-year-old Italian woman living in Switzerland was killed. According to the Italian news agency Ansa, the woman will be buried on Sunday.
Five people sustained gunshot wounds of varying severity during the rampage. According to the Aargau cantonal police, a further victim came forward later; they may have been slightly injured by a ricocheting bullet.
More
Swiss firearm laws: How Switzerland combines a passion for guns with safety
The shooter turned himself in to the Jura cantonal police in Delémont in the early hours of Monday morning. The Aargau cantonal police had been tracking the man and had already identified the vehicle used in the attack. The Swiss national is currently in pre-trial detention in Aargau.

The Watch World Went Crazy This Week. Here Are the 10 You Need to See
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

While Watches and Wonders every April is undoubtedly the watch world's main event of the year, Geneva Watch Days—which inauspiciously launched in 2020, the year Covid was declared a pandemic—is now establishing itself as a serious follow-up. Big brands can hold back key releases and gain valuable space to shout about new pieces away from the horological hubbub of W&W.
A second bite of the marketing apple in the latter half of the year seems like a good idea, as Swiss watch exports declined again in 2025 after a drop in 2024. However, despite America's tariff seesaw, the US is still by far the single largest market for Swiss watches. And, more positively for watch fans, signs suggest the industry downturn could be over.
Here are WIRED's picks of the best watches that dropped this week.
Inspired by the 1960s Breitling Navitimer 806 Mk5 worn by none other than Miles Davis, this manual-wind B09 with a display caseback takes cues from the original beyond the manual winding: the Twin Jet logo, reverse-panda dial, faux-aged cream-colored lume, and the original 41-mm dimensions. The pitch is that you get what made the 806 Mk5 great but with a modern overhaul. This model is limited to 500 pieces: You could go for the stainless steel on calf leather strap for $8,900, but we think you'd be kind of blue (sorry) to miss the superb bracelet model, complete with round vents, for $9,600.
Not part of Geneva Watch Days, here's something genuinely new from Casio's G-Shock line that's leaked and could break the internet. The GAC-2500 series is a resin analog lineup supposedly built from the DNA of the DW-5000C, the very first G-Shock made back in 1983. But that's not the real story of this piece. Much like the famous “CasiOak” that many G-Shock fans love for its passing resemblance to Audemars Piguet's Royal Oak, this GAC-2500 series has more than a whiff of Patek Philippe’s Nautilus about it.
So far, nicknames like “CasioNaut” and “CasioTilus” are being thrown around. Leaks suggest four resin colors at launch in November—white, black, green, and yellow—and the price is rumored to be 20,900 Japanese yen (about $134) each. There might be stainless-steel versions too—the GMC-2500D series, going for about $320.
Following Miss Piggy and Kermit editions, Oris clearly feels it's on to a winning formula with Muppets collaborations. This one is more interesting than the solid pink-and-green colors of the previous dalliances. The Gonzo is a reworking of Oris' ProPilot X but with subtle, classy nods to Gonzo the Great that chime perfectly with the subtle, classy performance art that is his trademark. While the showman himself appears on the watch’s mainspring, at 11 o’clock, the thumping 10-day power reserve indicator is a red chili, inspired by one of Gonzo’s favorite shirts. Such subtlety comes at a cost, however, as at $10,500, the Gonzo is twice the price of a Kermit.
A volume play from Zenith, and a good one. Bringing its famed El Primero movement to a cheaper—sorry, “more accessible”—price, the Solo Sport is a 40-mm steel diver watch, not a chronograph, with 200 meters of water resistance and a unidirectional rotating ceramic bezel. The black ceramic dial reveals the movement's capabilities, with a high-frequency pattern and “Shark tooth” minute track, showcasing the caliber’s prize feature: 5 Hz or 36,000 vph (vibrations per hour). You can grab this for $10,900 with a date window, but those in the know will get the cleaner no-date for $9,800.
Not physically at Geneva Watch Days either, Swatch Group's Hamilton decided to crash the party and release an upgraded version of its successful Interstellar Murph timepiece. Dialing up the model's association with Christopher Nolan's classic sci-fi film, Hamilton has added a version to its collection with a dappled “comet-inspired” face where the blue center is intended to reflect the glow of ionized gases in space. Whether you understand this cosmic connection is immaterial when the outcome is this pleasing. Sensibly, Hamilton has chosen to release the new Murph in the preferred 38-mm sizing at $995.
More comets? Yes indeed. Founded in 2017 by designer and photographer Ming Thein, this independent watch brand is known for a winning blend of refined aesthetics and innovative engineering. Here, this 40-mm stainless-steel worldtimer features a first-of-its-kind, patent-pending system for adjusting the time to account for daylight saving. Borrowing its name from the de Havilland Comet, the world’s first commercial jet airliner, the watch's split bezel divides cities according to whether they observe daylight saving. Those that don’t are fixed on the inner bezel, but the ones that do are on the outer ring. Rotating this outer bezel advances only the affected cities by one hour. Clever.
The limited run of 200 pieces has already been snapped up, but you can register online for future availability. If you get lucky, shun the $9,750 leather strap model for the $10,875 Polymesh bracelet version.
Another no-show at Geneva Watch Days was this new piece from Tudor. Well, not new exactly. After discontinuing the North Flag as recently as 2021, Tudor is bringing it back. Originally launched in 2015 at Baselworld, the North Flag was the first Tudor to boast one of the company's in-house movements. The new 40-mm “reissue” (now Northflag, not North Flag) sports a 24-hour hand for a second time zone. Water resistance is a respectable 100 meters, and there's a display caseback, too. Inside is Tudor's 4-Hz METAS-certified automatic movement. The uncluttered, functional black dial with yellow seconds and 24-hour hands is nicely contrasted by blue lume for the hands and markers. This watch, plus an integrated bracelet with Tudor's T-Fit micro-adjustment in the clasp, goes for $5,525.
Bulgari's multi-award-winning watch line now stars the “Dazzle,” an 80-piece limited-edition, super-thin Octo Finissimo built around the brand's 40-mm sandblasted titanium case. Despite its slender proportions, the watch manages a 60-hour power reserve. However, the highlight is the laser-engraved pattern on the case and bracelet, which looks more like it belongs in the world of Minecraft than horology. The geometric pattern is actually based upon “dazzle camouflage” devised by British zoologist John Graham Kerr, who proposed (to Winston Churchill, no less, in 1914) that the disruptive design would, much like zebra stripes, break up the perceived outline of ships at sea. Bulgari's Octo “Dazzle” will set you back $18,300.
The resurrection of Gallet, 200 years after its foundation in La Chaux-de-Fonds, completes Breitling's “House of Brands,” with Breitling taking on the center ground of the Swiss luxury watch market, Universal Genève going high-end, and now the relaunched Gallet slipping in below them both. The first model from the much-anticipated Gallet revival is the Flying Officer, and it's landing in two variations: the Flying Officer Chronograph 40 and the Flying Officer Automatic 40. The 40-mm chrono in light blue at $4,400 would be our pick, along with the orange Automatic 40 at $2,900.
Never a brand to shy away from doing something more than a little “out there,” Hublot has given its iconic Big Bang Original a new feel with a fabric makeover thanks to a velvet-like rubber invention. Two Soft Touch models see the case, bezel, dial, and strap wrapped in a specially developed textured rubber compound. Created through an overmolding process, the unique microscopic surface structure is composed of thousands of fine micro-elements, creating softness to the touch while supposedly keeping the durability and resistance of Hublot's signature rubber. The 43-mm model comes in black, but the red at $29,000 is tantalizing.

Reform continues to cast doubt on climate science. Do its supporters agree?
Fiona Harvey
On the second day of the Reform UK conference, in the wake of an undercover investigation alleging party officials plotted to evade the law on foreign donations, the deputy leader, Richard Tice, addressed the audience. Within minutes, a banner appeared behind him reading: “Collect £5m, burn the planet.”
It was taken down promptly and Tice, who has repeatedly called on people to enjoy the summer’s five successive heatwaves and record drought, rolled on. As Reform members at the Birmingham venue applauded Tice, there was plenty of agreement with his views. “I enjoyed the heat this summer,” said Jeanette Bowden, of Bexley. “I don’t think people need telling to take care of themselves.” Her partner, James, added, without scientific backing: “Carbon dioxide was much higher in the past, it was 10 times higher than this during the ice ages. It’s not a human problem.”
Amid stalls offering simulated helicopter rides, gold as an investment, tattoos and discounts on rum, climate scepticism was common. “It’s overhyped,” said Yvonne, who did not wish to give a surname.
“I don’t believe the predictions,” said Jim Langford. “They told us Norwich would be underwater by now and it’s not Atlantis yet.” Ed Rennie, a former Labour councillor from north London, said the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change had reduced some of its higher predictions.
But many of the same people who, like Tice, cast doubt on climate science, also criticised the government for failing to protect people against the hot weather. Bowden pointed to new-build houses. “They have really small windows,” she said. “That might be good in winter, but in summer it must be too hot, you can hardly open them. The government should not force this on people.”
Yvonne added: “The government were all on their holidays in the summer, not doing their jobs [to help people during the heatwaves]. Government should ensure there is clean water and sewage, but they’re not even doing that.”
The confusion among Reform supporters, explained Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, was to be expected given the party leadership’s peddling of “myths and lies” over the climate. Voters often say they want contradictory things, such as high standards of social care without tax rises to pay for them, Jacobs pointed out. But on the climate, they face an even more intense bombardment from contradictory viewpoints, as parties of the right try to turn the issue into a culture war.
Manchester model could unlock £80bn growth across England, report says
Pippa Crerar
In other news, a timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Andy Burnham’s biggest legacies as mayor – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.
Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.
Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.
While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold. Given the caution that exists in parts of the Treasury towards the prime minister’s more radical plans, Downing Street aides may read with interest.
Jenrick confirmed his promise to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 (see post at 11:09)
He said: “Here is my pledge to you and to the country. In the first 100 days of a Reform government, in our first Reform budget, we will raise the tax-free personal allowance from £12,570, not just with inflation, not just to £13,000, not just to £14,000, but to £15,000.
“The first 15 grand you earn is yours.”
He added that if he failed to deliver his promise, he will resign. “No ifs, not buts, I will be gone,” he said.
Dexys frontman ‘disgusted’ by Farage using Come on Eileen as entrance music

Police appeal after protester appears to be assaulted during Farage speech
Ben Quinn
Police are appealing for a woman who was among the climate activists protesting during Nigel Farage’s speech at Reform’s conference to come forward, after footage appeared to show her being manhandled by people in the crowd.
Security at the event on the outskirts of Birmingham removed several protesters who stood up and heckled the Reform UK leader at intervals during his speech.

Quarter of Reform supporters want Brexit reversed, poll finds
Peter Walker
A quarter of Reform UK supporters want to rejoin the EU, according to polling carried out to coincide with the party’s ongoing conference in Birmingham.
The study, which was to be set out at a fringe event on Saturday showed some attitudes among Reform backers were unexpected, as with Brexit. But on other subjects, notably immigration, Reform supporters’ views were very similar to what people expected.
The polling, carried out by Opinium for the Policy Institute at King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe, charted both what Reform supporters believe, and what backers of other parties think they believe.
In some areas there was a notable gap between the two. While 25% of Reform supporters said they want to see Brexit reversed, the public at large estimated the proportion at just 9%. In contrast, 76% of Reform supporters want to stop all immigration to the UK, close to the guess of 80%.
A more potentially alarming finding for Reform was that they are the party that voters at large most want to stop winning in their area, suggesting the possible damage to Nigel Farage’s party from tactical voting. Overall, 41% of voters named Reform as the party they would want to block.
Such is the strength of feeling that around a third of Labour and Green voters said they would consider voting Conservative tactically to keep Reform out.
Dover port disrupted as dozens of masked men block roads
Meanwhile, police are dealing with an apparent protest by groups of masked men in Dover, which a local councillor said appeared to be a “coordinated” demonstration related to “illegal migration”.
Dozens of men dressed in black and wearing balaclavas were pictured gathered at the port this morning, with the Port of Dover confirming that the disruption is affecting “all routes” in and out of the port, as well as around the town.
Chris Vinson, leader of the Conservative group at Dover District Council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”. He told the Press Association:
Overnight, clearly what appears to be several hundred masked men wearing black clothing and balaclavas seem to have coordinated and loaded into rental vans and then descended on roads leading in and out of Dover with the intent to block them, and that’s what they’ve successfully done, and it’s brought the town to a standstill.
There are stacks of people who are stuck in their cars or in their workplaces as a result.”
In a brief statement, Kent police said: “We are aware of a protest currently taking place at the Port of Dover. Officers are in attendance and engaging with protesters.”
Robert Jenrick is set to unveil a major tax-cutting pledge at Reform UK’s conference today, as the party seeks to shift the focus back to its economic agenda.
PA has the following report:
The party’s treasury spokesman is expected to tell the final day of the Reform conference in Birmingham that he would increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days of taking office.
The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.
Reform said the plan would save the average taxpayer £500 a year and take 2.9 million people out of income tax altogether, at a cost of £17.7 billion in its first year, rising to £21 billion five years later.

Five EU countries push ahead with migrant 'return hubs'
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:40:46 EEST
18:40:46 KST

Five European Union countries are seeking an agreement with a country outside the bloc to receive migrants who have no legal right to remain in the EU, as Denmark targets the end of 2027 for the first transfers. Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands agreed on steps towards establishing so-called return hubs.
The five governments, which refer to themselves as the Group of Five, want to reach an agreement with at least one partner country before the end of 2026.
Ministers meeting in Copenhagen on Friday did not identify a prospective host.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the governments wanted an agreement with third countries this year that would allow them to establish return hubs. The ministers plan another meeting in Munich at the end of September.
Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov said the group expected to have a common understanding with a partner country around the New Year. Denmark aims to start transferring people to such a facility by the end of 2027.
The planned centres would receive people who have no right to stay in the EU but who are not being returned to their countries of origin. Bødskov rejected descriptions of the proposed facilities as camps and said residents would have opportunities to live and work in the partner country.
“It’s a new chance to have a life in a partner country,” Bødskov told reporters in Copenhagen.
The identity of that partner remains under negotiation.
The initiative follows changes to EU migration rules. The European Parliament approved legislation in June aimed at accelerating returns and providing a legal basis for member states to establish return facilities outside the EU.
The proposal has drawn scrutiny over the treatment of people transferred beyond EU territory. The Council of Europe warned in July that return hubs posed “considerable human rights risks”.
Amnesty International warned that facilities outside the EU risk becoming “cruel black holes” for human rights.
Eve Geddie, director of Amnesty’s European Institutions Office, said the model carried risks including arbitrary detention, torture, ill-treatment and forced onward returns. The organisation said it was concerned by reported negotiations involving Uganda and Rwanda, citing its documentation of rights abuses in both countries.
Amnesty argued that transferring responsibility for migrants to states outside Europe would shift pressure onto countries with fewer resources and said past outsourcing schemes had exposed people to restrictions on due process and protection from refoulement.
The Centre for European Policy Studies has also questioned whether return hubs would achieve their stated purpose, arguing that they risk becoming long-term detention sites for people who still cannot be sent to their countries of origin.
CEPS said the new EU Return Regulation broadens the definition of a country of return by allowing member states to transfer people to third countries with which they have no previous connection, provided those countries agree to receive them.
The Brussels-based think tank criticised the use of non-binding arrangements with partner countries, saying such deals could reduce parliamentary and judicial scrutiny. It pointed to previous offshore migration schemes, including Italy’s centres in Albania and Australia’s offshore system, as examples of costly programmes that faced legal challenges and produced limited evidence of lasting deterrence.
CEPS also raised concerns over EU legislation under which families with children are no longer expressly excluded from return hubs, while only unaccompanied minors remain outside the scheme.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said the governments intended to protect human rights under the proposed system.
Bødskov said the International Organization for Migration and the UN refugee agency would take part in the next stages of the work. Reuters reported that a UNHCR spokesperson said the agency had not received details of the proposal and was therefore unable to comment on the arrangements under discussion.
Finland prepares for EU return rules
Finland is also preparing for the EU’s new return framework and has begun examining the return hub model with other Nordic countries.
Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said in June that preliminary work had started, while the Ministry of the Interior has since launched a legislative project to align Finnish law with the EU Return Regulation. The plans include longer detention periods during return procedures and longer fixed-term entry bans, while the return hub provisions are set to apply directly at EU level.
Finland has not identified a host country, but Rantanen has said future centres should focus on cases where deportations are difficult to enforce.
The government is also expanding migrant screening under the EU Migration and Asylum Pact through a €2.55 million project led by the Finnish Security and Intelligence Service, which will develop systems for security checks on people arriving in the country.

Details
"vladimir putin, seeking to take advantage of Ukraine's severely weakened air defense system, is intensifying a bombing campaign that he believes will force Kyiv to concede on some of its key territorial demands, possibly as early as this winter," the publication writes.

This allowed the Russian leadership to believe that it could still achieve gains regarding Ukraine, even though the chief economist of one of russia's largest state-owned banks publicly warned that russia cannot win a war of attrition against Ukraine as long as Kyiv is supported by the West, a Moscow businessman said.
"There is a view in the kremlin that a few more months of war are not a problem for russia and the Russian economy, but for Ukraine it is a huge problem," the Russian businessman said.

Rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese national alive on Saturday from a tunnel buried by debris, as emergency response teams dug with new vigour in the search for missing people 10 days after catastrophic flooding.
A joint rescue team comprising personnel from the Nepal Army and foreign experts rescued the man from 225 metres (738 feet) inside the tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Rasuwa district, a military statement said.
"His health is currently being assessed and further search and rescue operations are continuing," the army said.
The latest rescue brings to three the number of workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project.
Two Nepali workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.
About 900 workers remain missing from 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to authorities.
About 850 of those missing are foreigners, according to official figures from Nepal and China.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal’s Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 metres (17,060 feet), killing at least 1,300 people.
The fracture triggered an ice-and-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley.

UN backs effort to depict Africa correctly on maps despite US opposition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:35:55 UTC
18:35:55 KST

Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings. | iStock
The United Nations on Friday largely endorsed a resolution to promote maps that reflect the true scale of continents after an African-led campaign to move away from the ubiquitous 16th-century Mercator projection.
The United States was the only country to vote against the initiative, denouncing it as part of a “much larger and more radical ideological project” and urging “countries to instill common sense to this body.” Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine abstained.
Mercator, the world’s most commonly used map projection, was devised by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate using compass bearings.
Advertisement
But it distorts size, making landmasses appear larger the further they are from the Equator. As a result, Africa looks far smaller than it really is compared with countries in the Northern Hemisphere.
“A fair map does not change the geography of the world,” said Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign minister and lead negotiator on behalf of the African group, ahead of the U.N. vote.
The non-binding resolution stated that “correcting cartographic distortions of continental sizes constitutes an act of cognitive justice and memorial reparation,” and calls on countries to promote the so-called Equal Earth projection, including at schools.
“This decision is about much more than cartography. It is about justice, dignity, equality and the way we represent our world,” Dussey rejoiced on X after its adoption.

No registration number, no attendance: NMC warns medical colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:31:05 UTC
18:31:05 KST

Medical colleges have one month to update faculty registration numbers on the attendance system. Failure to comply will result in blocked daily attendance for specified teaching staff. The National Medical Commission issued this warning after finding blank registration fields. Colleges must review and update all medical faculty and resident profiles accurately. Non-medical faculty will have 'NA' entered in the registration number field.
NEW DELHI: Medical colleges have one month to update the National Medical Register (NMR) or State Medical Register (SMR) numbers of their faculty and specified teaching staff on the Aadhaar Enabled Biometric Attendance System (AEBAS), failing which their daily attendance could be blocked and automatically rejected.The National Medical Commission (NMC) has warned that this may adversely impact the compliance status of the medical college during NMC assessments and inspections.The warning was issued on September 3 after the NMC found that nodal officers at several medical colleges had left the NMR or SMR registration-number field blank while registering faculty on the attendance portal.The commission has directed colleges to review and update the profiles of all medical faculty, Junior Residents, Senior Residents, tutors and demonstrators with correct and valid NMR or SMR numbers.For non-medical faculty and tutors or demonstrators holding Master of Science (MSc) and Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) qualifications, colleges have been instructed to enter “NA” in the registration-number field.The NMC has made it clear that leaving the registration-number field blank will not be permitted.
The directive effectively makes faculty registration details part of the attendance compliance process, rather than a routine profile correction.
The memorandum has been sent to deans, principals and directors of all medical colleges and institutions, besides state and Union Territory medical education departments, directorates of medical education and State Medical Councils.The move is under the provisions of the Undergraduate and Postgraduate Minimum Standard Requirements and Medical Assessment and Rating Board regulations, which provide for periodic, transparent and digitally verified assessment of teaching staff in medical institutions.

The President of Argentina reiterated his country’s claims to the Falkland Islands and announced sanctions against companies operating on the islands without Argentina’s permission.
Javier Milei also announced the establishment of a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, which is located near the islands.
He also announced sanctions against companies planning to drill for oil off the coast of the Falkland Islands without permission from the Argentine government.
“We will use all diplomatic, economic, and legal tools to deter state and non-state actors who encroach on our sovereignty,” Milei stated in a televised address to the nation.

British Defence Minister Wes Streeting criticized the Argentine president’s statements.
“The Falkland Islands belong to the United Kingdom because their residents chose to be British,” he noted, referring to the 2013 referendum in which a majority of the islands’ residents voted to retain their status as a British Overseas Territory.
Milei’s statement came after U.S. President Donald Trump cast doubt on the previous support for the United Kingdom in the dispute over the Falkland Islands.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas, have been under British administration since 1833.
In 1982, hostilities broke out between the two countries over the archipelago, resulting in the deaths of about 900 people.
In 2013, the islands’ residents voted in a referendum to retain their British status. However, Argentina does not recognize the results of this referendum.

Third worker rescued from Nepal tunnel, woman found alive in rubble 10 days after devastating floods
Two people were rescued in separate operations in Nepal, 10 days after the devastating floods hit the country, officials said Saturday.
A man was rescued from a hydropower tunnel, according to a social media post by the country's prime minister's office, bringing the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.
Nepal's army said a joint rescue team of Nepalese military personnel and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 738-foot tunnel and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight.
A photo released by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV showed two rescuers carrying the man out of the tunnel.
Rescue efforts have increasingly focused on 12 hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects, hoping to find survivors.
In flood-hit Nuwakot town, a woman was rescued alive from a house, Nepal's army spokesperson said Saturday. Officials said she was being airlifted to Kathmandu.
Images released by Nepal's army showed rescuers finding the woman covered in mud. They gave her bottled water before pulling her to safety, wrapped in a gray blanket.
At least 1,300 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, which were likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency.

Line warns Taiwan users to add phone numbers to avoid account deletion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
09:20:29 UTC
18:20:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Some Line users risk losing access to their accounts, purchases, stickers, coins, and chat histories at the end of the year unless they add a phone number.
The rule applies to accounts linked only to Facebook that do not have a phone number set, with deletion scheduled after 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 31, per TVBS.
Users can check their status in the Line app by opening “Home,” tapping “Settings,” selecting “My Account,” and looking at the “Phone Number” field. A blank field means no number has been linked, and the setup can be completed entirely inside the app without using a webpage, per Line’s notice.
The company warned that phone numbers cannot be shared across Line accounts, while moving a number to another account can cause the original account to stop working.
Similar restrictions apply to email addresses and Apple and Google accounts. Reusing those credentials on a new Line account will remove their links from the original account and may render that account invalid, according to the notice.
Accounts should have an email address and password set, while at least one Apple or Google account should be connected. Both Apple and Google accounts can be added.
The phone-number requirement is intended to reduce dummy accounts and fraud risks and make the service safer. Users are also encouraged to help older relatives or friends who are less familiar with smartphone settings check their accounts.

Taiwan prepares testing facility for car imports from US

2026-09-05
09:19:53 UTC
18:19:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Transportation is budgeting NT$400 million (US$12.63 million) for next year to prepare for the liberalization of car imports from the US, reports said Friday.
As a result of the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed in February, Taiwan will have to remove its import limits on cars from the US. With safety test standards differing from country to country, Taiwan has to set up a new post-market surveillance system including a safety test lab, per CNA.
The import quotas will be removed for cars conforming to the US Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and to US emission regulations, the report said.
To improve its testing capacity, the ministry is proposing the NT$400 million budget, which includes the constructions of a test lab and other buildings, equipment, and machinery. The center will also require an environmental impact review, an evaluation of its power needs, and fire safety permits.
The ministry said it had discussed the required measures and legal amendments with associations representing Taiwan’s car industry, CNA reported. The changes will be designed to guarantee the safety of consumers, the ministry said, adding its proposals still required approval by the Cabinet.
