‘There is light at the end of this tunnel. But the tunnel is filled with sewage’: Marina Hyde on finding hope in political chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:28 UTC
14:00:28 KST

Let me kick off by letting a little daylight in on magic. If you’ve got a book out in September, you’re probably sending the publisher the final version of the introduction four months earlier. So I guess the moment I truly knew that Keir Starmer was finished was the moment, in the first days of May, when I typed the words “we’ve had three prime ministers since my last book”. At that point it became an absolute cast-iron cosmic inevitability that we would have had yet another prime minister by the time the book was out. Nailed on. It’s the equivalent of lighting a cigarette so the bus turns up immediately.
So, four prime ministers in four years … Good times, possibly, for someone whose job involves writing about prime ministers. But not good times for Britain, or indeed for the seemingly endless series of outgoing premiers. Being British prime minister has become the biggest ejector-seat job since the noughties, when the US would announce they’d killed “the al-Qaida No 3” about twice a month.
And yet, on a personal level, sometimes I think the weirdest thing about our weird times is that I actually remain a long-term optimist. But I’ll explain that strange little secret later.
Because, first up, it must be said that many, many people went too early on the optimism. In the couple of years leading up to the 2024 general election, I did a lot of audience events, and I got to notice that the same question would crop up again and again. And that question, as we inched towards the overwhelming likelihood of a Labour government, was: “What on earth will you find to write about when this is all over?”
Well, now. Short answer: this. All this. The long answer – which I gave as tactfully and sensitively as I could at the time, given the political horror show everyone had been living through for the past few years – was to say that while it was a lovely thought that “this” would be “over” with the dispatch of the Conservatives, I regretfully didn’t think it would be. I didn’t think the fundamentals of Britain’s decline were remotely easy to deal with, and I didn’t think the Labour leadership were any good, or had any realistic idea of how to get growth, or were so infinitely morally superior to the Tories that it would be like living in some kind of serene yesteryear utopia, where you went back to only having to check the news every week or so. And when you did, the news was still mostly as you left it. No one had kidnapped a president, attempted to annex a country, or done ketamine in the White House. Equally, I didn’t want to be a complete Debbie Downer, so I’d try to end the answer on an up note, saying stuff like, “But, you know, maybe it’ll all turn out great!”
If you’re watching the events of the past few years on catchup – or simply using this article to get you up to speed – then I apologise for dropping a spoiler in here. But, hand on heart, it all did not turn out great. If it’s possible to get buried by your own landslide, Starmer achieved it. Within months of “the grownups” being in charge, quite a few people already wanted the toddlers to be given the reins again. And a whole lot more wanted flashy Uncle Nigel to have his turn instead. I find it hard not to have at least some sympathy with many of these reactions in the abstract. After years of dysfunction and desperation, people are right to think they deserve better, even if you disagree with how they think that better will come about. It’s when they stop even expecting anything better at all that a country feels most lost.
Still, what a cast of characters has adorned public life in recent years. I’ve always found it helpful to think of the people I write about as characters in a drama/comedy/extreme horror movie. Maybe it puts things at one remove and makes it easier to find the jokes. In fact, my favourite emails are always from Guardian readers in far-flung corners of the globe who write and say things like, “I have zero idea who any of these people are, but I enjoy the soap opera.”
Even so, at no point during the last few years did I have an absolutely clear handle on who many of the lasting leading lights of this show would be. Some public figures who I thought would stick around ended up lasting the equivalent of a three-episode arc. Farewell, Rupert Murdoch’s dental nurse turned prison chaplain fiancee – we knew you too little. (Please remember, this was the year in which Murdoch – then 92 – got engaged twice.) I knew Liz Truss had deteriorated beyond safety standards – lettuce rejoice! – but her failure to reckon with her reckoning meant she kept popping back up, along with some of Britain’s other, worse exes. Boris Johnson, say, who protested his innocence from the maximum-security international lecture circuit, at least until Nigel Farage hit on the tactical masterstroke of naming an immigration wave after him. Even former president Donald Trump seemed like an ex after he was found to have broken a few laws – until he broke every law of politics and became current president Donald Trump once again.
Others were unexpectedly promoted from the chorus line and ended up becoming stars. Take Lauren Sánchez. You could be forgiven for thinking that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos placed a personal ad in Billionaire magazine – “Top 3 Croesus seeks force of nature” – and the rest was history. But just a few short years ago, Lauren was actually still just a “journalist and helicopter pilot” – not Mrs Bezos, nor the recipient of multiple philanthropy awards. Not, in fact, an astronaut. Or take Mark Zuckerberg. At his regular summonses to Washington, the Meta boss once used to apologise for things and dressed like the reluctant teenage best man at his mother’s third wedding. He now thinks all previous apologies were a mistake and dresses like an Armenian who owns an adult webcam business. Or take ChatGPT, which a few years back would itself have sounded like the name of a premium-rate adult sexline, but is now responsible for everything from your work presentation to an unspecified percentage of global policy drafting, to informing you why it is that guy won’t message you back.
Strange to think that just four years ago Farage was enjoying one of his 37 retirements from public life. Then in June 2024, he unresigned again, and this time it was serious. His party, which has had more previous aliases than a rogue double-glazing salesman, was now called Reform. Nigel rapidly gained a whole new friendship group – and, in typical Farage style, lost some of them pretty fast, too. Sad to see him go no-speaks with a trillionaire we came to know as the US president’s “first buddy”. But, thanks to Elon Musk, we got to see a president turning the White House lawn into an electric-car dealership. (“Wow! Everything’s computer!”) Love him or hate him, let’s just agree Mars would be a great place to keep Elon. In fact, if there’s space in the space compound, I’d love him to take Fifa president Gianni Infantino, whose baddie glow-up has been as swift as it was inevitable in his endlessly rancid organisation.
Upbeat moments? In terms of landmark events in legal history, we were gifted the no-stakes hilarity of the Gwyneth Paltrow ski-massacre trial. We got the tireless heroes of the Post Office scandal. We entered the jam‑pushing years of Duchess Meghan, Montecito’s most down-to-earth homemaker.
That said, some things don’t change. It was yet another difficult few years for “difficult” men, with female TV stars and beloved female authors still lagging vanishingly far behind in the sexual misconduct stakes. Come on, gals – harassing, grooming or assaulting much younger juniors is an absolutely essential part of the artistic/retail mogul process!
Meanwhile, Gregg Wallace, hemmed in for lucrative decades by a BBC that simply failed to recognise his behaviour was some kind of disability, finally released himself back into the wild.
And we had Jeffrey Epstein, a guy who bizarrely turned out to be one of the most consequential figures in transatlantic public life, capable of wreaking the highest-level havoc from beyond his grave. Some got away with posthumous exposure; Russell Brand simply rebirthed himself as a messiah figure in a Thames baptism performed by Bear Grylls. And all the many, many hangers-on and enablers who stood discreetly by for these men simply melted back into the world, presumably waiting for the next situation vacant.
As for the whole tenor of the period we have just lived through – in fact, are still living through – it’s hard not to look back on it and feel that chaos and disorder is now the norm. In fact, it’s hard not to look out of the window on any day and not feel it’s now the state in which we live. Let’s face it, the arc of history hasn’t been having a normal one for a while. Or, to put it another way, we seem to be living through a period of political and social entropy, having moved from a state of something that felt more like order towards increasing instability and an agonising loss of institutional effectiveness. Nothing brings it home like the US president using his private social media platform to share an AI-generated video of a swimming-trunked him and Benjamin Netanyahu sipping cocktails on sun-loungers in a lavishly redeveloped “Gaza riviera”. No, wait – nothing brings it home like the US national security adviser accidentally adding a journalist to a Real Housewives-style group chat that also included the defence secretary and the vice-president, in which live and operational details of a US forces mission were shared alongside punching fist emojis and metaphorical drink tosses at the Europeans.
But I do want to end this on an up note, because – strange as it might seem, in the circumstances – I am an optimist. No, but really. Always have been. I do have faith that humans can get ourselves out of a lot of the holes we’re in, even if we fall into some others in the process. We’ll fix a lot of the problems that right now feel intractable. And, sure, we’ll create some more seemingly intractable problems along the way. That’s inevitable. But I just cannot help feeling that humans are amazing and ingenious and hardwired to make it. To quote The Big Lebowski: “I guess that’s the way the whole darned human comedy keeps perpetuating itself, down through the generations, westward the wagons, across the sands of time.” Strikes and gutters, ups and downs. Yep, I truly do believe there is light at the end of this tunnel. Unfortunately, the tunnel is filled with sewage – but the glimmer is there.
Can I let one other chink of daylight in? Like a lot of deadlines, in my experience, that final, final book introduction deadline that I mentioned up the top of this article turned out to not actually be final. And so it is that I contrived to do a genuine last‑minute rewrite to keep pace with the sheer warp‑speed churn of leaders charged with rescuing the UK from the mess it’s in. But I swear to God, if anything happens to Andy Burnham between you reading this and the book being published in a couple of weeks, I will not be responsible for my actions. OK, OK. I will be responsible for my actions – but you’re going to need to give me a pass on being responsible for the error. Because, if we’ve learned anything over the past four years – and I’m not especially convinced we have – it’s that life moves pretty fast.

Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

Five British prime ministers ago – and six French ones – when Emmanuel Macron first confirmed that France would return the Bayeux tapestry to Britain after 1,000 years, he told an audience at Sandhurst and Theresa May – the No 10 seat-warmer of the day – that when it came to France and Britain there were “two things that nothing can change, be it a vote or a political decision: our history and our geography”.
It was January 2018, 18 months after the UK had voted to leave the EU, and relations between the near neighbours were not good. The French political establishment had been shocked and angered by Brexit; personal relations were frazzled, and cross-Channel government contacts measurably dwindling. This was not a rupture that a piece of embroidered medieval linen, however perfectly it represented that tangled history, was going to solve on its own.
It took only eight and a half years and many, many changes in personnel, but this week Macron finally made good on that pledge with the unveiling of the tapestry at the British Museum in London, in scenes of such amitié that one could almost forget the bilateral chill that had gone before.
No one pretends that the Bayeux tapestry alone has been responsible for stitching together two nations whose connections had visibly frayed. (When it comes to the tapestry, as every commentator this week has shown, the needlework metaphors are hard to resist.) But the French president’s single-minded commitment to drive through a loan that he has previously called “seemingly impossible” illustrates that, in diplomatic terms, the London exhibition is not just a decorative sideshow.
“It is much more than just a linen canvas embroidered with wool,” Macron told an audience at the museum on Wednesday. “It represents a whole chapter of French, British and European history.”
In that context, it was notable that he speculated that people “decades or even centuries from now” would look back not only on the tapestry itself but on “what we did here today” – the very fact of its loan to the British Museum – as being a significant marker in the long span of Franco-British relations. “Two countries which, after centuries of shared history, [chose] to forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery,” he said.
The latest UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, agreed in language tailored to suit his own political project. As a “tremendous demonstration of goodwill”, he said, the loan “says so much about the friendship of our two nations … It shows the power of collaboration to lift people’s lives.”
The Bayeux tapestry, of course, was always a highly political artefact, even before it acquired its status as a foundational text for the English nation (1066, the date of the Battle of Hastings, is “the nation’s pincode”, the British Museum chair, George Osborne, noted drily on Wednesday).
Much remains unknown about the circumstances of its commission and creation, but a vast artwork showing a clash of kings and wholesale invasion of a nation is not a neutral object. “It was definitely designed with a political purpose in mind when it was first made,” says the historian Dr David Musgrove, who has written a book, The Story of the Bayeux Tapestry, with Prof Michael Lewis, the curator of the exhibition.
“That political purpose was essentially to legitimise the invasion of William the Conqueror, to explain why he did it, why he chose to send his fleet across the Channel,” argues Musgrove, who is the content director of HistoryExtra magazine and podcast. The “crux scene”, he argues, is not the famous bit where Harold takes an arrow to the eye, but an earlier portion that shows the then English earl Harold making an oath to support William’s future claim to the English throne.
Harold reneges on this later when he has himself crowned king of England. “So he perjures himself and that gives William the reason to invade,” Musgrove says. “My take is that the tapestry is entirely predicated on making that justification. So it’s very modern in that sense; people trying to justify military action today is kind of the same thing. It’s a retrospective justification for what happened.”
Most historians believe it was made in Canterbury, but “just about everything around [the tapestry’s creation] is a little bit uncertain”, according to Leonie Hicks, a professor of medieval studies at Canterbury Christ Church University. She says historians’ “best assumption” – based on the internal evidence of the embroidery itself and other contemporary documents – “is that it was likely commissioned by Bishop Odo, who was William the Conqueror’s half-brother, bishop of Bayeux and also earl of Kent after the conquest. Or somebody very close to Odo.”
Odo and Willliam had fallen out, so an elaborate narrative wall covering at Odo’s Norman cathedral celebrating the new English king could be seen as an attempt to regain favour. But if the tapestry undoubtedly flatters William, it is not a piece of crude propaganda, argues Hicks, and the politics of its depiction are nuanced. “It’s not a straightforward piece of ‘Yay, aren’t the Normans great, they dumped the English and took the throne.’”
Among the most intriguing details, she notes, are the depictions in the margins of the human cost of war – all stitched, most likely, by English women who may have lost husbands and sons in the battle. “We have the scene where a house is being burnt and a woman is holding a child’s hand and leaving the house. [There are] very graphic depictions in the margins of decapitated soldiers, and bodies being looted. It does give that sense that war is horrific and terrible.”
It is context which, we can assume, was lost during the tapestry’s long afterlife. History records nothing about it until it turns up in an inventory of the Bayeux Cathedral treasury in 1476. The tapestry, it noted, was hung around the cathedral for a few days each year. During the French Revolution it was narrowly rescued from being used as a wagon cover.
It would not be long, however, before the tapestry’s political usefulness would again be recognised. Napoleon, planning an English invasion of his own in 1803, displayed it in Paris where “it was quite a sensation”, says Musgrove. “I think Napoleon probably thought it was useful to have an artefact which showed a previous cross-Channel invasion by forces from France into Britain.” When the invasion plans foundered, the tapestry was quietly returned to Bayeux.
The Nazis were “obsessed” with the tapestry – “they basically saw it as part of their worldview of Aryan Teutonic supremacy”, says Musgrove – and in the days before the liberation of Paris planned to whisk it away to Germany. They were, however, frustrated by the French resistance, who had been alerted by codebreakers at Bletchley Park.
Eight quiet decades followed before the renovation of the museum where it is housed in Bayeux prompted its removal from display. But if that immediate circumstance opened the possibility of the artwork being loaned to Britain, there was certainly no inevitability that this would happen.
Britain first made a request almost a century ago, in 1931. A request to borrow the artwork in 1953 to mark Elizabeth II’s coronation was initially agreed by France, before it reversed the decision over conservation concerns. Another attempt in 1966, to commemorate 900 years since the battle, foundered in the face of local and national French opposition. Another bid in the 1980s came to nothing.
Macron could easily have come to the same judgment, not least because there was plenty of opposition in France to the loan, including from artists and conservation experts. Why, then, such commitment to making happen a loan which, he only half joked last year, had been more complicated to negotiate than the Brexit withdrawal agreements?
To Helen Drake, a professor of French and European studies at Loughborough University London, making the loan happen fits with Macron’s view of himself as a cultured international statesman – but also with the value he attaches to repairing the Franco-British relationship in the face of mutually threatening global forces.
“Macron is a French president who has pulled the maximum levers that the constitution give him to operate on the international stage, and that will probably be his legacy. So from that perspective it would make sense to him to be seen to be behind the transfer of the tapestry.
“But he has also very much made it part of his mandate to be at the forefront of ameliorating France’s relations with the UK.” On Ukraine, defence and security, migration and Trump, British and French shared interests have become ever more pressing, she says. “The external environment, to put it bluntly, has pushed the two together.”
But for all the genuine bonhomie over a dazzling piece of history, Drake says, neither side has any illusions about the dynamic tension that has always characterised their love-hate relationship. “The fact is that France habitually plays hardball with the UK in its negotiations with the EU post-Brexit,” she says. “You can have all the warmth you like in the British Museum, [but] the Quai d’Orsay will still drive a hard bargain. The two co-exist and they’re not even contradictory – they’re just part of how we see the Franco-British relationship.”

Malta off the beaten track: Discover the quieter and more authentic side of this busy island nation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

If you want to beat the crowds in Malta, then skip the capital Valletta and head to Gozo, Mdina or one of the charming fishing villages.
Do you know the two countries you can reach by ferry from Sicily? Even boat travel geeks might struggle with this one. One is Tunisia - reachable from Palermo in 11 hours (in the six years I’ve lived in Sicily, I’ve still only known one person who’s ever taken that boat). The other is Malta.
Luckily for me, the most frequent ferry to Malta goes from my local town. Pozzallo to Valletta is a pleasant 1hr45 minute journey, on a catamaran mostly staffed, curiously, by people from the Philippines. With three or four crossings a day, Malta is quicker to reach than most parts of mainland Italy, so I’ve visited regularly during the six years I’ve been living on Sicily’s south-east coast.
On most of my trips, I’ve stayed in Valletta, Malta’s capital. An ancient fortified city full of gorgeous architecture, buzzy outdoor bars and restaurants and rooftop views to die for.
What does all of that gorgeousness mean? You guessed it - it’s packed with tourists.
Spend time in Valletta and you'll understand why you’re often told Malta is one of the most densely populated countries in the world. During the summer high season, it’s hard to move on Valletta’s cobbled streets. While there’s plenty of good shopping, it’s hard to enjoy it when you’re in fear of, at best, being ripped off for tourist tat and, at worst, being pickpocketed.
So, on my most recent trip I decided to try and beat the crowds in Malta. I planned a hotel stay and itinerary that would let me experience the more authentic parts of the country, taking in Gozo, one of the islands, and Mdina, an atmospheric walled city.
Where to stay in Malta for a group trip
Malta's busiest tourist hotspots are concentrated in the south of the country - Valletta, St Paul’s Bay, St Julian’s and Sliema are all in this region, as well as being where most visitors will arrive thanks to the airport.
Many of them will take taxis or buses to the northern region for day trips to Comino and Gozo, islands home to popular spots like the Blue Lagoon and Gozo’s many beautiful beaches.
Knowing that most tourists just come to Malta’s most northern tip to leave it on a ferry, I surmised that hotels there would be less oversubscribed.
I decided on the Riviera Spa Resort, a large adults-only hotel with views across to Comino. The property is right in front of Marfa Jetty so we watched tourists line up to take speed boats across to Comino - most go there seeking the Blue Lagoon.
The Riviera is also very well positioned for trips to Gozo - more on that below.
One of the main reasons we chose the Riviera was for the adults-only promise. I was away with eight others and almost all of us had left babies or children at home. While we love our own, we didn’t want to have to listen to other people’s screaming children.
Having gathered here from all over Europe, our time at the Riviera revolved around long catch-ups and leisurely meals. Lurid-coloured cocktails from the poolside bar kept us hydrated while relaxing on sun loungers. With four restaurants and two bars to choose from, there was something to suit everyone’s tastes and budgets.
While it’s not a luxury property, Riviera was perfect for a group trip thanks to its many services and being able to book it through tour companies (including Jet2 and EasyJet Holidays). There was high energy aqua aerobics and a gym for those that couldn’t miss out on their workouts. For a more relaxed start to the day, a few of us joined a pilates class which was expertly taught in a lovely studio. For full relaxation, the on-site spa had one of the longest massage menus I’ve ever seen.
One of the hotel’s standout features is its staff. Coming from all over the world, they’re multilingual and seemed genuinely proud of the newly renovated Riviera. There were plenty of people to help so, despite the hotel being busy, we were always helped quickly and with a smile.
I’d recommend the Riviera for group or multi-generational trips, and for anyone who wants everything you could need under one roof.
Mdina: Malta's silent city
Venturing off the beaten track in Malta was worth it just for our trip to Mdina (pronounced um-dee-nah). Meaning ‘fortified place’ in Arabic, this walled city on a hilltop in the middle of the island has a very different feeling than anywhere else I’ve been in Malta.
At 3,000 years old, Mdina has a fascinating history. It served as the nation's capital and the seat of the Maltese nobility until the mid-16th century arrival of the Knights of St. John. As the knights chose another part of Malta, Birgu, as their new capital the Great Siege of 1565 by the Turks was directed there and not at Mdina. Under the knights and even more so under the British the importance of Mdina as the seat of power faded steadily, and what was once known as the 'Citta Notabile' became the 'silent city', almost a ghost town. Only 400 people live within Mdina’s walls now.
While shops, small museums and lookout points mean it’s no longer a ghost town, it does feel closed off and peaceful. This is in part thanks to there being no vehicles driving around - the cobbled streets are far too narrow for that.
We spent a gorgeous afternoon wandering the city’s streets, with stops to admire the gorgeous buildings or pick up a drink or an ice cream. I recommend arriving mid to late afternoon, especially in summer.
As the sun gets lower, it washes the sandstone buildings with a golden glow, giving Mdina a dreamy, ethereal atmosphere.
Gozo: One of the best places in Europe for diving
Gozo has a very different feeling to the main island in Malta, making it a perfect alternative destination. It has been spared the development that’s overrun its neighbour. Inland is mostly still countryside with small towns or villages dotted throughout.
The preservation of the land means the soil here is very fertile and it feeds the main island with some foods, though most of Malta’s food is imported from Sicily. This makes it worth seeking out local specialties, like the cheese 'gbejna', made from sheep's milk.
Gozo has a stunning coastline and this is where it shines for me - especially as I’m a qualified scuba diver. Many European divers think they need to fly to south-east Asia or the Caribbean to see reefs and marine life, not realising that Malta has world-class diving.
It has sites for everyone from beginner to advanced divers - there are plenty of dive schools to choose from and they’ll know where to go and when. You can expect good visibility and gentle currents in most places, though be careful if you're swimming and not with a dive guide.
If you’re not into diving, the Azure Window, the Inland Sea and the Blue Hole can all be enjoyed from the beach or boats.
For sightseeing, check out the Ggantija Temples in Xagħra (thought to be one of the oldest free-standing Neolithic structures in the world) and Ta' Pinu Basilica if you’re in need of some luck - an ancient church where some believe miracles have happened.
If you want to visit Gozo for a day trip, Gozo Fast Ferry has frequent departures from Valletta, arriving at Mgarr in 45 minutes. Once you’re on Gozo, there are public buses to get around and it’s also suitable for walking around.
Marsascala, Marsaxlokk and Birżebbuġa: Malta’s fishing villages
Fishing village probably conjures up images of a quaint harbour with the sound of seagulls overhead. While these three small towns are much quieter than Valletta and its surroundings, the harbours are still designed to attract tourists. But since Malta is hot for much of the year, the bars and restaurants are a welcome pit stop for refreshments.
You can reach all of them by bus from Valletta. They’re not too far from the airport but if you have a flight to catch, allow plenty of time - Malta’s traffic can be brutal.
There’s not a huge amount to do in Marsascala, Marsaxlokk and Birżebbuġa other than wander around, discover the beaches and meet some locals
Sunday is the best day to visit Marsaxlokk for its famous fish market, which some say is the best place to buy fish in the whole country.
Ruth Wright was a guest of the Riviera Spa Resort.

Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for kacang pool, or Malaysian bean stew
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

This is a dish with roots in ancient Egypt. There, it started life as ful medames, the famous fava bean dish lightly seasoned with cumin, garlic and lemon. Then it was, reportedly, brought to Johor in Malaysia by Arab traders. It has since been adopted and adapted with a fierce sort of love, plus more spice and a tin of baked beans. I adore it. It’s a very delicious dinner and a triumphant blend of two cuisines.
Kacang pool
Traditionally, this dish is made with minced beef, but I’ve used soya mince. I ignore the packet instructions to rehydrate it before using, though.
Prep 10 min
Cook 35 min
Serves 4
30g unsalted butter
   3 tbsp rapeseed oil, plus extra for frying the eggs
2 red onions, peeled and very finely chopped
¾ tsp fine sea salt
   3 garlic cloves, peeled and minced
1½cm x 1½cm piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped
1 tsp ground cumin
   1 tsp mild curry powder
   ¾ tsp ground coriander
   ¾ tsp ground fennel
   60g dried soya mince – I like Clearspring
1 415g tin baked beans
   1 400g tin borlotti beans in water, not drained
To serve
4 eggs
  Buttered dinner rolls, or Greek-style flatbreads or baguette
2 green finger chillies, finely sliced
1 lime, quartered
Put the butter and oil in a wide frying pan or a medium-sized casserole pot for which you have a lid on a medium heat. When it’s hot, add three-quarters of the chopped onions and three-quarters of a teaspoon of salt, and cook, stirring, for 10 minutes, until soft, glossy and easily squashed with a wooden spoon. Add the garlic and ginger, cook for a further three or four minutes, until the garlic no longer smells raw, then add all the spices and the soya mince, stir to mix and cook for about three minutes more.
Add both tins of beans, including the borlotti bean water, then half-fill one of the empty tins with water, and add half of that to the pan (so, a quarter of a tin’s worth). Stir, pop on the lid and leave to cook for about five minutes. Mash with a potato masher to a consistency you like – I like mine quite chunky – add more water, if need be, to loosen, then pop on the lid again and cook for another five minutes. Taste, add salt, if need be, then take off the heat and leave covered.
Heat a tablespoon of oil in a wide, nonstick pan and, when it’s hot, crack in as many eggs as you can fit comfortably into the pan. Fry until the whites are set and the yolks are runny. Meanwhile, warm the bread.
To serve, spoon a quarter of the bean mix into four lipped plates or wide bowls, top each serving with a fried egg, then sprinkle over a little green chilli and as much of the leftover chopped red onion as you like. Put a lime quarter on each plate, then dig in, serving the bread on the side for mopping.

Japan, US to advance cooperation on US$550 billion trade deal

Japan, US to advance cooperation on US$550 billion trade deal
Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa affirms no higher US tariffs on Japanese goods and supply chains for critical minerals to be reinforced
Japan and the United States have confirmed they will advance cooperation on investing in strategic sectors and honour the other terms of a trade deal they reached last year, even though President Donald Trump’s tariff policies have changed significantly over time.
“We reaffirmed that last year’s agreement remains unchanged,” Japan’s Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa told reporters in Washington on Friday, after meeting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer separately.
Akazawa said the US would not impose any higher tariff rates on goods from Japan than those agreed to bilaterally in July last year.
He also said he agreed with the US officials that the two countries would reinforce supply chains for critical minerals.
During his meeting with Greer on Friday, Akazawa said they shared the view that China’s “arbitrary export controls” posed a risk of causing “significant damage to the supply chains of both Japan and the United States”.
Japan has stuck to the trade deal’s terms, even after the US Supreme Court invalidated Trump’s sweeping country-specific tariffs in February.

From Trump’s takeover threats to a ‘northern neighborhood,’ why the EU chief is going to Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will travel to Greenland's capital on Sunday, seeking to shore up support for the Arctic island against a backdrop of repeated threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.
The EU chief is widely expected to announce fresh funding for the self-governing Danish territory, when she makes her second trip to Nuuk, in the company of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
It comes shortly after Icelanders voted to reject restarting EU membership negotiations and as Trump renews his push to acquire Greenland on national security grounds.
Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen made a thinly veiled reference to Trump's pursuit to acquire the island ahead of Von der Leyen's visit.
"The EU has made clear its support for us in the geopolitical situation, while responding to our desire for even greater partnership. I look very much forward to the coming days and to share more about the importance of the Joint Declaration for Greenland," Nielsen said in a statement shared with CNBC.
Analysts highlighted three key reasons for Von der Leyen's Greenland visit: Arctic security, economic and infrastructure investment and broader cooperation in the North Atlantic and wider Arctic theater.
The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, did not respond to a CNBC request for comment ahead of Von der Leyen's visit. A spokesperson for Denmark's Foreign Ministry declined to comment.
Arctic security
The EU chief's trip to Nuuk serves as a show of solidarity to both Greenland and Denmark at a time of heightened geopolitical tensions, according to Kristina Spohr, professor in the Department of International History at the London School of Economics.
"We must never lose sight with what's going on with Russia and China. By that, I don't just mean the sabotage activity and hybrid warfare that we see, and the focus has now been on Germany, but actually again we have question marks over Russian trawlers around Svalbard," Spohr told CNBC by video call.
"We also see that the Chinese and Russians are doing dual-use scientific action in the Chukchi Sea, through the Bering Strait further north. And, of course, America has said they must not enter American national waters."
These security concerns also extend to the so-called GIUK gap, Spohr said, referring to a strategic maritime passage between Greenland, Iceland and the U.K. that links the Arctic to the Atlantic Ocean.
"So, it's very, very volatile … when actually one of our most important allies in the global scheme of things, the United States, is making life incredibly difficult, especially when it comes to Greenland and Denmark," she added.
Trump has long advocated for control of Greenland, a vast, sparsely populated and largely frozen island, but the U.S. president's fixation on the territory became a major trans-Atlantic issue at the start of the year.
Trump, who had refused to rule out the use of military force to annex Greenland, abruptly announced in late January, however, that he and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had formed a "framework of a future deal" with respect to the territory.
A working group of representatives from the U.S., Denmark and Greenland have since been meeting to discuss the way forward.
Local investment
The EU's Greenland funding package for 2026 and 2027, which the Financial Times reported may amount to 200 million euros ($232.4 million), could target areas such as critical minerals, renewable energy and undersea cables, among other priorities.
Von der Leyen had previously opened the European Commission's office in Nuuk in March 2024, establishing a permanent European presence in the country. The EU chief also signed cooperation agreements worth close to 94 million euros at the time.
"There are several layers but the one layer we should never forget is the Greenland-Denmark relationship," Andreas Raspotnik, senior fellow at The Arctic Institute think tank, told CNBC by telephone.
Read more
"The approach now is very clear: What can we really do? We can invest, we can offer support on pre-agreed issues such as infrastructure, investments in education and increasing our presence there."
Jozef Síkela, the EU's commissioner for international partnerships, recently highlighted some of the EU's investments in Greenland during a gathering to discuss Arctic affairs in Brussels.
"The EU has invested in Arctic education, fisheries and sustainable tourism for decades. €372 million into Arctic research through Horizon, €273 million through Interreg," Síkela said Tuesday at the EU Arctic Forum. "We are not newcomers here. But today's environment demands more," he added.
'Northern neighborhood'
Von der Leyen's visit to Greenland is also seen as a prime opportunity for the EU to coordinate closely with regional leaders on issues such as defense and economic resilience, particularly given the bloc is in the process of updating its Arctic policy.
"I think that the strategic thinking is changing in Brussels as they consider how they can even better include Greenland into, maybe you want to call it the northern neighborhood," Raspotnik said.
"I hear that term as well now, you know, we have an eastern neighborhood, we have a southern neighborhood but how can we define the north? And by north, that means Iceland, it means Canada and it means the U.K.," he continued.
"How can we more strategically think about these partners, those states that are outside the EU in the north?"
Greenland is scheduled to host on Monday a biannual national meeting with Denmark's Frederiksen and Faroese Premier Beinir Johannesen.
"These times commit us to working closely together. Like being three people in the same boat, we must row together and ensure a common direction that is the way it is in the current system," Nielsen said.

Lithuanian comedians take stage at Edinburgh Fringe: ‘Here you are naked’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Amid 4,000-plus shows at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, four Lithuanian artists took to the stage in theatre and stand-up shows, including award-winning actress Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė and rising stars of the British comedy circuit Evaldas Karosas, Justina Seselskaitė and Donatas Staneika.
In Scotland’s capital city, the world’s largest international arts festival was in full swing for three weeks from 7-31 August, with more than 61,000 performances taking place.
LRT met four Lithuanian artists performing solo Fringe shows.
Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė: a family history and the story of a nation on stage
With no props other than a single chair, Ingeborga Dapkūnaitė invites the audience to imagine her childhood apartment in Soviet-occupied Vilnius through storytelling and mime.
In four Christmas Eve scenes, she conjures her family around the dinner table, sharing kleckai dumplings, herring, as well as poppyseed milk with kūčiukai biscuits. While the number of people changes over time, the traditions remain.
Dapkūnaitė’s one-woman play, A Pebble in the Road, follows three generations of Lithuanian women and the turbulent history shaping the country around them.
Fond memories are interwoven with snapshots of dark history and double lives, of arrests, deportations, bullets and death.
The story was inspired by Dapkūnaitė’s grandmother Genovaitė – her beloved babutė –who was born in 1905 and lived to 103, spanning the final years of the Russian Empire, two world wars, Soviet occupation and the restoration of Lithuanian independence.
At the end of the show – just one of Dapkūnaitė’s 24 performances – a Lithuanian fan runs onto the stage with flowers. Soon after, she receives a second bouquet.
“My grandmother represents the 20th century of Lithuania for me,” Dapkūnaitė said. “But I realised that I couldn’t tell her story without my family story. Then I realised that my family story might be interesting not only to Lithuanians, but it reflects the story of a country. We cannot talk about anybody, in my view, in a vacuum.”
She recalls her Soviet diplomat father responding to the question ‘How’s life?’ with: “Like a pebble in the road, whoever isn’t lazy kicks me” – a response that speaks to the violence and upheaval inflicted on Lithuania throughout the 20th century.
Dapkūnaitė also echoes her grandfather Stasys, who said: “You should speak the languages of your neighbours because you never know who’s going to march in and when.”
Above all, it’s a story of resilience and the joy that can coexist alongside trauma.
“All of these people tried to survive in their own way, and as a family,” Dapkūnaitė said. “Life passes very quickly, and all you remember is the most vivid memories, whether it’s a hook that held granny’s door open, or the food you had.”
‘Close to home’
Many Lithuanians have come to watch the performance, including Lithuania’s ambassador to the UK, Asta Radikaitė and cultural attaché Ūla Tornau.
But in addition to the Baltic and Eastern European audience, for whom this history is so familiar, the show has opened the eyes of other visitors.
“A lot of Americans say: ‘Oh my God, we found out so many things that we didn’t know about,’” Dapkūnaitė said. “It’s educational.”
As Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and hybrid threats to the Baltic region persist, the history recounted in the play takes on contemporary significance. Dapkūnaitė left Moscow in 2022 and now lives in London.
“Many Ukrainians come, and they say very nice things, but also tell very painful things,” Dapkūnaitė said. “The show is very close to home for them.”
Dapkūnaitė has performed on some of the world’s biggest stages, from London to New York. On screen, she was the lead actress in the 1994 Oscar-winning film Burnt By The Sun and starred in Mission Impossible and Seven Years in Tibet. But the more intimate, intense Fringe theatre format provides a unique challenge.
“Here, you are naked,” she said. “People either come, or they don’t. You have ten minutes to get into the venue, ten minutes to get out, and you either connect with your audience or you don’t. You develop your show by listening to the audience.”
Evaldas Karosas: A very capable – and funny – man
Striking a different tone is 32-year-old Evaldas Karosas, who is performing a debut Fringe hour of comedy in his set A Very Capable Man. His show promises a dose of cynical objectivity applied to the art of Western stand-up and is billed as an “uncomfortably accurate” hour exposing unspoken thoughts.
After growing up in Antanašė and Rokiškis, Karosas gigged in Vilnius before moving to Manchester, England in 2018 and later settling in London.
In Lithuania's smaller comedy scene, he couldn't work jokes to their full potential: "If you've told a new joke even just 50 times in Lithuania, everyone and their mother has heard it.”
He became a full-time comedian three years ago and reached the finals of the BBC New Comedy Awards in 2025. Earlier this year, he signed with Off The Kerb, one of the UK’s top talent agencies representing some of the biggest names in British comedy.
Karosas previously performed at the Fringe five years ago in a split bill with another comedian. Like many Fringe acts, they struggled to attract an audience – the average Fringe audience is rumoured to be somewhere between six and 20 people in size, with many performances attracting fewer, or none at all.
“I have a documentary on my YouTube channel about doing the Fringe back then, and it’s fun to watch,” Karosas said. “We just kept cancelling shows because we had no audience.”
Comedy that crosses borders
On the evening of September 3, however, the seats in an underground vault in one of Edinburgh’s most iconic music venues are filled. Karosas delivers an energetic set, skewering themes ranging from culture clashes between the Baltics, Eastern Europe and the UK, to men’s mental health and dating.
The audience responds with belly laughs – even if Karosas claims that by performing in his second language, he’s only at sixty percent of his comedic power.
But Karosas doesn’t plan to gig in Lithuanian anytime soon. “Changing languages is like boxing and then changing to karate,” he explains. “It’s still another martial art, but you have to relearn, and even if you have the fitness, the moves are different.”
Karosas assumes that his audiences will know little about Lithuania – and perhaps even struggle to place it on a map. A friend made a video game for audiences to play on their phones, introducing them to his backstory while they wait for the show.
“You have to find a common denominator and talk about being from a small country, which immediately adds context to make it more relatable,” he said. “But I think we now live in such a globalised world that it’s no longer about where you’re from, it’s about how old you are.”
A testing ground for bigger ambitions
While most comedians place importance on winning one of the many Fringe awards, Karosas is not here for prizes.
“For me, the Fringe is more like a tool than the goal,” he said. “It’s the only place where I can do 30 hours in a month. It’s crafting the hour slowly, to be very precise about what you cut.”
Scottish audiences in particular respond well to Karosas’s comedy, and he is supporting acclaimed Glaswegian comedian Kevin Bridges in his 2026 international tour alongside more hour-long London gigs.
Reviews of Karosas’s Fringe show are overwhelmingly positive, but during the festival, he’s avoiding the critics and staying firmly in a bubble.
“I think I’m having a good run objectively,” he said. “But once I leave Edinburgh, I’ll allow myself to peer out of the bubble and read the reviews.”
Justina Seselskaitė: a Lithuanian with a northern English soul
Also making her solo Fringe debut, Justina Seselskaitė is performing in Settled, a 45-minute stand-up show exploring her journey as an immigrant in northern England. She jokes about locals mistaking her nationality and quizzes the audience on Lithuanian covers of British and American songs.
32-year-old Seselskaitė moved from Šiauliai to Manchester in 2014 and had made a name for herself in the city’s booming comedy circuit.
In 2025, she performed in a split-bill and became a finalist in the Fringe’s So You Think You’re Funny? newcomer competition – a launchpad for some of Britain’s top comedians.
‘Shock’ recognition
This year – on top of glowing reviews – Seselskaitė was longlisted for the ISH Edinburgh Comedy Awards for Best Newcomer, which she described as “a total shock.”
“When you’ve worked so hard on something, having that recognised really puts everything into perspective.”
Some audience members relate to her through Lithuanian acquaintances.
“They love telling me about every Lithuanian they’ve ever met,” she said. “I genuinely love it every time! It’s always really sweet.”
Seselskaitė will be back at the Fringe next year for a debut hour of stand-up, but before then, she’ll be “gigging as much as possible, all over the place” and working on her new podcast, The Favourites Pod.
Donatas Staneika: the prolific gigger
Also looking to fill seats and raise laughs is 27-year-old comedian Donatas Staneika from Vilnius, who is performing for 30 minutes in a split-bill stand-up show called 1 British, 1 Immigrant *Continental Breakfast, alongside British-born Bangladeshi comedian Ridwan Hussain.
Staneika is eager to make the most of the Fringe. He has performed at more than 100 gigs and smaller spots during the festival so far, and has done eight gigs in a single day.
“It’s a lot, I’m constantly moving,” he said. “Stand-up is my favourite thing to do, so just getting to do it is a reward. It gives very quick feedback – if you come up with a joke on stage and it doesn’t work, you know immediately.”
The experience has enabled him to practise crowd work, improvisation and refine his set, which pokes fun at everything from Eastern European stereotypes, British accents and immigrant life.
“If my family came to the UK to live with me, I would have them deported myself,” he joked.
‘I think of comedy in English’
Staneika moved to London in 2020 to pursue a stand-up career, having never set foot on stage in Lithuania. He performs observational stand-up across London’s comedy clubs.
This year is Staneika’s second Fringe visit. In 2023, he entered the So You Think You’re Funny? competition and made the semi-finals. He has since been shortlisted twice in the BBC New Comedy Awards.
In October, Staneika might be performing in Lithuania – in English: “The comedy scene in Lithuania is growing and a few clubs have opened, so there is more stand-up now than ever before.” Whether he ever performs in Lithuanian remains to be seen.
“I grew up watching American and British stand-up comedians, so even though I have my own style, I think of comedy in English,” he said. “I feel like English is made for stand-up, as you can play on words.”
Between his Fringe gigs, he’s enjoying connecting with performers and visitors from all over the world.
“Comedy is universal,” he said.

Argentina sanctions 45 firms, individuals over UK-linked Falklands oil drilling
Unknown

04:57:23 UTC
13:57:23 KST

Argentina initiated on Friday sanction proceedings against 45 individuals and companies suspected of carrying out unauthorised hydrocarbon exploration and exploitation on the Falkland Islands, which Buenos Aires calls Islas Malvinas.
President Javier Milei's office announced that the legal measures target not only active oil firms but also "their shareholders and companies that have been providing services" to facilitate the operations.
It said those trying to profit by violating Argentinian sovereignty "will find in the Argentine State the full force of the law."
The government reaffirmed its claim on the Falkland Islands, South Georgia, and the South Sandwich Islands and their "corresponding maritime and insular spaces," declaring they are Argentine "by history and by law" and that there is "no question about it."
Milei warned earlier that the Sea Lion oil project, a major offshore hydrocarbon development near the Falklands operated by British firm Rockhopper Exploration and Israel-based Navitas Petroleum, poses an imminent threat.
He noted that without swift action, foreign entities will "appropriate the oil reserves that lie beneath our sea" and deepen their "occupation."
Falkland dispute
London dismissed the sanctions as domestic politics, asserting its commitment to the islands, while Navitas and its partners said they expect to proceed with drilling under UK licensing.
The long-standing sovereignty dispute between Buenos Aires and London was recently reignited as offshore projects move toward active drilling.
The Falklands are a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic, about 300 miles (483 kilometres) east of the Argentine coast, with a small population. 
Argentina argues that it inherited sovereignty from Spain, and Britain has “illegally occupied” the islands since 1833; it calls the islands Islas Malvinas and rejects the residents’ right to self‑determination as decisive.

Arieh Warshel first Nobel Prize winner to receive Taiwan Employment Gold Card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:56:41 UTC
13:56:41 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Chemical scientist Arieh Warshel has become the first Nobel Prize winner to receive an Employment Gold Card, a milestone the National Development Council said underscores the nation’s growing appeal to elite global scientists.
NDC Minister Yeh Chun-hsien (葉俊顯) presented the card to Warshel at a National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) hosted ceremony, CNA reported Friday. Yeh described the move as a new benchmark for Taiwan’s efforts to attract and retain major talents.
Warshel is the first person with a Nobel Prize to obtain Taiwan’s Employment Gold Card since the program launched in 2018. The NDC commented that the award demonstrates Taiwan’s ability to draw talent, particularly in fields tied to semiconductors, AI computing and biomedicine.
Yeh described the Gold Card as a “Taiwan VIP pass,” saying it makes coming to Taiwan “as easy as going home” for top-tier experts like Warshel, per Liberty Times.
Warshel, a professor at the University of Southern California and member of the US National Academy of Sciences, shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Martin Karplus and Michael Levitt for the development of multiscale models for complex chemical systems.
In the 1970s, he pioneered methods combining quantum and classical mechanics to simulate biological processes such as enzyme catalysis. His work became foundational for computer-aided drug design, enzyme research and protein engineering — earning recognition as a pioneer of computational structural biology.
Warshel accepted an invitation earlier this year from NYCU’s International Graduate Program of Semiconductor Technology to serve as an honorary professor, CNA further reported. It is a role the NDC said will deepen cooperation in talent development, semiconductors and other key technologies.
The Employment Gold Card combines a work permit, resident visa, Alien Resident Certificate and re-entry permit. Key benefits include freedom to seek employment, change jobs or start a business without needing an employer-sponsored work permit. It also provides a shortened path to permanent residency.
Liberty Times reported the NDC as saying that attracting talent is not just about bringing people to Taiwan but ensuring they stay.

Interview: Australia-China PV collaboration powers world: Australian solar pioneer
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:44:44 CST
13:44:44 KST

Scientia Professor Martin Green of the University of New South Wales introduces solar modules in Sydney, Australia, Aug. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)
SYDNEY, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- The winter sun shined bright outside the window of Scientia Professor Martin Green's office at the University of New South Wales (UNSW), Sydney, a quiet reminder of the very element he has spent a lifetime converting into energy.
The energetic 78-year-old engineer from UNSW's School of Photovoltaic and Renewable Energy Engineering is a leading pioneer in modern photovoltaics thanks to his decades of relentless innovation that changed the way the world harnesses solar power.
Green and his team have made pioneering contributions to the advancement of photovoltaic (PV) technology, particularly in improving the performance of silicon solar cells. The two technological pathways they pioneered have both become fundamental to modern silicon solar cell design.
Yet "an even more important achievement" and "the most exciting stuff" is "helping to get the PV industry established in China through the researchers and engineers that we had trained, who did so well in setting up a very competitive industry in China," Green told Xinhua just weeks after returning from Beijing, where he received the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award for the year 2025.
The contact with China all started in 1981. Green's lab welcomed its first Chinese visiting researcher, and batches of them were trained here over the following decades. Some of them founded China's earliest PV companies.
In 1984, Green published a paper on the fundamental efficiency limit of silicon solar cells -- around 30 percent. That same year, he visited China for the first time, invited to lecture at Huazhong University of Science and Technology. He sensed the country's unmistakable potential as it was just beginning to modernize.
In Green's view, mainly with solar and batteries, China's green development has made a massive contribution to the world's green transition. It was the combination of China's massive manufacturing scale and Australia's continuous technological advancement that drove photovoltaics to become one of the world's cheapest sources of electricity.
"Without China's involvement, we definitely wouldn't have solar cells as cheap as now. It could be 10 times the price that they are now. Solar would still be an interesting technology for the future rather than the best option for now."
According to a report Green released in 2016, the flow-on economic benefits to Australia from decades of local photovoltaic research were worth well over 8 billion Australian dollars (about 5.74 billion U.S. dollars), heavily underpinned by the solar manufacturing industry in China.
"If I did the calculation again now, it would be hundreds of billions that it saved Australia by providing a cheap way of generating electricity and avoiding the imputed costs of all the carbon dioxide that we would have been emitting," he told Xinhua,
A frequent visitor to China's PV research institutes and manufacturers, Green observed that they are evolving rapidly. "All the companies are continually building new production lines to accommodate the improved equipment that's going to be available as well as the improved cell technology."
Today, silicon solar cells are approaching the fundamental efficiency limit of around 30 percent. To go further, Green said, the industry must stack new materials on top of silicon. The next chapter of solar power will be defined not by efficiency records, but by whether new cell technologies can stand the test of time in the real world. That is where his latest collaboration with China comes in.
"China dominates the industry, so that makes the collaboration sort of unique," Green said. "Working with China, we feel we're in a position to improve the solar performance more quickly."
"We've just started a big project using AI to find other candidates for stacking onto silicon," Green said. "With AI, it might provide a more systematic way of finding such new materials."
China, he noted, has been pushing hard on AI development, and that makes it an even more attractive partner for this next phase of discovery. "The more China improves AI, the more options we'll have using different AI to explore the available space and see if they can come up with ideas for new compounds," he said. ■
Scientia Professor Martin Green of the University of New South Wales poses for a photo with his certificate of the China International Science and Technology Cooperation Award for the year 2025 in Sydney, Australia, Aug. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)
Scientia Professor Martin Green of the University of New South Wales introduces solar modules in Sydney, Australia, Aug. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)

Researchers in Australia develop new approach to deliver cancer drugs into brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:44:32 CST
13:44:32 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia are developing a new class of cancer drugs that can break through the blood-brain barrier, a protective shield that currently blocks most drugs from ever entering the brain.
The national project, which has received 18.8 million Australian dollars (about 13.54 million U.S. dollars) in government funding, aims to develop brain-penetrating drugs that can overcome one of the biggest barriers to brain cancer treatment, according to a statement released recently by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI).
The blood-brain barrier strictly controls what can enter the brain to prevent toxins and infections from passing through, blocking around 98 percent of cancer drugs from reaching brain tissue, essential to maintaining the brain's overall health, the statement said.
Researchers plan to "hijack" the blood-brain barrier's natural nutrient delivery pathways to "smuggle cancer-killing molecules into the brain," said lead investigator Associate Professor Jim Whittle, a WEHI laboratory head.
The brain relies on the natural delivery systems to transport essential nutrients such as iron and glucose from the bloodstream. Cells in the blood-brain barrier contain specialized "docking stations" that recognize and actively draw these nutrients into the brain, according to researchers.
The approach could unlock a new class of brain-penetrating drugs and create an opportunity to test existing cancer drugs that have previously failed to reach the brain, Whittle said.
The researchers said the team will initially target high-grade gliomas, including glioblastoma in adults and diffuse midline glioma in children. ■

Seattle Times, Newsday sue OpenAI, Microsoft, alleging copyright infringement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:35:00 UTC
13:35:00 KST

Seattle Times, Newsday sue OpenAI, Microsoft, alleging copyright infringement
NEW YORK - The Seattle Times and Newsday sued OpenAI and Microsoft on Sept 4, alleging in federal court that the US tech companies copied the US newspapers’ journalism without permission to train their AI systems.
The suit in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York alleges that OpenAI and Microsoft scraped the newspapers’ websites, including content behind paywalls, and incorporated articles into datasets used to train and operate products including ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Bing’s AI features.
The newspapers, based in Seattle and Long Island, New York, said the companies’ AI products can reproduce passages from their reporting, closely paraphrase articles and provide users with answers that reduce the need to visit their websites or buy subscriptions.
“We feel strongly that we must defend our content - which we spend millions of dollars a year to produce - from being used without our consent or compensation,” Seattle Times President and CEO Alan Fisco wrote to employees, according to the newspaper.
A spokesperson for San Francisco-based OpenAI said its models are trained on publicly available data and grounded in fair use, without commenting specifically on the lawsuit.
A spokesperson for Microsoft, based near Seattle in Washington state, said in an email: “While we’re surprised by the lawsuit, we appreciate the importance of local journalism and we’re always happy to sit down and explore solutions to this type of dispute.”
The Seattle Times and Newsday are seeking an order requiring the destruction of copies of their works as well as training datasets or AI models incorporating them.
The lawsuit echoes a case filed by the New York Times in 2023, which accused OpenAI and Microsoft of using millions of newspaper articles without permission to train OpenAI’s popular chatbot. 
The case is ongoing, and is one of dozens brought by copyright holders against tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta for what they say is misuse of their material to train AI systems. REUTERS

The agency named Nehru, his relatives and several officials as accused.The allegations include a Rs 888-crore cash-for-jobs scam, in which money was allegedly collected from candidates in exchange for government jobs, as well as irregularities in contracts worth around Rs 1,020 crore and illegal transfers and postings linked to the department.The Enforcement Directorate (ED) had earlier shared details of the alleged irregularities with Tamil Nadu authorities, following which the matter came under scrutiny.However, the Madras high court later granted an interim stay on further action by the vigilance agency and proceedings against the accused. Legal proceedings in the matter are continuing.(With ANI inputs)

‘Mini-dictatorship’: students slam far-right turn at Argentina-run residence in Paris
Residents allege surveillance and far-right meetings as they claim Argentina House at Cite Universitaire has become ‘a space of fear’
Weeks before President Javier Milei visits France, scrutiny has grown around an Argentina-run university residence in Paris supposed to promote peaceful coexistence but which activists say instead restricts lodger freedoms and hosts European far-right figures.
Paris city officials have demanded the foreign ministry investigate Argentina House, one of dozens of homes run by foreign nations or French institutions on an international campus in the French capital.
The Cite Universitaire campus, or Cite U, was set up after World War I as lodgings for youth to form lasting connections with their peers across the globe.
But campus sources and former house residents, most speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, say that the one run by Argentina had gone awry since a Milei appointee, fervent Catholic lawyer Santiago Muzio, became its director in 2024.
“The house used to be a space for community, culture, and art. Today it’s a space of fear, control, surveillance, cameras,” said an Argentine who lived there during the last academic year.
Residents said their access to common areas such as the lounge or the outdoor barbecue – an epicentre for socialising in Argentine culture – had been restricted.

Japan will invest $550 billion in the U.S. in exchange for lower tariffs – AI and chips now at the center of the deal
Kyiv • UNN
Japan has advanced a $550 billion investment deal in the U.S. in exchange for a 15% tariff. The new package will focus on AI and chips.
Japan and the United States have made progress in implementing a large-scale $550 billion investment deal, which became a key part of the agreement to reduce U.S. tariffs on Japanese goods. Artificial intelligence and semiconductors may now play an increasingly important role in new projects, Bloomberg reports, writes UNN.
Details
Japan's Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa announced the progress following talks in Washington with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.
With the growing presence of the artificial intelligence and semiconductor industries, we continue to develop and implement projects that promote mutual benefit
Why the $550 billion deal matters
The investment mechanism became a central part of the trade agreement under which U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to impose a 15% tariff on Japanese goods and reduce the tariff on automobiles – an export sector that is critically important to Japan's economy.
The first package provides for $36 billion in investment in oil, gas, and raw materials projects in the United States. The second – another $73 billion in nuclear power and gas-fired power plants.
The parties are now working on a third package. Akazawa did not disclose its parameters, but noted that AI and semiconductors would carry "very significant weight" in the negotiations.
For Japan, there is another important outcome of the negotiations: the parties confirmed that the United States would not impose additional tariffs on Japanese goods beyond those already provided for by the trade agreement.

Country diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battle | Cal Flyn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
04:30:26 UTC
13:30:26 KST

I hear them before I see them: a wailing, or something more like ululation. High-pitched, repeated vocalisations that are neither man nor cat, but somewhere in between. I throw open the cabin door, unsure what to look for, and for a moment see nothing new: only the rocky strand and the sweep of dark wrack high above the shoreline.
The strange, warbling sound comes again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. Not quite screaming, not quite howling, not quite trilling, but all of those things at once.
A flash of movement in the water, perhaps 50 metres out. A small, dark body leaps from the surf, followed smartly by another. My eyes struggle to understand what I’m looking at. Tiny figures catch a millisecond of clear air, then slice back through the surface, like dolphins or porpoises. But the silhouette is all wrong. And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle.
Ai-ai-ai-ai. Are they playing? Fighting? Their forms are slick and dark. When one launches again from the water, I see it clearly: four limbs, and a long tail – two otters, locked in battle. Over a fish perhaps, or one of the crabs we were watching earlier from the rowing boat as we drifted on the breeze, hands trailing through saline, watching the tiny creatures on the seabed below like tourists from a cable car.
They tussle and twist. Then one breaks free and makes a dash for the shoreline. The other shrieks and follows, both now skimming over the surface like stones.
What drama! You would hear them a mile away. The otters disappear behind a boulder, and for a moment all is silent but for the wash of the waves.
It has gone 8pm. The sun is lowering in the sky, ready for bed. The wind ruffles the heads of the trees on the island in the bay. A pair of little egrets pick their way through the shallows, pause to examine their surroundings, then move on, feet lifted high and deliberate. Then the voices come again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. The soap opera continues unseen.
