Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:45:31 UTC
08:45:31 KST

Putin announced battlefield encirclements that the evidence doesn’t show, but Russia’s real offensive is accelerating elsewhere
At a late-night press conference in Bishkek on September 1, Vladimir Putin said what he believed was happening on the battlefield. Once again, his account clashed with the Russian military’s documented gains. Putin is evidently aware that even troops at the front do not accept his reports, so he cited sources in the General Staff and “other agencies.” He said the picture, as it “appears” to him, is “fairly objective.” He immediately said that Ukrainian units had been encircled in two places in the Kharkiv region and that Sviatohirsk, near Sloviansk, had been captured. The claims surprised even the people behind Telegram channels close to the Russian military command, who likely work at the headquarters of the units responsible for the sectors Putin mentioned. Yet, strange as it may seem, Putin’s optimism about these operations is not detached from reality: Russia’s offensive accelerated in late summer and again pushed Ukrainian defenses into crisis along several important axes in early fall.
The Kharkiv region
- Putin said several thousand Ukrainian troops were encircled near Vovchansk and pinned against the border. Russian forces have indeed broken through from two directions southeast of the city, which Russia captured by mid-2026 after two years of heavy fighting. One group advanced from Vovchansk in the north and approached the large settlement of Bilyi Kolodiaz; another is advancing toward it from the Russian border to the east.
- Russia’s Defense Ministry said a month ago that Bilyi Kolodiaz had also been captured. Since then, however, published videos filmed by Russian units have shown strikes on Ukrainian positions inside the settlement. The nearest Russian positions are in tree lines several kilometers to the north.
- Published videos indicate that the force advancing from the east has not moved past Kupyne, 25 kilometers (16 miles) from Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- To be fair, the most recent videos from the area date to mid-August, and the situation may well have changed considerably in the weeks since. Still, it would be unusual for such changes to leave no visual trace at all — the Russian push toward Bilyi Kolodiaz in early August and the Ukrainian counterattacks that followed were both well documented.
- In any case, Russia does not have enough troops in this sector to encircle a 25-by-25-kilometer (16-by-16-mile) area. No encirclement of that size has been completed since May 2022, despite many attempts by both sides.
- An encirclement of Ukrainian units near Pisky-Radkivske, south of Kupiansk, seems even less likely. The Ukrainian army has maintained a large bridgehead on the eastern bank of the Oskil River for four years, centered on Borova, north of Pisky-Radkivske. Ukrainian forces also have numerous crossings over the shallow Krasnooskilske Reservoir. From the bridgehead, they periodically attack near the junction of the Kharkiv and Luhansk regions, trying to keep a small part of the Luhansk region under Ukrainian control so Russia cannot capture the entire region. Overall, this stretch of the front remains a “backwater.” Most troops in the area are fighting either near Kupiansk to the north or near Lyman to the south.
- Russian forces have made gains around Kupiansk and inside the city in recent months, retaking territory Russia lost during Ukraine’s counteroffensive last winter. They have also seized large areas on the eastern bank of the Oskil between Borova and Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi. But Putin said last fall that Russia already fully controlled Kupiansk, so this time he did not mention these actual gains. Nor did he mention a new Ukrainian attempt to pressure the northwestern flank of the Russian force advancing on Kupiansk near Dvorichna and Zapadne.
Lyman and Sviatohirsk
- Putin said Russian forces had captured Sviatohirsk, a city on the northern bank of the Siverskyi Donets River, 20 kilometers (12 miles) from Sloviansk. But no Russian positions have been documented in the immediate vicinity of Sviatohirsk in recent months. Moreover, Ukrainian forces have rolled back Russian incursions into the nearby villages of Yarova and Pryshyb, on a small Russian bridgehead on the river’s southern bank.
- Ukrainian forces are also trying to push Russian troops farther from Lyman, a city Russian forces tried and failed to storm in early summer.
- Overall, Ukrainian forces have managed to halt the Russian advance toward Sloviansk on the river’s northern bank, but not on its southern bank.
Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Dobropillia
- After capturing most of Kostiantynivka — where scattered groups of Ukrainian troops still remain — Russian forces found themselves in early August in a situation they had hoped to avoid. Despite their success in the center of the front, which stretches more than 100 kilometers (62 miles) from the Siverskyi Donets River to Pokrovsk, they could not advance directly on the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area. Attacks on the flanks — the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia, Dobropillia–Druzhkivka, and Lyman–Sviatohirsk sectors — were stalling, and a direct push toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from Kostiantynivka or Chasiv Yar was difficult without support from the flanks.
- In recent weeks, Russia’s offensive on the western flank, from Dobropillia to Druzhkivka, has intensified sharply.
- Russian forces captured settlements south of Dobropillia and then reached Annivka on the city’s eastern outskirts. Exactly a year after a failed attempt to break through to the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, Russian troops struck again at the same point, this time with far larger forces and more extensive preparation. They captured Kucheriv Yar — which Russian forces had also occupied in August–September 2025 — and Rubizhne. Farther east, Russian forces also pushed toward the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road, reaching the area around Novoandriivka.
- Russian forces continue to advance toward Druzhkivka along the Kazennyi Torets River. They have crossed the river and taken up positions in Raiske, 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the city. Along the entire stretch from Dobropillia to the northwestern approaches to Druzhkivka, Ukrainian defenses are in a full-blown crisis requiring urgent measures — such as redeploying major reserves, as Ukraine did in the same area a year ago.
- The situation is also deteriorating southeast of Druzhkivka, where Russian troops are advancing rapidly — by the standards of this war — from the direction of Chasiv Yar. They have already reached Izhivka on the approaches to Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka.
- Farther north, on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets, Russian forces have reached the outskirts of Mykolaivka, which shields Sloviansk.
- The two sides’ starting positions for the battle over the Kramatorsk–Sloviansk urban area will depend on how Ukrainian commanders respond to these advances from several directions. A delayed or inadequate response could mean the battle begins as early as winter. Kyiv has created new command structures but has not yet transferred additional troops, which could be freed up only by weakening other sectors of the front. Ukrainian forces in the northern Donetsk region are clearly feeling the absence of an army corps — an air assault formation. The formation was sent southwest in the spring to the junction of the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk regions to stop the Russian advance deeper into the Zaporizhzhia region, particularly toward Orikhiv.
Orikhiv and Mala Tokmachka
- In August, Ukrainian forces made another attempt to advance near the junction of the three regions. They broke through near the Donetsk–Zaporizhzhia road and advanced 10–12 kilometers (6–7 miles) to the Mokri Yaly River. The breakthrough point seemed well chosen: it was right at the junction of the Russian “Vostok” and “Tsentr” groups, bringing Ukrainian troops onto the western flank of the “Tsentr” group’s 90th Tank Division, whose positions faced north.
- Russian commanders, however, quickly brought in forces from the 90th Tank Division and the neighboring 41st Combined Arms Army to repel the Ukrainian attack from the west. In mid-August, both sides published videos showing their flags raised in about 10 villages. Ukrainian forces did so first, followed by units of the “Tsentr” and “Vostok” groups. The situation has remained unclear since then, but the lack of new information suggests that the Ukrainian advance was stopped, perhaps only temporarily, and that Ukrainian forces lost some of the territory they had previously retaken.
- Ukrainian forces also failed to achieve the offensive’s primary goal. Strikes on the northern flank of the “Vostok” group, which began in the spring, were meant to halt its advance eastward toward Orikhiv, in the central Zaporizhzhia region. The advance was only slowed, and it has now resumed with renewed force.
- Russian forces have reached the Orikhiv–Novomykolaivka road in several places. It is one of the main supply routes for the Orikhiv garrison. Russian troops have often failed to hold positions along the road or in nearby villages, however: Ukrainian forces continue to hold positions behind and on the flanks of the advancing Russian troops and are even counterattacking.
- The clash between small groups of assault troops on the steppe has already had dire consequences for Orikhiv itself. The “Dnipro” group’s 42nd Motorized Rifle Division had failed for two years to break through the Novodanylivka–Mala Tokmachka line south and southeast of Orikhiv; it did so in just two weeks. Russian forces have captured all of Novodanylivka, and assault troops from the 42nd Division have also established positions on the southern outskirts of Orikhiv.
- For the first time in a long while, Russian assault troops have also reached the center of Mala Tokmachka, a large village familiar from its frequent appearances in reports by pro-war commentators. Russian troops have cut the road from the village to Orikhiv. It remains unclear whether the 118th Mechanized Brigade, which had held Mala Tokmachka since early 2024, managed to retain positions even on the village’s outskirts. With Russian forces in their rear and the road to Orikhiv cut, doing so will be extremely difficult.

A private spacecraft approached NASA’s doomed telescope, but could no longer save it

The private spacecraft Link operated by Katalyst Space Technologies approached NASA’s Swift telescope to within about 15 km and collected data on its condition, but was unable to complete the rescue mission due to insufficient fuel. Associated Press reports, as UNN writes.
Details
Link was launched in July in an attempt to raise the aging Swift to a higher orbit and extend its operational life. However, shortly after launch, the spacecraft began spinning uncontrollably.
Controllers managed to stabilize Link, but this consumed a significant portion of its fuel reserves. In August, the rescue operation was canceled, although the company decided to use the spacecraft for an additional rendezvous with the telescope and to collect data.
Link managed to approach Swift to within 15 km
This week, Link approached Swift to within about 15 km and took images of the telescope.
We got so close, yet at the same time so far away
NASA paid the company about $30 million for the attempt to rescue the telescope. From the outset, the agency regarded the mission as experimental, in part because of the risk of the spacecraft colliding and creating space debris.
According to Lee, Link likely no longer has enough fuel for another rendezvous with Swift. The spacecraft itself may remain in orbit for several more weeks, after which it will enter the atmosphere and burn up.

US judge blocks Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:40:33 UTC
08:40:33 KST

Muhammed Yasin Güngör
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
A federal court in the state of Massachusetts issued a nationwide preliminary injunction on Friday to block the US government from implementing restrictive new mail-in ballot rules for the 2026 midterm elections.
Judge Indira Talwani ruled that the United States Postal Service (USPS) overstepped its legal authority by attempting to regulate the "time, place, and manner" of elections. The court emphasized that under the Elections Clause of the US Constitution, the powers are reserved for individual states and the US Congress, leaving the executive branch with no inherent authority to intervene.
Talwani warned that forcing states to redesign envelopes and upload voter data to an unproven digital portal weeks before the Nov. 3 election would cause "inevitable" disenfranchisement.
The ruling noted that the policy stemming from President Donald Trump’s executive order would allow the USPS to "refuse to transmit" ballots that did not meet the new standards. It means millions of Americans could lose their right to vote if the USPS withheld ballots that did not comply with the new, complex standards.
The court found that many small rural jurisdictions lack the technology to print the required specialized barcodes. Additionally, the digital portal the government intended to use is not yet operational. The judge said the record contained "no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting" to justify the sudden policy shift.
The ruling prevents the government from refusing to transmit mail-in or absentee ballots based on the new requirements.
While Trump has frequently advocated for tighter voting restrictions, the court denied the administration's request to pause the injunction.

Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:35:59 UTC
08:35:59 KST

Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
Historian and writer Artem Kirpichenok flew to Tel Aviv on August 2 to attend an international conference, his support group said. Officers from Israel’s General Security Service (Shin Bet) detained him at the airport. Kirpichenok, a citizen of both Russia and Israel, has remained in custody ever since. Officials have not disclosed the reason for his detention.
Little is known about Artem Kirpichenok’s case. Israeli authorities may suspect him of espionage.
Family representatives told Meduza that, based on “unofficial information,” investigators suspect Kirpichenok of espionage and of contacting an agent of a foreign intelligence service.
But “there’s no Arab angle [to the case],” the source said. According to the source, the agent Kirpichenok allegedly contacted is not from Lebanon or Iran.
“Who could it be, then? If it’s Russia, the whole case is built on sand, as Israelis say. He’s a Russian citizen who has lived in Russia permanently since 2005. And Russia is hardly a stranger to Israel: the two countries conduct joint intelligence operations and share information despite friction over Iran and other issues,” the source told Meduza.
The alleged offenses are considered serious, according to the source, but even Kirpichenok’s lawyer does not know exactly what he is accused of. Israeli law has more than a dozen statutes that can apply in espionage cases, with penalties of up to life imprisonment.
“The fact that someone is held in a Shin Bet detention facility indicates that the person is suspected of crimes against state security,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family said.
A separate charge may stem from Kirpichenok’s 2018 trip to Iran, which he wrote about on social media at the time. Israel considers Iran an enemy state, and traveling there without special permission from the Israeli Interior Ministry carries a prison sentence of up to four years.
Nika Dubrovskaya, an artist and friend of Kirpichenok’s, told the outlet Bumaga that he visited Israel several times after his trip to Iran without running into problems at the border. Another friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza the account was accurate and said the historian had also visited Israel the previous winter, before his August trip.
He rented out his apartment in Ashkelon, which was one reason he returned to the country several times a year.
Kirpichenok’s research and columns
Kirpichenok, 51, holds a Doctor of Sciences degree and works as a journalist and researcher specializing in the Middle East and Central Asia. A family representative told Meduza that he is cautious — an “armchair scholar” who dislikes fieldwork.
A friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza that she met him in Israel in the mid-1990s, when she was living there and he was still studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She said that after he graduated, Kirpichenok could not find work in his field in Israel and was “very unhappy.”
Kirpichenok, a St. Petersburg native, returned to Russia in the 2000s and inherited an apartment there, she said. During those years, he worked as a tour guide, gave lectures, and wrote articles: “He worked with all kinds of publications and held, I’d say, Trotskyist views. Some minor grassroots activity: tours, and during COVID, he developed routes like ‘Sick Petersburg.’ A kind of intellectual precariat.”
Drawing on his dissertation about Hungarian nationalist movements at the turn of the 20th century, Kirpichenok wrote a book titled Vengriya-1956: drugoy vzglyad (“Hungary-1956: A Different View”). Kirpichenok criticized the 1956 Hungarian uprising, viewing it not as a progressive movement against the Soviet regime but as a far-right conservative revolt.
In recent years, Kirpichenok headed the Slavic studies department at the Center for Arab-Eurasian Studies, which was founded by Amr Abdel-Hamid, an Egyptian journalist, media manager, and former head of Al Jazeera’s Moscow bureau.
He also wrote about the Middle East for the Turkish broadcaster TRT and the Azerbaijani outlet Caliber, sharply criticizing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s actions in Gaza, and its policies toward Palestinians.
In his book Izrail’. Put’ k katastrofe (“Israel: The Road to Catastrophe”), Kirpichenok says Israel is not “the revived state of the Jewish people” but “the last bastion of Western colonialism.”
“Artem never wrote anything that went beyond what he read in the newspaper Haaretz and a couple dozen other sources, like B’Tselem,” his friend said. “I mean, some criticism of the existing regime. Geez, that exists in every country, and it’s a good thing — that’s what the intelligentsia is for.”
She was surprised by the possibility of espionage charges: “He doesn’t have any [classified] information. How would he have access to any?”
Kirpichenok flew to Israel for an academic conference — but officials in the city where it was supposed to take place had never heard of it
Kirpichenok is now being held in a Shin Bet pretrial detention facility in Petah Tikva.
He is alone in a cell where the lights stay on around the clock, with no outdoor exercise and no access to reading or writing materials. “All he can do in his cell is sit or lie down, sleep, or think,” a family representative said.
“Before October 7, 2023, only Arab Muslims were subjected to this kind of repression,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family told Meduza.
A support group of Kirpichenok’s friends believes the international conference may have been a trap set by security services to get the scholar into the country, according to the independent Russian outlet Doxa. Kirpichenok arrived in Israel on August 2 and had planned to leave six days later.
Representatives of Kirpichenok’s family contacted the municipality of the city where the conference was supposedly scheduled to take place, but officials there said no such event had been held. The family said Kirpichenok avoided answering questions about exactly who had invited him to Israel.
Israeli security officers pressured Kirpichenok, according to a family representative
The fourth court hearing in Kirpichenok’s case took place in Ashkelon on Thursday, August 27. The proceedings are closed to the public.
Kirpichenok was brought to court from the pretrial detention facility. Family representatives said he was held in a soundproof glass booth during the hearing. His lawyer, Inna Lebedinskaya-Katz, was unable to speak with her client during the proceedings, a Meduza source said. (Lebedinskaya-Katz declined to comment, citing a court order barring publication of details about Kirpichenok’s case.)
That day, the court extended the gag order on details of Kirpichenok’s case through August 31. A formal declaration of charges — roughly equivalent to an indictment in Russian legal procedure — was due to be filed on September 4. At that point, the defense would be able to access the investigation files, a family representative told Meduza. The family representative expects prosecutors to seek Kirpichenok’s continued detention through the end of the trial.
At the hearing, Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to exclude her client’s confession, arguing that Kirpichenok had been pressured into making it. Israel Shamir, a left-wing Israeli writer and columnist covering the case, said on Telegram that Lebedinskaya-Katz had filed the motion.
Kirpichenok had not been allowed to contact his lawyer, a family representative told Meduza. His only meeting with his defense attorney came on August 23, when he told Lebedinskaya-Katz that he had falsely incriminated himself “under pressure from investigators.”
During that meeting, Kirpichenok, in handcuffs, was held in a glass booth and spoke with his lawyer by phone. He feared the conversation might be monitored and worried that he would “be sent back down to the basement” where the interrogations took place, a family representative told Meduza.
Investigators allegedly threatened to confiscate his apartment in Israel and deport him to Ukraine. “He never supported the ‘special military operation’ that Russia launched, but because he holds left-wing views, he has spoken out against imperialism, including Russian imperialism,” a family representative told Meduza. There is no independent confirmation that investigators pressured Kirpichenok.
At the August 27 hearing, Kirpichenok “looked much worse” than he had when he met with his lawyer. According to Shamir, the defense attorney said: “His face seemed to sag, his eyes were dull, and he could barely smile.”
Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to move Kirpichenok from pretrial detention to house arrest because he has an apartment in Ashkelon, but the judge denied the request, citing the severity of the charges.
Kirpichenok also asked for an interpreter at future hearings — a request that surprised representatives of his family, since he had begun living in Israel as a teenager, served in the Israel Defense Forces, and later graduated from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The lawyer asked the court to allow a psychiatrist to see her client, citing his depressed state and post-traumatic stress disorder.
How Russia reacted to Kirpichenok’s detention
“The irony of Artem’s situation is that he holds two toxic passports. Neither country is particularly eager to stand up for him, you know?” the historian’s friend told Meduza.
Kirpichenok’s support group only recently contacted Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and Russian diplomats “have been emphatic in promising their support,” a family representative told Meduza. But because Kirpichenok also holds Israeli citizenship, Russian Embassy staff have not yet been allowed to see him.
Russia’s ambassador to Israel, Anatoly Viktorov, said the diplomatic mission “had sent a request to the appropriate Israeli authorities.”
Valery Fadeev, head of the Presidential Human Rights Council, sent a letter to Matthew Gillett, chair-rapporteur of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, on August 28. In the letter, Fadeev said: “In Israel, this kind of detention is usually linked to suspected crimes against state security.”
“This suggests that his detention was motivated by [Kirpichenok’s] political views,” the letter says. “Of particular concern is his health: he suffers from hypertension with a risk of retinal detachment, which requires constant medical monitoring.”
The Presidential Human Rights Council called on the United Nations to demand that Israeli authorities clarify the grounds for Kirpichenok’s detention and ensure that he has immediate access to a lawyer and qualified medical care.
Shin Bet had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment as of publication.

Five European nations seek deals to send migrants out of the EU

Breadcrumb
Five European nations seek deals to send migrants out of the EU
Five European nations aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency to countries outside the European Union, they said at a meeting hosted by Denmark on Friday.
Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands said they had agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with a non-European Union country on return facilities, the latest effort by European nations to reduce immigration.
The countries, known as the Group of Five, did not name the nations they expect to host return centres.
"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at a press conference in Copenhagen.
The group, which has held a series of meetings this year, plans to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what critics say could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.
HUMAN RIGHTS CONCERNS
The Council of Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the continent, in July said return hubs posed "considerable human rights risks", and several other groups have also criticised the plan.
Danish Refugee Council Secretary General Charlotte Slente said it would be better to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses on stricter border screening, faster asylum and return procedures, and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.
"Return hubs focus on a small number of returns, they will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and they could violate basic human rights," Slente said.
Denmark expects to be ready to send migrants to the return hub by the end of 2027, Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov said.
"It's a new chance to have a life in a partner country," he said, adding that the five nations would be in dialogue with the UN body, the International Organization for Migration, and the UN Refugee Agency for their next steps.
A UNHCR spokesperson said the agency had not been approached with details of a proposal and could not comment on the arrangements being discussed.

UN approves world map reflecting true size of Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:34:00 UTC
08:34:00 KST

UN approves world map reflecting true size of Africa
September 5, 2026
A yearslong push to change the default view of the Earth came to a vote at the United Nations General Assembly on Friday with 164 countries in favor of a new map, the United States against it and six abstentions.
Known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection, the map "offers a more accurate representation of the sizes of continental landmasses and to this end is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," according to the resolution, which was spearheaded by several African countries.
Togo's foreign minister, Robert Dussey, told the UN maps "shape our understanding of the world."
"They guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions," he said. "They are, therefore, never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."
No, Greenland is nowhere near as big as Africa
The resolution pushes for countries to adopt the Equal Earth projection rather than the traditional Mercator projection, which was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.
The Mercator projection accurately depicts the shapes and angles of landmasses, necessary for shipping, but distorts their relative sizes: landmasses near the Earth's poles appear larger while those near the equator look smaller. This makes Greenland appear about as big as Africa, despite the African continent being about 14 times larger.
Togo's Dussey said his country aims to replace the maps used in its schools by the end of the year.
The Mercator projection's use is a result of colonization, Dussey said, adding, "The world is changing. Africa also is changing."
US, China, India, Japan, Mexico and part of EU fit in Africa
France, which co-sponsored the resolution, said on Friday that it would also abandon the Mercator projection.
In that projection, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in statement.
"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he acknowledged. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."
In support of the new projection, online campaign group #CorrectTheMap said, "You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare."
The UN General Assembly vote is not legally binding and "in no way challenges the use of Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited," the ministry said in a statement.
Equal Earth a 'distraction,' US says
As the only country to vote against the resolution, the United States said the Equal Earth projection pushed an "ideological agenda" and distracted attention from "genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations."
"Instead of focusing on genuine problems... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.
Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Morocco, Serbia and Ukraine abstained from voting on the resolution.

In Bulgaria, the skeleton of a man was found who may have hidden from an attack in a huge jar 1,600 years ago
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:23:18 EEST
08:23:18 KST

In Bulgaria, the skeleton of a man was found who may have hidden from an attack in a huge jar 1,600 years ago
Kyiv • UNN
In Deultum, a man's skeleton was found in a dolium with weapons. He may have hidden during an attack when the city was engulfed in flames.
Archaeologists discovered the remains of a man inside a large storage vessel—a dolium—at the site of the ancient Roman city of Deultum in southeastern Bulgaria. Scientists presume that he may have climbed inside it to escape an attack. Live Science reports this, UNN writes.
Details
Two iron knives and a belt were found next to the man. One knife remained tucked into the belt, while the second lay between his legs, as if the man had been ready to defend himself.
In the 4th–5th centuries, the Romans in Deultum confronted East Germanic tribes and the Huns. Around the dolium that was found, archaeologists discovered traces of a large-scale fire—ash, charcoal, blackened walls, melted glass, coins, and the burned bones of domestic animals.
Archaeologist Lyudmil Vagalinski of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences presumes that, before the attack, residents may have driven livestock inside the fortifications. Since a layer of ash also lay beneath the man's remains, he likely hid in the vessel after the fire had already begun.
After the attack, the city's residents dismantled and leveled the ruins of the tower, then arranged a new, higher floor level above them. It was beneath this floor that the man's remains were preserved for about 1,600 years.

The head of Memorial, Russia’s Nobel Peace Prize-winning rights group, has told AFP she fears a fresh crackdown after September’s legislative elections, with more people arrested and sent to fight in Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, I think that now everything is getting worse, but not so fast,” the 65-year-old said. “But after the elections, there will be a very sharp deterioration.”
Last month, Russia’s Supreme Court banned the only anti-war party, Yabloko, from running in the elections, where opposition to Russian President Vladimir Putin will be minimal.
“More people will be arrested for insignificant things and sent to prison. They are interested in sending people to prison. For them, prison is a way to the front,” she said, referring to the main line of combat in Ukraine.
“The situation at the front is very fragile.”
Memorial was founded in the late 1980s to document victims of Soviet-era political repression during which millions of people perished in the Gulag penal system.
Earlier this year, a court labelled the group “extremist”, making its supporters subject to prosecution and effectively outlawing any cooperation with it.
Will Russia Honor Zelensky’s Proposed Truce for US Envoys?
Memorial group received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022 – months after Russia launched its offensive on Ukraine – alongside jailed Belarusian activist Ales Bialiatski and Ukraine’s Centre for Civil Liberties.
Zhemkova herself has fled the country and keeps the organization running from Berlin where she acts as executive director.
“The more they try to silence or erase the name of Memorial in Russia, the louder it will sound outside Russia,” she promised.
Zhemkova was speaking on the sidelines of an exhibition entitled “Artists Against the Kremlin: Memory Remains”, at the De Balie cultural centre in Amsterdam.
The exhibition features work from artists forced into exile, silenced or persecuted and Zhemkova said it was a good example of Memorial’s work outside Russia.
“If we don’t understand and take lessons from the past, we will repeat mistakes and our present and future will be terrible,” she said.
‘Sophisticated propaganda’
With Russia apparently escalating its offensive in Ukraine and testing Western unity with “hybrid” attacks in Europe, Zhemkova urged a strong response.
When Europe hesitates, Putin “sees this as weakness,” she said.
“And for Putin, what does weakness mean? It means that victory is around the corner and we need to push further,” said Zhemkova.
She highlighted what she described as a “huge repressive mechanism” in Russia and “very powerful and sophisticated propaganda.”
She pointed to a plan to replace Moscow’s Gulag museum with a new exhibition documenting Nazi crimes against the Soviet Union during World War II, the latest move in a crackdown on institutions documenting Soviet-era repression.
“It’s only a part of what they do,” she said, referring to the museum.
“Unfortunately, the process of rewriting history is much bigger, much deeper. It’s also the destruction of monuments,” said Zhemkova.
The human rights leader said she felt safe in Berlin, despite being distanced from friends and home and her family, which she said was now disbursed over eight countries.
“That’s the reason why our meeting point is Zoom every week,” she laughed.
And despite the situation in Russia seeming to get worse by the day, she said she still feels hopeful.
“We are trying to explain that not everybody turned into criminals. That there is another Russia. Even now,” she told AFP.
She said what gives her hope is the bravery of her fellow campaigners and the creative protests of artists such as those exhibiting in Amsterdam.
The objects in the exhibition often tell a sad and tragic story of repression, she said.
“And on the other hand, the other side of the object is always a story about solidarity, love, friendship, family.”

DNA of a dangerous virus that raged thousands of years ago was found in medieval manuscripts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
02:18:49 EEST
08:18:49 KST

DNA of a dangerous virus that raged thousands of years ago was found in medieval manuscripts
Kyiv • UNN
Scientists discovered sheep pox DNA in ancient parchments and traced its history back 3,700 years. The virus was found in medieval manuscripts.
Scientists have discovered traces of sheep pox virus DNA on the pages of ancient parchment manuscripts and traced its history back at least 3,700 years. University College Dublin reported this, UNN writes.
Details
Researchers analyzed parchment made from animal skins and found that it can preserve genetic traces of ancient pathogens.
The recovery of ancient pathogen DNA has completely changed our understanding of infectious diseases in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve the DNA of animal pathogens
The virus was found in a 1,000-year-old Gospel
Traces of sheep pox were found, in particular, in the 1,000-year-old illuminated manuscript "The York Gospels," as well as in an early English dictionary known as the "Corpus Glossary."
The virus's DNA was also found in parchment made from calfskin and goatskin. Scientists suggest that this may have occurred through interspecies transmission of the virus or contamination during the manufacture of the parchment.
According to the researchers, libraries and archives around the world may contain similar genetic traces of ancient outbreaks of animal diseases. The study's findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

Poland ranked first in the European Union in terms of gas storage levels—as of September 1, its facilities were 93.5% full. LRT reports this, citing polskieradio.pl, writes UNN.

Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:07:23 BST
08:07:23 KST

Germany's far-right AfD bids for first taste of power in eastern vote
- Published
Germany is holding its breath this weekend as there is a seismic election in the country's east.
The Alternative für Deutschland party is aiming to secure a majority in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt.
An outright win would mark the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in the nation's post-war era.
For the AfD's opponents, this is a point of serious peril. But the party sees it as a stepping stone towards its dreams of nationwide power.
This is an election that could change German history.
The result could also spell fresh trouble for embattled conservative (CDU) Chancellor Friedrich Merz, as rumours persist about whether he can see out his term in office.
Booed during recent public appearances, Merz is hardly seen as an electoral asset.
Perhaps the chancellor regrets a pledge to halt the rise of the far right, given that the exact opposite has happened.
By contrast, the charismatic AfD lead candidate in the state - Ulrich Siegmund - appears to have enjoyed dominating discussion and media coverage.
Dubbed "Germany's Most Dangerous Man" by Der Spiegel magazine, he has brushed off reports that people previously in the neo-Nazi scene are among those to hold influential roles around him.
The 35-year-old can often be seen, including in his own many social media posts, amongst adoring crowds or happily riding a retro East German scooter.
A lingering nostalgia for the past, alongside an acute dissatisfaction with the present, has fed the party's popularity in its eastern strongholds.
Voters voice frustration with immigration, public safety, Germany's struggling economy, high energy costs and aid being sent abroad to countries like Ukraine.
Some people I have spoken to passionately believe that the AfD is offering a real chance for radical change - and say Ulrich Siegmund has given them hope.
Other supporters are less certain, but say they have lost faith with mainstream parties that have dominated politics for decades.
An AfD lawmaker once told me that if they got a shot at regional government, then people would see the "sky won't fall in".
Some of the movement's detractors may disagree. Its plans, for Saxony-Anhalt, are highly controversial within Germany.
The party wants to segregate child refugees into special classes: "The refugee children should be given the message that their stay in Germany is only temporary."
The manifesto claims that "sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles" have been aggressively promoted over "normal family" structures.
LGBT rainbow flags should be banned from being flown at schools, the party argues, while children should be taught less about the Nazis and more about positive aspects of German history.
On immigration, a task-force would be set up as part of plans to detain and deport migrants who no longer have the right to be in the state, while the party also calls for an end to "illegal, culturally alien" mass migration.
The AfD's pro-Russia sympathies have also sparked claims that it cannot be trusted with sensitive intelligence. When a Russian army mug was spotted in the office of leading AfD figure Hans-Thomas Tillschneider in Saxony-Anhalt, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".
That was as Berlin, this week, publicly blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. The Kremlin has denied involvement.
Meanwhile, German security sources have warned that Russian-backed disinformation campaigns, often against AfD rivals, have been escalating - something Moscow's representatives describe as "anti-Russian hysteria".
State-level governments hold significant powers over areas including local education, policing and culture, while their delegates sit in the federal government's second chamber – the Bundesrat.
An AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt would be able to implement changes locally and gain a louder voice on the national stage.
The party remains strongest in the former communist east Germany but it is also leading the polls nationwide.
That is despite warnings that it has morphed from a Eurosceptic party, founded in 2013, into one that flirts with, or attracts, extremist support.
At one AfD rally, we saw a man wearing a T-shirt that read Arisch - the German word for Aryan that the Nazis used to promote their false theories of a master race.
We do not know whether the man was a party supporter, a member or merely an attendee. He would not talk to us.
Saxony-Anhalt is one of several states where the party is officially classed as right-wing extremist.
Domestic intelligence charges the local branch with being infused by a "racist ideology" and anti-constitutional aims.
The AfD, which says it is a conservative, libertarian movement, dismisses these designations as politicised smears and rejects any comparisons with National Socialism.
Ulrich Siegmund has not ruled out getting rid of domestic intelligence (BfV) in the state if the AfD wins a majority.
Other parties won't go into coalition with the AfD, as part of what is known as the Brandmauer or firewall that keeps the far right from government.
That is why it must seek a parliamentary majority in order to be sure of securing power.
In Saxony-Anhalt, it is no longer about creating cracks in the firewall but rather trying to bypass it altogether.
Pulling that off will likely depend on whether other, smaller parties get enough votes in order to pass a 5% threshold that allows them to enter parliament.
Politics is maths and Germany is no different, even if the maths can be quite convoluted.
But if the AfD does score a decisive victory, then a party that uses anti-establishment rhetoric to grow its support will face a test it has never faced before.
Grievances could still be laid at the door of the federal government in Berlin, but the AfD would no longer solely be able to rail against those in office because it would be in office itself.
Saxony-Anhalt may be a relatively small state, by population, but it is about to host one hell of an election.

EXPLAINER - How the White House turned its deportation policies into online arcade games
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
23:03:14 UTC
08:03:14 KST

“Build the Wall.” “Rio Run.” “Supply Line.” “Flappy Bill.” “Trump Savings Tycoon.”
On the White House website, they are the names of five games in which players stack bricks against a border “horde,” round up pixelated migrants, remove unhealthy food from school lunch lines, keep legislation in the air and catch money for children’s savings accounts.
Behind the deliberately nostalgic graphics are policies, parts of which have faced declining public support, with real consequences for migrants, families and children, cast as targets in a game to capture and points to accumulate.
The online “Arcade,” launched Thursday, packages parts of US President Donald Trump’s political agenda as low-resolution entertainment, drawing criticism from a state lawmaker and social media users who say the administration is trivializing immigration enforcement and stripping it of its human cost.  
How are migrants depicted?
Two of the games focus directly on Trump’s border and deportation policies.
“Build the Wall,” presented with “Zombie Border Siege” imagery, copies the mechanics of Tetris. Players arrange falling blocks to construct a barrier while the game instructs them to “protect the border from the coming horde.”
“Rio Run” adapts the Snake format, placing a pixelated likeness of Trump’s border czar, Tom Homan, on a grid representing the Rio Grande. Players direct the character toward people depicted as border crossers, collecting them one by one while being warned not to double back.
The migrants, shown as small figures with different skin tones, effectively become collectibles in a game built around an administration policy that has resulted in mass arrests, detention and deportation.
The other titles give similar treatment to domestic initiatives.
“Supply Line” asks players to knock products containing seed oils, coloring or additives off a school-food conveyor belt under the banner of the administration’s “Make America Healthy Again” campaign.
In “Flappy Bill,” a bald eagle carries legislation through obstacles above Washington’s monuments, while “Trump Savings Tycoon” has players swing a net at falling cash and gold bars to fund “Trump Accounts,” the administration’s investment program for children born during Trump’s second term.
The White House promoted the arcade through videos imitating the loading screens of major gaming consoles, including one that transformed the Sega logo into “MAGA,” an abbreviation of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan.
It later posted “CAN’T STOP WINNING” on X alongside a link to the games. 
How popular are the policies behind the games?
The arcade also arrives as public support for Trump’s immigration agenda has weakened, particularly over deportations.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published in February found that 38% of Americans approved of Trump’s handling of immigration, down from 50% shortly after he returned to the White House.
Polling by the Pew Research Center has shown a similar shift on deportations.
In February 2025, 44% of Americans said the Trump administration was doing “too much” to deport immigrants living in the US illegally. By April 2026, that figure had risen to 52%.
Over the same period, the share saying the administration was doing “about the right amount” fell from 47% to 31%. 
Why has the arcade drawn criticism?
The arcade was launched as Trump faces criticism over rising living costs and the economic fallout from the war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy and fertilizer supplies through the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Connecticut state Sen. Matt Lesser pointed to the contrast between the website and the financial pressure facing households, noting that heating-oil prices were near record levels while the administration offered a game featuring Homan.
“Heating oil is near an all-time high but hey you can play Border Czar Tom Homan in a video game. #outoftouch,” Lesser wrote on X.
Adam Cochran, a professor, policy consultant and independent journalist, described the launch on X as “a pathetic and shameful moment in American history.”
The White House defended its approach as a way to communicate Trump’s record and contrast its culture of “fun and winning” with its political opponents. A White House official made the remarks to the Washington Examiner.

Judge again halts USPS mail ballot plan as Trump administration seeks Supreme Court relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:58:11 UTC
07:58:11 KST

Judge again halts USPS mail ballot plan as Trump administration seeks Supreme Court relief
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A federal judge again blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enforcing President Trump’s sweeping new mail ballot rules.
- California has led the legal charge against the rules, arguing they could cause chaos and disenfranchise millions of voters.
- Judge Indira Talwani’s ruling follows a whistleblower’s claims that USPS is rushing out untested and flawed computer systems to implement the new rules.
A federal judge again Friday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from enacting President Trump’s sweeping new mail ballot rules for the November election, finding that the Postal Service lacks such authority over elections and that neither it nor states such as California are capable of implementing the changes without causing chaos and disenfranchising voters.
U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani noted that election officials from across the country told the court that it is “likely impossible” to comply with the rules, which “makes disenfranchisement more than likely, if not probable” if the Postal Service were to proceed with them.
Talwani’s order — her latest of several halting the plan this summer — came after a Postal Service whistleblower alleged the agency’s new computer systems for the project are fundamentally flawed, a top Postal Service official acknowledged a key online portal was unfinished and the Trump administration filed an emergency petition asking the U.S. Supreme Court to allow the plans to proceed anyway.
All this unfolded this week as some of the first mail ballots of the election cycle started to go out.
The new rules — which Trump required in a March executive order — would require states to submit complete voter lists to the Postal Service and to adopt new ballot envelopes with individualized voter bar codes designed by the Postal Service, and empower the Postal Service to reject any mail ballots that don’t match those lists.
Trump’s executive order also required the Department of Homeland Security to develop its own lists of eligible citizen voters, ostensibly to be compared against the state lists.
Trump has said the changes are necessary to combat widespread voter fraud, including by noncitizens, though independent election experts say there is no evidence that such fraud exists in large numbers.
The effort is part of the implementation of President Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting and has been temporarily halted by a federal judge. The ruling is being appealed by the administration and the directive may ultimately end up back before the U.S. Supreme Court.
Leading Democrats and elections officials in California and other states say the new rules constitute an unlawful federal overreach into state-run elections and a thinly veiled effort by the Trump administration to suppress the vote in a midterm election the GOP is expected to lose.
Talwani, an appointee of President Obama, agreed, finding that the states and voting rights groups are likely to succeed in their claims that the U.S. Constitution reserves the right to regulate elections to the states and Congress — not the executive branch.
Talwani issued her order after holding a contentious hearing in federal court in Boston on Thursday, where she questioned the Postal Service and the dozen conservative-led states supporting it on their ability to implement the changes in time for the Nov. 3 elections. She also heard from California, other liberal-led states and voting rights groups that it would be impossible.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, whose office is helping lead the states’ challenge, hailed Talwani’s order as a crucial reprieve.
“We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” Bonta said in a statement to The Times. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.”
Bonta’s office also criticized Department of Justice attorneys for rushing to the Supreme Court before Talwani could issue her order or the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals could weigh in on an appeal the department had already filed on the matter.
Walter Garcia, a Bonta spokesperson, said the Justice Department had “flouted standard procedural rules” by approaching the high court before the lower courts had weighed in, despite the fact that the Postal Service acknowledged Thursday that it was not ready to launch its new portal.
“It defies common sense that they would seek emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court when USPS is unprepared to implement the rule now,” Garcia said.
State law requires that all registered voters be sent a ballot in the mail, and more than 80% of California voters have used those ballots to vote in recent elections.
President Trump has spent months waging an unusually aggressive campaign to reshape how states run elections.
In its emergency petition to the Supreme Court, the Trump administration argued that an earlier temporary restraining order by Talwani to halt the new rules from taking effect was “baseless” and would cause “serious irreparable harm” to the federal government, states and voting public.
“To forestall those harms and protect the public interest, this Court should grant an immediate stay, making clear to States that they should begin efforts to comply if they have not done so already,” wrote Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer.
The swirl of litigation has created uncertainty around the Nov. 3 election. It also reflects the Trump administration’s desperate race to get the lower court orders lifted and the new rules implemented in time for that election — the rushed nature of which was a prime focus of the whistleblower.
The unidentified Postal Service employee alleged in a statement released Tuesday by congressional Democrats and submitted in court by Bonta’s office that the agency has been rushing to implement the changes — in defiance of an earlier court order — using “an entirely new and untested set of IT systems” that could cause “catastrophic problems” and disenfranchise millions of voters nationwide.
The Postal Service in a statement Friday said that while its system was developed on an “accelerated schedule,” quality and security standards “were not compromised,” and the agency stands behind “both the rigor of our process and the resulting system.”
At Thursday’s hearing, Talwani appeared frustrated when a Justice Department attorney was unable to tell her the status of the portal.
In a subsequent declaration hours later, Steven W. Monteith, the Postal Service’s chief customer and marketing officer, said officials were still making “refinements” to the portal, but anticipated being able to make it available “for voluntary use by sometime next week.”
Talwani previously issued an order blocking the Postal Service changes from being implemented in California and more than 20 other states suing in June. The Trump administration appealed that decision to the 1st Circuit, which declined to lift it, and then on an emergency basis to the U.S. Supreme Court. In early August, Talwani issued a second ruling for the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups, blocking the changes nationwide.
On Aug. 24, the Supreme Court set aside Talwani’s order in the states’ case, finding that the states’ challenge was essentially premature because the Postal Service had yet to formally initiate the changes or require state compliance. However, the court explicitly noted that it was not reaching any conclusions as to the legality of the pending rules themselves. “On that score, time will tell,” it said.
The states and voting rights groups promptly filed new lawsuits challenging the legality of the rules, which the Postal Service formally issued Aug. 21. And it is in those cases that Talwani issued her ruling Friday.
She wrote that the voting rights groups had standing to challenge the Postal Service rules nationwide in part because the “chaos” created by the rules’ stiff deadlines significantly interfered with their mission to provide voters with accurate and reliable information about how to vote — and whether to use mail ballots to do so.
David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, said in remarks prior to Talwani’s Friday order that he was “very, very confident” that the Postal Service changes will be blocked for the upcoming elections, and that “mail voting is going to go forward as conveniently and securely as it always has.”
That’s in part because election officials nationwide are “telling the courts that even if they wanted to, they could not implement it,” he said — including in a legal filing Becker helped nearly 100 local elections officials from red and blue states file in separate litigation challenging the rules.

Mock Republican convention website tops Google, redirects to Epstein files
Democratic lawmakers poke fun at prank website, while Republicans slam ‘fake news’ and redirect users to real one.
A mock website that directs users to the Epstein Files appears to be the primary search result on Google for the Republican Party’s upcoming midterm convention in Dallas, Texas.
For hours on Friday, the website gopdallas2026.com soared to the top of the search results, with preview text that offered viewers the chance to “discover details about the 2026 RNC [Republican National Committee] Midterm Convention”.

Democratic lawmakers used the prank to revive discussion of the Epstein Files, which has been a long-running source of criticism for the administration of President Donald Trump, a speaker at the two-day convention.

Some critics have pointed out that certain records published by the Justice Department appear unnecessarily redacted, while others reveal the identities of victims.
Trump has also faced scrutiny for his personal relationship with Epstein, which he says ended decades ago.
There has long been speculation, however, that powerful figures in Epstein’s orbit turned a blind eye to his crimes. He was convicted in 2008 of soliciting a minor, and he faced sex-trafficking charges at the time of his death in 2019. His victims are thought to number in the hundreds.

The centre of the website prompted users to input their contact information to “get exclusive updates”.
But, in small text at the bottom, the website included a caveat that it was not the official source for information related to the midterm convention.
“This website is an independent informational resource and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by the Republican National Committee (RNC), the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention, the American Airlines Center, or any official convention entity,” it said.
“For official convention information, please visit the appropriate official websites.”
This month’s event is the first-ever midterm convention hosted by the Republican Party.
It is slated to take place from September 9 to 10. A press release from the Republican National Committee indicates that the event is expected to be the party’s largest convention since 2016.
Trump is reportedly slated to speak on both nights, as he tries to rouse enthusiasm for his party ahead of the November midterm elections.
Republicans hope to hold onto their majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate as Trump’s popularity slides to new lows amid continued fallout from the war on Iran.
“Never before in history has any major party held a midterm convention, and President Trump wants to focus in on that and open this up to the American people, because all of his work has been about improving their lives,” RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft said in an interview with CBS Texas.
Democrats, however, held national midterm party conferences in 1974, 1978 and 1982.

Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:42:39 UTC
07:42:39 KST

Chants, applause, and hundreds of supporters: A report from the Moscow courthouse where children’s hospice founder Lida Moniava faced a charge of spreading ‘fakes’ about the Russian military
On the evening of September 3, Simonovsky Court placed Lida Moniava, founder of Dom s Mayakom (“Lighthouse Charity Foundation”), under a set of restrictions in a criminal case accusing her of spreading “fake” information about the Russian military. Moniava is one of the leading figures in contemporary Russian philanthropy: she founded the Dom s Mayakom charity and its hospices for children with severe and incurable illnesses. Dozens of people came to Simonovsky Court in Moscow to support her. The news outlet Bereg recounts what happened — and shows how Moniava’s supporters celebrated her release. Meduza is translating the report in full.
A hearing on pretrial restrictions for Lida Moniava, founder of the Lighthouse Charity Foundation, is scheduled for 5 p.m. on September 3. A full hour before the hearing, Muscovites who have come to support Moniava are already gathering outside the Simonovsky Court building.
Police searched Moniava’s home early on the morning of August 2 as part of a criminal case over spreading “fake” information about the Russian military, then arrested her. The case stems from a post Moniava published on her Telegram channel to mark the first anniversary of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “For a year now, my country has been sending missiles, tanks, and soldiers into Ukraine. For a year now, innocent people have been dying because of it,” she wrote.
A short young woman named Nadezhda stands in the parking lot reserved for official vehicles directly in front of the courthouse. She is visibly nervous. She introduces herself as Moniava’s goddaughter.
“I’m waiting for justice. If someone like Lida is sent to prison, something truly terrible will happen to the world,” Nadezhda says.
A mixed crowd gradually gathers by the parking lot: young people who might be described as part of the alternative scene, middle-aged people, and elderly members of the support group. Some call themselves Moniava’s friends and acquaintances; others, like red-haired Makar, dressed all in black, learned about her from recent news coverage.
“When I read about Lida, I realized she’s just an incredibly good person — kind, with the noblest intentions,” Makar tells the independent Russian outlet Bereg. “Of course, it’s a real shame things turned out this way.”
Makar says he is trying not to get his hopes up that the charges against Moniava will be dropped or that she will be released from custody, “so I don’t end up disappointed.”
Mikhail, an acquaintance of Moniava’s, is also there to support her. He speaks about her much as dozens of others have in Facebook posts supporting her over the past day.
“I admire what she does, what she stands for, and the fact that she’s open about it. That’s genuinely brave,” Mikhail says. “You can do charity work and still be a conformist because you think charity makes up for everything. But Lida did good work without becoming a conformist just to keep doing it.”
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moniava stayed in the country and continued helping children with incurable illnesses. She also set up a fund to help refugees from Ukraine and Nagorno-Karabakh, as well as residents of the Kursk region’s border areas affected by the Ukrainian military’s incursion in August 2024.
While helping people affected by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Moniava also wrote antiwar posts on Facebook. In February 2026, Russian authorities fined her 45,000 rubles for “discrediting” the Russian military over those posts. She wrote about children killed in a Russian missile strike on Kryvyi Rih and the deaths of the Martynenko family — a father, a mother, and their 11-year-old son — in a strike on Sumy.
After the February hearing at which a judge imposed the fine, Moniava thanked her followers for their support and said in a post that she had “received a lot of advice to leave Russia”:
When Center E is banging on your apartment door, it’s scary, of course. But look at this photo — Anya and I are having such a great time on our shift [at the hospice]. She’s a girl who spent 19 years behind the walls of a residential institution. If I leave, children in palliative care will spend more time in residential institutions and intensive care units. I doubt I could live happily in some other country knowing that. So emigration isn’t in the plans.
In the same post, Moniava added: “I also can’t stay silent as if there’s no war. Trying to live honestly comes first for me.”
Natalya, who came to Simonovsky Court, does not know Moniava personally but has long followed her work. “I’m just in shock over what’s happening,” she says. “It’s probably to be expected, but it’s still very hard for me to accept. I’m an outsider looking on, and I simply respect her work, so I came here to support her. Lida is a wonderful person who helps others live and survive. That’s very important in our world. In turbulent times, we need to support each other somehow and do something.”
Others who came to support the Dom s Mayakom founder included Nobel laureate Dmitry Muratov, former editor-in-chief of the independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta; Nyuta Federmesser, founder of the Vera Fund, which helps people with incurable illnesses; actress Tatyana Drubich, co-chair of the same fund; and Daniil Maksimov, a Vera Fund employee and founder of an inclusive magazine about sex for people with disabilities.
Maksimov, a blogger, writes on social media about living with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and the problems wheelchair users face. Several people in motorized wheelchairs gathered outside Simonovsky Court on the day of Moniava’s hearing.
The Lighthouse Charity Foundation needs support. In recent days, it has lost many donations and some of its donors. You can donate from Russia in rubles on the foundation’s website.
Shortly before 5 p.m., a prison transport van parked outside the courthouse pulls away. By now, around 200 people have gathered. Someone in the crowd says, “This one’s probably leaving now, and the next one will have Lida in it.” When another prison van drives onto the court grounds soon afterward, people start chanting, “Lida! Lida!”
The van’s barred windows make it impossible to see who is inside. The van pulls into the garage.
People line up to enter the courthouse, and the line moves very slowly. One woman in a blue jacket stands out among the crowd, holding a copy of Viktor Vilisov’s book Nas Vsekh Toshnit (We’re All Sick to Our Stomachs) with a bright orange cover. Off to one side stands Yekaterina Duntsova, head of the Rassvet (“Dawn”) party; somewhere in the same crowd are Tatyana and Valery Yashin, the parents of convicted politician Ilya Yashin, who was sent to Germany in a prisoner exchange.
“So many people showed up. This is a really high-profile case,” someone in the crowd says.
“Yeah, this isn’t Remeslo.”
Forty minutes later, the line still has not cleared. Two young men carrying tripods come out of the courthouse toward the line. Someone in the crowd asks hopefully:
“So, any news?”
“No, nothing at all.”
It is a little after 5 p.m. when Nyuta Federmesser, who had entered the courthouse near the front of the line, comes back outside. “Lida hasn’t arrived yet,” she says. “We came down because it’s impossible to breathe in there. There’s no point in standing here anymore because they’ll start kicking everyone out soon. The court closes at 6 p.m.”
Some of those who came are in no hurry to leave, even though it is very stuffy inside. Dmitry Muratov takes a spot right by the courtroom entrance. One woman who came to support Moniava offers people postcards to write warm messages on, which will later be delivered to Moniava. A police officer comes upstairs and asks everyone to leave the building: the court has closed for the day.
Everyone heads down to the courtyard, which is packed with people. In the middle, a group shares a pie. Police soon drive everyone out of the courtyard as well, and the gates close. Now everyone waits for Moniava by the fence.
Traffic police officers watch the crowd from cars with their emergency lights on. One of them approaches the crowd. What he says is familiar from rallies and pickets:
“Citizens, do not obstruct the passage of other citizens!”
“We’ve heard that one before,” a woman over 60 says. “I’m so sick of you!”
Word eventually spreads that Moniava has been brought to the courthouse after all and that the hearing has begun. The press is not allowed to attend.
“I know Lida personally,” says Fatima, who came to Simonovsky Court to support her. “Lida is a wonderful person. She’s done a lot in our country to help children with severe and incurable illnesses, and she built a palliative care system. Of course, it’s pretty horrifying that she’s inside the Simonovsky Court building at all.”
Neither Fatima nor Mikhail, who respects Moniava for refusing to conform, expects “anything good” to come of the judge’s decision.
Half an hour later, the crowd starts to stir. The courthouse doors open, and two security officers appear in the doorway. Several people start chanting “Lida!” but she is nowhere in sight. A few men come out, followed by a woman. “The workday is over,” someone in the crowd says.
As they wait, someone starts singing, but the words are impossible to make out.
Finally, Moniava’s defense attorney, Mikhail Biryukov, says from inside the courtroom that the court is releasing Moniava from custody and placing her under a “ban on certain activities.” While the investigation continues, she is barred from going outside between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., communicating with witnesses, or using the internet.
Sometime between 8 and 9 p.m., Moniava and Biryukov emerge from the courthouse. The people waiting behind the fence chant Moniava’s name and applaud. Once outside the gates, she tells the crowd: “I thought I was going to get 10 years in prison. Some kind of miracle.”
She says investigators spent “many hours” trying to persuade her to admit guilt: “For some reason, it’s very important that the defendant say they feel guilty. I don’t feel guilty. I want the war to end as soon as possible.”
“Is there anything you want to do right now?” journalists ask Moniava.
“See my friends,” she says with a smile.

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Hurricane Lowell, located several hundred miles south of the Hawaiian Islands, has been rapidly strengthening, prompting Hawaii Governor Josh Green to declare a statewide emergency on Thursday to support preparations for potential impacts from the storm.
Hurricane Lowell has strengthened back to Category 4, with sustained winds of about 240 kilometers per hour and a central pressure of 926 millibars. It was located about 985 kilometers south of Lihue, Hawaii, as of Friday morning local time, according to an update of the U.S. National Hurricane Center on Friday.

The latest forecast track shows Lowell will remain near major hurricane strength as it moves closer to the western Hawaiian Islands late Monday and Monday night. Weather impacts such as high surf and heavy rain may extend hundreds of miles from the center of Hurricane Lowell, according to the NWS.
Green signed an emergency proclamation on Thursday covering the entire state to support preparations for and potential impacts from Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina, Tropical Storm Marie and any additional storms that could affect Hawaii.
The proclamation allows state and county agencies to mobilize personnel, equipment and resources more quickly as Hawaii continues recovering from Tropical Cyclone Lala.
"This proclamation gives our agencies and counties the flexibility to move people, equipment and resources quickly so we can protect communities across every island. We encourage everyone to remain prepared and continue following official weather updates," Green said. ■

U.S. measles cases surpass 3,000 as vaccination coverage declines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
06:38:49 CST
07:38:49 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- The United States had recorded 3,134 confirmed measles cases this year as of Thursday, with the nationwide total continuing to rise amid declining childhood vaccination coverage, according to data released Friday by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The figure has already surpassed the 2,289 confirmed cases reported for the whole of 2025. The 2026 total is the highest annual number recorded in the United States since 1991, according to the CDC.
Of the cases reported this year, 3,118 were identified across 47 U.S. jurisdictions, while 16 were among international visitors. A total of 248 people have been hospitalized, accounting for about 8 percent of confirmed cases, and 38 measles outbreaks have been reported so far this year.
About 94 percent of confirmed cases involved people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, the CDC said. The agency recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine as the best protection against measles.
The CDC said measles vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell to 92.4 percent in the 2025-2026 school year, down from 95.2 percent in the 2019-2020 school year. About 280,000 kindergartners did not have documentation of completing the MMR vaccine series.
The agency has said that when more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity. ■

In Germany, production of thousands of long-range drones for Ukraine has begun—one of them can strike at a distance of 1,500 km

01:37:01 EEST

In Germany, production of thousands of long-range drones for Ukraine has begun—one of them can strike at a distance of 1,500 km
Kyiv • UNN
Auterion Airlogix will produce 5,000 drones for Ukraine by 2027. Anubis has a range of up to 1,500 km and a 40–50 kg warhead.
The American-German-Ukrainian company Auterion Airlogix has launched serial production of 5,000 Anubis and Seth-X drones for the Defense Forces of Ukraine. This was reported by Defense Express, according to UNN.
Details
Production was launched at a plant near Munich. The contract is worth approximately €300 million, with funding provided by the German government. The order is planned to be completed by mid-2027.
Under the joint project, Auterion is responsible for the software, while the Ukrainian company Airlogix is responsible for the hardware of the drones.
What is known about Anubis and Seth-X
Anubis belongs to the class of long-range strike drones. According to Defense Express, it has a range of up to 1,500 km and a warhead weighing 40–50 kg. The company also emphasizes that the drones are adapted to operate in conditions of intensive use of electronic warfare systems.
Less is known about the Seth-X. It is designed to engage personnel, lightly armored vehicles and logistics vehicles at medium range.
Both models have already been documented in use by Ukrainian military personnel. Anubis has appeared in official materials from the Unmanned Systems Forces, as well as in photos from the Russian side.
In the future, the company plans to open another plant in eastern Germany. According to Defense Express, the project will provide Ukraine with an additional production line for strike drones, while giving Germany the opportunity to strengthen its own defense-industrial potential at the same time.
