Breadcrumb
US and allies want IAEA board to report Iran to UN Security Council, diplomats say
The US and its allies Britain, France and Germany are pushing other countries on the UN nuclear watchdog's board to pass a resolution next week reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, diplomats said on Friday.
If passed, the resolution would follow up on one adopted on June 12 of last year declaring Iran in breach of its non-proliferation obligations for not fully cooperating with an investigation into uranium traces found at undeclared sites.
Israel started bombing Iran's nuclear facilities the next day, soon joined by the United States, destroying or badly damaging Iran's uranium-enrichment plants.
Iran has not let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors return to the bombed sites since then or verify what remains of its stocks of enriched uranium, some of which was enriched to up to 60% purity, a short step from weapons grade.
A resolution by the IAEA's 35-nation board reporting Iran to the Security Council would also be the culmination of a standoff over IAEA access to those sites, since the board has passed two resolutions in the past year demanding Iran declare its enriched uranium stocks and grant the IAEA full access to verify them.
A draft text for the resolution has yet to be formally submitted to the board and negotiations between countries over the exact wording are ongoing, diplomats said. A draft is usually formally submitted early in the week of a board meeting.
As a party to the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), Iran has the right to develop nuclear technology, including enrichment, for peaceful purposes. Iran says it would never produce nuclear weapons.
It is, however, the only country to enrich to 60% without making a bomb. The amount it has enriched to that level is "a matter of serious concern" to the IAEA.
The IAEA believes well over 200 kg of that highly enriched uranium has survived the bombardments and is held in a tunnel complex at Isfahan and at the Natanz facility.

Details
Milei said that the Falkland, or Malvinas, Islands, as they are called in Argentina, belong to his country "by history and law." In addition, he announced the acceleration of sanctions against foreign oil companies operating near the islands without Buenos Aires’ permission.
The impetus for the renewed activity surrounding Argentina’s claims came from Trump’s remarks. Responding to journalists’ questions about a possible review of the U.S. position on the Falklands, the American president said that he was "reviewing every position" and that this issue was one of many.

Milei attached considerably greater significance to these remarks, saying that Washington was reviewing its "historical position" regarding the islands.
Trump may be pressuring Britain over Iran

What Sputnik couldn’t do to American science, Beijing has
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
21:30:04 UTC
06:30:04 KST

The US government owns 9.9 per cent of Intel, converted out of US Chips Act grants, alongside a golden share in US Steel, US$400 million in the rare earth mining firm MP Materials and stakes in roughly 30 firms worth US$26.7 billion. In 2025, Nvidia and AMD gave up 15 per cent of their China chip sale revenues in exchange for export licences. The country that spent four decades advising its allies against picking winners now runs a portfolio.
The United States has not fully turned to state capitalism, but it has accepted something it resisted for 80 years. Technological leadership is a security objective in its own right, pursued with the instruments of security policy rather than an economic advantage that pays security dividends.
The National Security Science and Technology Strategy, unveiled on August 18 and the first such document bearing this name since Bill Clinton’s in 1995, is where that proposition appears in writing. Most of it reads as such documents often do. Then comes a sentence that gives away the game: the US should avoid contests where capable adversaries can readily counter its moves and should not spend on replicating what a rival has already built better.
Countries do not redraw the board while they are winning. Washington has adopted the tactics of a fighter with reach who declines to trade blows in the clinch: keep it long, concede the inside, win where your arms are. That is rational enough, and also what fighters do once they have felt their opponent’s power.
The rest of the document follows from that concession. Foreign investment, firms and personnel touching American research face tighter scrutiny, though a presidential memorandum had already turned the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US against Chinese money in strategic sectors in February 2025. Research security has gone from a compliance chore to a branch of statecraft. Three domains are ring-fenced for battlefield advantage – undersea, space, artificial intelligence and autonomy – above an enabling technologies list running through hypersonics, directed energy, semiconductors and nuclear energy.
The strategy document reaches furthest into American life through alignment. Agencies are steered towards milestone contracts with competing vendors, told to place federal money where it complements private capital rather than crowding it out, and to expedite clearances so expertise moves between laboratory, firm and department at commercial speed. The universities enter the same architecture through vetting.

Part of Saint Sophia of Kyiv Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Damaged in Russian Drone Attack
Unknown

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Part of Saint Sophia of Kyiv Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Damaged in Russian Drone Attack
A Russian drone in central Kyiv on September 4 caused damage to the 18th-century Consistory Building, also known as the Khlibnya, within the National Sanctuary Complex of Saint Sophia of Kyiv.
A blast wave shattered several windows and destroyed interior glass vestibules, according to LB.ua.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The main cathedral structure, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, sustained no initial visible damage, though specialists will conduct a thorough inspection. No staff members were injured during the incident, as everyone reached shelter in time.
Sanctuary director Nelya Kukovalska confirmed that management is looking for restoration funds, noting that offers for assistance have come in from colleagues and UNESCO representatives in Ukraine.
Originally constructed between 1722 and 1730 to serve as a bakery for the Saint Sophia Monastery, the Consistory Building was repurposed for ecclesiastical administration and court facilities after the monastery closed.
Modern modifications included a new wing built along Volodymyrska Street between 1851 and 1853 under architect Pavlo Sparro, followed by additional alterations from 1884 to 1886 by Volodymyr Nikolayev.
Although earlier alterations stripped the structure of its original Baroque appearance, restoration efforts between 1976 and 1984 partially restored its historical forms, and the building currently serves as the Khlibnya exhibition halls.
“We will look for funds for restoration. I don't know where yet. Many people are offering help — colleagues, the UNESCO office in Ukraine. We will make use of it,” said Kukovalska.
At least 7 people were injured in the broader central area attack, with 6 requiring hospitalization. The strike hit an SBU security service building situated across the street from the sanctuary grounds.
This marks the second time the complex has suffered damage from Russian air strikes. An earlier attack during the night of June 10, 2025, damaged the 11th-century Saint Sophia Cathedral in Kyiv when a blast wave caused part of the cornice on its main apse to collapse. Former Ukrainian Minister of Culture Mykola Tochytskyi stated that the strike hit the heart of Ukraine’s identity, targeting a sacred site that had withstood centuries and symbolized the birth of Ukrainian statehood.
Russia has previously been linked to attacks on Ukrainian civilians and cultural sites. On February 16, Ukraine’s Office of the Prosecutor General identified senior commanders from Russia’s Black Sea Fleet as suspects in the missile strike on Lviv and the nearby UNESCO buffer zone on July 6, 2023.
The investigation determined that the strike involved 3M-14 Kalibr sea-launched cruise missiles fired from submarines and surface ships of the Black Sea Fleet, which were on combat duty in the region at the time. One missile hit a residential area, killing nine civilians and causing significant damage to buildings, vehicles, and other civilian infrastructure.

Senior aides to U.K.'s Nigel Farage step down in scandal over undercover report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Senior aides to U.K.'s Nigel Farage step down in donation scandal where reporter posed as wealthy American's son
Two senior aides to Nigel Farage, the firebrand leader of the U.K.'s populist Reform party, have stepped down after the party was accused of breaking British electoral law concerning foreign funding in the wake of an investigative news report where a journalist posed as a wealthy American's son who wanted to donate to the party.
In a statement, a spokesperson for the party said it was launching an internal probe after the report aired on Britain's Channel 4 news late Thursday. Two Reform party officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, have left their positions pending the outcome of that investigation, the spokesperson said.
"The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing," the spokesperson said.
Jukes is widely regarded as Farage's right-hand man, with an "innate sense of his boss' instinct," according to CBS News' partner network BBC News. Orr, an influential figure in the British national conservative movement, served as Reform's head of policy until his resignation. He is a theologian and associate professor of the philosophy of religion at the University of Cambridge. Both men denied any wrongdoing.
In an interview with a London radio station early Friday, Farage insisted the party had broken no laws.
"The party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever," Farage told LBC Radio. "However, it is a clear case of entrapment, and they worked at it for a very long time, and they got a couple of our contractors to say things that perhaps should not have been said. And as a result of that, they have been removed this morning and yeah, you know, I'm not happy about it."
Channel 4 stood by the report, with a spokesperson telling BBC News the investigation "has been rigorously verified to ensure accuracy. We would encourage people to watch the investigation in full."
The allegations pile further pressure on Farage just as his party's annual conference was getting underway. It also unfolds against the backdrop of scrutiny over donations linked to the party, including an ongoing parliamentary investigation over a multimillion-pound donation from cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. Farage denies any wrongdoing.
Speaking to CBS News at the party's conference, Zia Yusuf, a spokesperson for domestic affairs, downplayed any immediate blowback the allegations would have on the party's internal operations.
"Look, Reform has had many great people who have helped get us to where we are. And I have no doubt, given the talent pipeline that I do have visibility of, both at parliamentary level, potentially, and beyond it, we will withstand this, and ultimately, ultimately will come out strong on the other side," Yusuf said.
On Thursday night, Channel 4 aired the investigation that it said was carried out by an undercover team of journalists from a group called Verbatim, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting.
The investigation follows one journalist who poses as the British-educated son of a wealthy American businessman from Wyoming, who both appeared eager to support the party, which shares aspects of ideology and policy positions with elements of the MAGA movement, as well as other right-leaning populist movements around the world.
British law regards a permissible donor to a U.K. political party as either a U.K.-registered voter or a company. In the scenario that unfolds in the undercover investigation, the son is a permissible donor, and the father is not.
Secretly filmed footage purports to show the two party aides arranging donations from the undercover journalist to fund the commissioning of a number of political polls. According to Channel 4, the donations added up to 32,500 British pounds, which is about $44,000.
Some of those polls later appeared in news articles for British newspapers such as The Telegraph and the Times of London. The articles, which reflect favorably on the party on issues such as its fortunes in local elections and support among labor union members, do not mention how Reform allegedly commissioned the polls.
Jukes is heard telling the undercover journalist that the donation made a "huge impact" for the party while not "showing up anywhere in public records."
Orr denied Reform's involvement in the polling, saying in a video posted to social media an "independent person had paid an independent pollster." "No money reached Reform UK at all, no donation reached Reform UK at all — whether it was in cash or in kind," he said.
The investigation also includes a discussion between Jukes and the journalist on how to circumvent electoral law to secure a separate foreign donation to the party of 500,000 British pounds, or about $675,000. Channel 4 says that donation was never made.
The investigation culminates in a four-way lunch between the journalist posing as the son of the American businessman, an actor playing the businessman, Jukes and Farage.
During that meeting, Farage appears to have knowledge that the funding for the polls came from the businessman, and does not appear to be concerned when the son proposes the method by which the 500,000-pound foreign donation could reach the party, saying, "Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you."
Jukes released a statement to BBC News calling the report "entrapment over a prolonged period of nearly a year by foreign-funded climate change activists."
"I totally deny any wrongdoing but have stepped back from politics in order to clear my name," Jukes said.
In a statement to Sky News, Orr said, "I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully."
At least two of Reform's opponents, the ruling Labour Party and the centrist Liberal Democrats, have written to the Metropolitan Police, alleging breaches of electoral law.
In a statement to CBS News, the police said it was aware of reporting "involving political party donations" and alleged breaches of British law relating to polling.
The police have not launched an investigation so far, saying it would "assess the matter and any information provided to us."
The U.K.'s Electoral Commission, which regulates party and election finance, confirmed it was in contact with the police.
"The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500," the commission said. "Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."

"Financial institutions continue to find out the hard way that we are serious about Operation Economic Outcast," said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement.
"While we hope no more banks will need to be sanctioned, that ultimately depends on how quickly the international community comes to its senses and ceases support of the murderous Iranian regime," he added.
Bessent had said Tuesday that Washington would likely announce a bank sanction this week and one next week, as it tries to choke off Tehran economically.
He was speaking on the sidelines of a Group of 20 finance leaders' gathering in Asheville, North Carolina, where he also sought to rally support from partners to put pressure on Iran.
Iran has been at war since late February, when the United States and Israel launched a surprise bombing campaign that killed the Islamic republic's supreme leader.
Bessent recently vowed that the United States was declaring an "economic D-Day" on Iran, and warned of harsh consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.

Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level
NEW DELHI: Coal stocks at thermal power plants across the country have fallen to less than half the recommended level, with 50 plants classified as having 'critically low' inventories as on Sept 2 amid high electricity demand and monsoon-led disruptions in supplies, Central Electricity Authority data showed.The plants, with a combined capacity of around 224 GW, had 28.2 million tonnes (MT) of coal as of Wednesday, 48% of the prescribed requirement of 58.7 MT. The available stock is equivalent to about nine days of coal requirement at 85% plant load factor, against the normal requirement of around 19 days.
The plants classified as short on coal stocks have less than 25% of their normative inventories. Coal ministry officials, however, said all critical plants were being monitored by an inter-ministerial team of officials on a day-to-day basis and regular fuel supplies were being provided to them.
Of the 50 plants, 45 are based on domestic fuel
Of the 50 plants, 45 are based on domestic fuel, four are designed for imported coal and one runs on washery rejects.A senior coal ministry official said, "Classification of a thermal power plant as critical is a routine monitoring parameter under norms laid down by CEA. It simply means closer tracking and priority action. These plants are not running out of supply."
Though the normative coal requirement at power plants is calculated at 3.1 MT every day at 85% plant load factor, officials said the actual requirement is around 2.4 MT.
The monsoon sees supply disruptions every year. The situation starts improving from Sept onwards as rains begin to recede.While the power ministry did not respond to requests for a reaction, sources said some coal-fired plants had been asked to defer scheduled maintenance to ensure continuity of electricity generation.

====================================================================================================

When AI Meets Language Class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:53:15 UTC
05:53:15 KST

Why Language Teachers Need a Different AI Conversation
Generative AI tools are increasingly visible in educational spaces, often accompanied by excitement, uncertainty, and uneven guidance. Much of the practical guidance around AI in education emphasizes efficiency, accuracy, and productivity (Case et al., 2025). While this framing may be useful in some contexts, it does not fully reflect the goals of language teaching.
Language education is not only about correctness. It is about meaning-making, voice, identity, relationships, and context. Across ESL, bilingual, and world language classrooms, students learn to communicate with real audiences and make linguistic choices shaped by social and cultural norms. When generative AI enters these classrooms, it raises important pedagogical questions: whose language does AI treat as “correct”? Which voices and varieties are made visible or marginalized? How might AI feedback shape students’ sense of authorship, confidence, and agency as language users?
At the same time, generative AI is already embedded in many students’ everyday language practices beyond school, from drafting messages and translating texts to seeking explanations. Language classrooms therefore offer a meaningful opportunity to engage AI deliberately, helping students learn to question, evaluate, and make informed choices when interacting with AI systems.
This moment invites a different conversation about AI in language education: one that moves beyond tools or productivity claims and instead centers pedagogy, ethics, and equity. Rather than starting with what AI can do, we suggest beginning with language learning goals and the social and ethical commitments educators want students to develop. From there, teachers can consider how AI might be used to expand opportunities for language practice, voice, and critical engagement with meaning.
Our Stance: A Human-Centered Approach to Generative AI
Before discussing specific tools or classroom strategies, we begin with a shared stance: generative AI should be approached as part of a broader pedagogical and ethical ecosystem in language education (Godwin-Jones, 2025). Language learning is fundamentally social, involving interaction, negotiation of meaning, and reflection on how language is used across contexts and communities. Any engagement with AI needs to be grounded in these core purposes.
A human-centered approach begins with instructional intent rather than technological capability. Instead of focusing on what AI can produce, teachers consider what students are meant to learn and practice, such as communicating ideas, shaping messages for different audiences, making strategic language choices, and developing confidence as multilingual or emerging multilingual speakers. From this perspective, generative AI becomes one possible resource among many, and its value depends on how it is designed into learning tasks.
This stance foregrounds teacher agency and professional judgment. Language teachers routinely make decisions about scaffolding, modeling, feedback, and assessment in response to their students and instructional goals. Similar judgment is required when integrating AI, particularly when deciding when its use supports learning and when it may limit opportunities for student engagement or reflection.
Finally, a human-centered stance treats ethical and social responsibility as central to language teaching. Generative AI systems reflect particular language norms and values, shaping whose language is recognized and whose voices are less visible. Questions of equity, representation, ownership, and accountability are therefore inseparable from pedagogy.
Introducing the Position–Design–Enact (PDE) Framework
To move from stance to practice, language teachers need a way to think systematically and flexibly about how generative AI enters their classrooms. Building on a human-centered approach, we propose the position–design–enact (PDE) framework (see Figure 1) to support instructional decision-making that is pedagogically grounded and ethically informed.
The PDE framework consists of four interrelated dimensions. Position refers to how generative AI is situated within the classroom ecology: its relation to students, teachers, and language learning goals. Design focuses on intentional planning, including task structure, timing, and expectations for AI use. Enact centers on what happens in practice as teachers and students interact with AI during instruction. Running through all three dimensions is criticality, which involves sustained attention to language ideologies, representation and bias, authority and agency, and ownership and ethics. These considerations inform how AI is positioned, how tasks are designed, and how classroom interactions unfold.
The PDE framework is not a linear sequence. Decisions about positioning, design, and enactment inform one another and often need to be revisited as contexts and learners change. For this reason, the framework is adaptable across ESL, bilingual, and world language classrooms and can be taken up from different entry points depending on instructional needs.
A P-D-E Centered Critical GenAI Pedagogy for Language Teaching
Figure 1. The PDE Framework for Critical AI Integration
Unpacking the PDE Framework with a Classroom Example
Position: Locating Generative AI in the Classroom Ecology
The first dimension of the PDE framework, position, invites teachers to consider how generative AI is situated within the classroom ecology. Rather than beginning with specific tools or features, positioning focuses on relationships: the relationship between students and language, between teachers and instructional goals, and between AI and the learning environment as a whole.
Positioning involves clarifying what role generative AI plays in relation to language learning. At different points in instruction, AI may function as a source of feedback, a planning support, a model for analysis, or a partner for reflection. What matters is not assigning a fixed role but making that role visible and intentional. How AI is positioned shapes how students interpret its authority, how they engage with feedback, and how responsibility for learning is shared.
For language teachers, positioning is closely tied to instructional purpose. Tools that support noticing patterns in language use may be positioned differently from ones that generate sample texts for discussion. In language classrooms, these decisions are further shaped by students’ linguistic repertoires, proficiency levels, and prior experiences with AI. Thoughtful positioning helps ensure that AI use aligns with learning goals rather than quietly redefining them.
Positioning also involves setting boundaries. Teachers decide when the use of AI is appropriate, when it should be postponed, and when it should be set aside entirely in favor of human interaction. Making these boundaries explicit through classroom norms, task instructions, or classroom conversation helps students understand why AI is used in some contexts and not in others.
In Practice
In this example, the setting is a high school world language classroom. The learning goal is for intermediate-level students to write an informal inquiry email in response to an online roommate advertisement in a target-language-speaking context. With the goal established, the teacher determines how generative AI will function in the lesson. 
In this case, AI is positioned as a writing coach. Its role is to help students notice potential issues in their drafts, explain relevant grammar patterns, and suggest alternative ways to express ideas. With this role defined, appropriate tools can be selected. Most commonly available generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) are suitable for this task, provided they are accessible to students and permitted by school or district policy.
Design: Planning with Critical Awareness
Design focuses on finding appropriate instructional spaces for the role of AI that has already been established through positioning. Once teachers are clear about what AI is meant to do in a lesson, design addresses how and when that role is taken up within learning tasks. This includes decisions about task structure, timing, prompts, and expectations, as well as how AI use is coordinated with other forms of instruction and interaction. Design translates positioning into concrete learning opportunities that support language development. 
Design decisions should always be guided by language-learning objectives and planned with critical awareness. When generative AI is introduced, teachers need to consider what beliefs about language the tool may reinforce (language ideologies); whose cultures, experiences, and knowledge are included or excluded (representation and bias); who is positioned as the expert in the learning process (authority and voice); and who owns the work that is produced (ownerships and ethics). Designing with criticality means anticipating where these issues may shape student learning and intentionally structuring tasks to address them. This can involve adjusting prompts, planning opportunities for discussion and reflection, and creating space for students to question AI output instead of accepting it directly.
In Practice
Following the positioning of AI as a writing coach in a high school world language classroom, the design of the lesson turns to the four critical domains. In this context, generative AI is likely to favor standardized and formal language, given the types of texts it draws on. It may not recognize informal registers, region-specific conventions, or culturally situated ways of writing. There is also a risk that students may treat AI feedback as authoritative, especially when it is delivered with confidence.
These considerations guide several design decisions. AI feedback is not positioned as the sole source of input, so students receive multiple forms of feedback. The lesson is structured to support students in questioning and evaluating AI suggestions, rather than accepting them automatically. Time is also built into the lesson for explicit discussion of language norms and biases, so that students can reflect on how AI treats register, appropriateness, and correctness.
To support these goals, the lesson sequence includes several stages. Students begin by drafting their emails independently and completing a self-evaluation. They then receive AI feedback. As students review this feedback, they complete a structured worksheet that prompts them to consider each suggestion, decide whether to accept it, and explain their reasoning. Peer feedback follows, allowing students to compare perspectives. A whole-class discussion takes place before revision, giving students space to compare feedback sources and reflect on differences. Students revise their writing using insights from all sources, with responsibility for final language choices remaining with the writer.
Enact: When Generative AI Meets Classroom Practice
While positioning and design shape the conditions for AI use, enactment focuses on what happens when generative AI is taken up in everyday classroom practice. It brings attention to classroom moments as they unfold, including how students interpret AI output, how they respond to it, and how teachers adjust instruction in response. Enactment is where planning meets practice and where assumptions about AI use are tested through interaction.
In language classrooms, enactment makes visible how authority and agency circulate during AI-supported activities. Even when AI use is carefully planned and scaffolded, students may still respond to AI feedback in different ways. Some may treat suggestions as authoritative, others may question them, and some may adopt them selectively based on their communicative intentions. These responses are shaped not only by how AI has been positioned and how tasks have been designed but also by students’ prior experiences, language identities, and comfort with risk-taking. Observing and responding to these dynamics is an important part of teaching with AI.
Enactment also brings ethical considerations into classroom practice in concrete ways. Questions of ownership, authorship, and responsibility often emerge as students decide which AI suggestions to accept, revise, or reject. Classroom conversations, peer interaction, and guided reflection can help make these decisions visible. Through these interactions, students articulate their reasoning and develop greater awareness of how AI influences language use and meaning-making.
A key feature of enactment is responsiveness. Teachers observe how students engage with AI and make adjustments during the lesson. This might include pausing to address misconceptions, reframing instructions, or creating additional space for discussion. These in-the-moment decisions often lead teachers to revisit earlier choices about how AI is positioned or how tasks are designed. The enact dimension therefore highlights the ongoing and adaptive nature of teaching with AI.
In Practice
Instruction begins with familiar language-teaching practices. Students examine an authentic roommate advertisement to understand the communicative context and expectations of the task. They then analyze a model response and co-construct a sample email as a class before moving into independent writing. These steps establish a shared understanding of purpose, register, and audience before any AI use occurs.
After students draft their emails and complete a self-evaluation, generative AI is introduced in its previously defined role as a writing coach. Students submit their drafts using a guided prompt and review the AI feedback with the support of a worksheet. As students work through the suggestions, classroom interaction reveals differences in how AI feedback is interpreted. Some students focus closely on surface-level corrections, while others question whether suggested changes fit the informal register of the task. These moments allow the teacher to circulate, listen, and respond by prompting students to explain their reasoning and compare AI suggestions with their original intentions.
Whole-class discussion becomes an important enactment space. Students are invited to share patterns they notice in AI feedback, including instances where suggestions conflict with the norms of informal writing. Discussion also surfaces questions about whose version of correct language AI appears to prioritize and how the types of texts AI draws on may shape its responses. Through guided conversation, students consider when AI feedback is useful for their goals and when it should be questioned or set aside.
Looking Ahead
As generative AI develops rapidly, new tools appear almost every day. Many teachers feel pressure to try these tools or uncertainty about where to begin. This sense of urgency is familiar. Past waves of educational technology have brought similar excitement and overload. There is little doubt that AI will shape teaching and learning in many domains. At the same time, these changes call for a broader human-centered view of what teaching and learning are meant to do (Lu et al., 2025). The PDE framework was developed with this context in mind. It is intended to help language educators orient themselves in a fast-changing landscape without feeling compelled to chase tools or trends. The framework does not promote any specific technology or prescribe a single way of using AI. Instead, it offers a way to approach AI use thoughtfully by grounding decisions in language-learning goals, critical awareness, and professional judgment. 
In this sense, the PDE framework aligns with calls in the field to move beyond simple judgments about whether AI is “good” or “bad” (Tian and Wang, 2025). We believe that the value of AI in language education lies less in the tools themselves and more in how educators use them. The PDE framework offers one way to support this work by keeping criticality and human judgment at the center of language education in this new era.

He serves as associate editor for the International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism and The Modern Language Journal.

Diesel in the US has risen to a historic record, which could make food and goods more expensive
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04

Diesel in the US has risen to a historic record, which could make food and goods more expensive
Kyiv • UNN
The price of diesel in the US has reached a record $5.85 per gallon due to supply disruptions amid the war with Iran. This is increasing transportation costs.
The average price of diesel fuel in the United States has reached a record $5.85 per gallon for the first time amid disruptions to global supplies due to the war with Iran. Higher fuel prices increase transportation costs and could lead to another rise in prices across a wide range of goods. AP reports, UNN writes.
Details
The food sector is under the greatest pressure, as vegetables, meat, and other perishable products require regular transportation, while diesel-powered machinery is widely used in agriculture. More expensive transportation also affects the cost of clothing, cosmetics, furniture, and other goods.
Some companies are already passing the additional costs on to consumers through fees for online orders and parcel delivery. Experts warn that the longer diesel remains expensive, the more strongly this will affect final prices.
Fuel prices surged after the start of the war with Iran
Diesel in the United States now costs nearly 56% more than before the start of the U.S. and Israeli war against Iran at the end of February, when the average price was about $3.76 per gallon.
One of the main reasons was the rise in oil prices caused by supply disruptions in the Middle East and restrictions on tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. On Friday, Brent was trading above $95 per barrel, compared with approximately $70 before the start of the war.
The cost of regular gasoline is also rising—averaging $4.15 per gallon, compared with $3.20 a year earlier. AP notes that high fuel prices could become an additional political problem for Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Italy and the U.S. Renew Their Scientific Collaboration in Washington
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
22:42:42 CEST
05:42:42 KST

On September 2 and 3, the Italian Embassy in Washington hosted the bilateral meeting between Italy and the United States, aimed at strengthening and renewing the long-standing scientific cooperation between the two countries and taking stock of joint initiatives in the fields of fundamental physics and emerging technologies.
                                    
                                       
				      The two-day meeting, held annually, brought together a delegation from the National Institute of Nuclear Physics and U.S. delegations from the Department of Energy (DOE) and the National Science Foundation (NSF), the main federal agencies that fund scientific research in the United States. The discussions addressed numerous topics of interest to the physics community, starting with large accelerators for particle physics research. In particular, the discussions delved into ongoing activities at CERN and potential future collaborations within the Future Circular Collider project, as well as the progress of the Electron-Ion Collider—the future electron-ion collider currently under construction at Brookhaven National Laboratory—for the study of the properties of nuclear matter. Ample attention was also given to neutrino physics, with an update on the DUNE project in the United States and on the future LEGEND experiment for the search for neutrino-less double beta decay, which will be hosted at the INFN’s Gran Sasso National Laboratories. 
     Research in the field of gravitational waves was also discussed, ranging from the current collaborations between the Virgo and LIGO teams to future prospects related to the next generation of observatories, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer. Discussions also focused on the direct search for dark matter, with particular reference to the DarkSide and XENON experiments, housed at the INFN’s Gran Sasso National Laboratories.
                                    
                                       
				     Cooperation between Italy and the United States also extends to emerging technologies: advanced computing, artificial intelligence, high-performance computing, and quantum technologies. During the meeting, the development of quantum computing was discussed, with an update on the project coordinated by Fermilab’s Superconducting Quantum Materials and Systems (SQMS) Center to build a future quantum computer, for which the INFN was the first international partner outside the United States. “Scientific cooperation between Italy and the United States stems from a solid relationship built over time between our research communities,” emphasized Marco Peronaci, Italy’s ambassador to the United States. “In a rapidly evolving field, pooling expertise, infrastructure, and technological capabilities means fostering innovation and creating new opportunities for collaboration between the two countries.”
 “The meeting in Washington was an important opportunity to renew scientific collaboration between Italy and the United States,” stated Antonio Zoccoli, president of the INFN. “There are numerous strategic projects in which our scientific communities are working side by side: from particle physics to neutrino research, from gravitational waves to dark matter, and on to quantum technologies and the new frontiers of computing. This collaboration is based on shared expertise, infrastructure, and projects, to which Italy makes a leading scientific and technological contribution. For the INFN, it is a source of great satisfaction to be able to make the expertise of its community available to these major international programs and, at the same time, to continue building new opportunities for research and innovation with our U.S. colleagues.”

US Army doctor claims 28 troops died from Covid vaccines – Politico
A US Army doctor has testified that she knows of 28 US military deaths caused by Covid-19 vaccines, Politico has reported citing a court deposition. The US government is investigating 2,544 deaths reported following the jabs, the official has said.
Theresa Long, who also serves as an adviser to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., reportedly gave the testimony during an August 14 deposition in a federal court case in Virginia. Neither her testimony nor her role at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) had previously been reported.
Long allegedly said that the 2,544 unverified deaths were reported to the department’s Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS).
Former US President Joe Biden ordered all US military staff to be vaccinated or be discharged from service, resulting in over 9,000 dismissals. After returning to office, President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to offer reinstatement to those who had been discharged for refusing a vaccine.
Mass-produced Covid-19 vaccines using mRNA technology were fast-tracked for deployment. Pharma giants that made billions in profit – Pfizer and Moderna – later acknowledged that their vaccines could, in rare cases, increase the risk of inflammation of the heart muscle.
Long testified for the defense in a lawsuit being heard by District Court Judge Michael Nachmanoff over the dismissal of Terry Adirim as director of the CIA’s Center for Global Health Services. Adirim alleges that the intelligence agency fired her for political reasons, specifically because of her advocacy for Covid-19 vaccination.
Adirim served as acting assistant secretary for health affairs at the Department of Defense during the pandemic. The CIA fired her in April 2025, a move highlighted at the time by several conservative political commentators, including Ivan Raiklin, who is a defendant in the lawsuit. Her termination came about a month before she would have qualified for full federal retirement benefits.
In May 2025, Nachmanoff expressed skepticism about Adirim’s chances of prevailing in the case when he declined to issue an injunction reversing her termination. The CIA has argued that the matter is an ordinary contract dispute.
Kennedy has repeatedly argued that some vaccines have been insufficiently studied and may carry serious side effects. Critics have accused him of promoting anti-vaccine views and argued that they make him unsuitable to serve as health secretary.

Sochi Airport Limits Flights and Rosneft Halts Refueling After Ukrainian Drone Strikes

Sochi Airport Limits Flights and Rosneft Halts Refueling After Ukrainian Drone Strikes
Operations at Sochi International Airport have been severely disrupted following overnight drone strikes, forcing a subsidiary of state oil giant Rosneft to halt aircraft refueling services and prompting strict limits on incoming flights, an independent Russian news outlet ASTRA reported on September 3.
Since September 4, following the Ukrainian strikes, only Lukoil is currently authorized to refuel planes at the major Black Sea hub.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The reliance on Lukoil in Sochi comes as the oil giant faces severe operational strain across Russia due to escalating Ukrainian drone strikes. Just days earlier, Lukoil’s massive LUKOIL-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez refinery in Kstovo—which accounts for up to 11% of Russia’s total gasoline production—was forced to completely halt operations.
According to reports, an August 26 drone attack caused significant damage to multiple primary crude-processing units and a vacuum gas oil hydrotreatment unit, effectively forcing the facility to suspend all refining activities while repairs are carried out.
An official international Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) cited by ASTRA informed pilots that aircraft refueling in Sochi is exclusively being provided by the Lukoil fuel operator due to “technical reasons.” The directive, which requires airlines to confirm refueling availability in advance, remains in effect until September 5 afternoon, according to the independent outlet.
Under normal circumstances, the airport is serviced by both Lukoil-Aero-West and Rosneft-Aero, ASTRA noted, adding that Rosneft has not yet issued an official comment regarding its subsidiary’s suspension.
A separate aviation notice highlighted by ASTRA restricted the airport’s capacity to a maximum of eight landings per hour, explicitly citing “security measures introduced due to the threat of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in the airport area.” Airlines are now required to re-confirm their arrival slots with the airport operator under these heightened restrictions, which remain active until early Saturday morning, ASTRA reported.
The airport disruptions follow Ukrainian drone strikes on local military and energy infrastructure. An OSINT expert for ASTRA determined that an air defense division in Sochi was attacked overnight, resulting in a fire.
While local authorities acknowledged a blaze at a fuel depot that blanketed the resort city in black smoke, ASTRA established that fires actually broke out at two separate facilities—one owned by Rosneft and another by LUKOIL-Yugnefteprodukt—noting that physical anti-drone barriers failed to protect the sites.
In the aftermath of the strikes, Russia’s consumer protection agency, Rospotrebnadzor, began conducting air quality measurements across Sochi, ASTRA reported.
Meanwhile, residents described to the independent outlet the surreal contrast of watching massive fuel fires burning outside their windows while state television broadcast footage of Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin laughing and clapping at a forum.
The disruption in Sochi comes amid record-breaking disruptions across Russia’s civilian aviation network driven by escalating Ukrainian drone operations. Russian airports have previously temporarily shut down 993 times in August alone, a more than 30% increase from July.
An estimated 16,000 Ukrainian drones entered Russian airspace during the month, and from June through August, Russia experienced 2,182 temporary airport shutdowns, already surpassing the 1,923 total closures recorded throughout all of 2025.

le studio d’orphée and the home-studio of new wave director jean-luc godard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:35:26 UTC
05:35:26 KST

Jean-Luc Godard’s Le Studio d’Orphée at Fondazione Prada, Milan
At Fondazione Prada, the fashion house’s home for contemporary art in Italy, there is not one, but two spaces that are dedicated to the late French-Swiss New Wave auteur, Jean-Luc Godard. One is the mirrored Cinema Godard, renamed during the summer of 2023, a year after his passing. The second is Le Studio d’Orphée, a version of his home studio in Rolle, Switzerland, recreated in the Milan exhibition space. Covered in layered Persian rugs, photos tacked to the wall, and a Dyson handheld vacuum tucked in a corner, the space, opened in 2019, is at once home and atelier, editing studio and creative sanctuary.
Just last year, the American filmmaker Richard Linklater’s film Nouvelle Vague came out with a lighthearted retelling of the making of Godard’s debut feature film, Breathless. The 1960 film, memorable for Jean Seberg in the New York Herald Tribune shirt, put the former film critic on the map for his experimental approach to cinema. He went on to pursue over sixty years of filmmaking that resulted in the likes of Contempt (1963), Vivre sa vie (1962), and Pierrot le Fou (1965). His images were striking in their peculiarity, and his ideas could often be challenging. At Fondazione Prada, when they invited actress Juliette Binoche to speak, she reflected on her experience on Hail Mary, or Je vous salue, Marie (1985), in the cinema that held the director’s name. She didn’t shy away from the difficulties around working with the director, while at the same time lauding his impact on modern cinema.
Breathless (1960) put the former film critic on the map for his experimental approach to cinema
Finding Le Studio d’Orphée
Visitors who find time between visiting Fondazione Prada’s Damien Hirst or Louise Bourgeois masterpieces can climb the narrow stairs to the upper floor of the Sud Gallery and enter the intimate space that gave birth to the later works of the nouvelle vague, or French New Wave, icon. Entering the room, you have to pass through a tastefully unkempt room with a fold-out chair, a lamp resting on the table, and a director’s block in mid-swing. The walls have humbly tacked-up photos and other clippings that look as though they were taken out of the plastic sheaths of a photo album.
a look at Le Studio d’Orphée in Milan’s Fondazione Prada
Jean-Luc Godard’s many monitors
Inside the main ‘studio’ there are benches on the back wall where visitors can sit and look onto a version of the home studio once occupied by Jean-Luc Godard. There are two simple wooden tables, pushed up next to each other to create a kind of editing bay. One monitor has a gray mixing interface from updates and updates ago; another shows a film playing. That same video is simultaneously being screened on a larger television that sits on the other side of the room. Here, there’s the opportunity to see Le livre d’image (2018) and nine other short films created by Godard between 1981 and 2008. Le livre d’image was actually created amongst this equipment when it was still in Switzerland, simulating the actual conditions of the artist when he was in the midst of cutting, pasting, and reviewing his work. The space holds fragments of the film, suspending the installation between the real—his studio—and the imagined—a physical display of the inspiration and ideas moving through his mind at the time. This straddle, between a lived and imagined world, is where the studio installation takes its name, referencing the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, where the musician goes to the land of the dead to find his wife.
media readers are precariously stacked on an ornately painted wooden table
The tchotchkes of a home studio
There is an undeniable homeliness to the space. Le Studio d’Orphée looks more to be a salon or a living room, one that collects dust and has been lived in for more years, than a professional production space like those that show up in behind-the-scenes footage for major blockbusters. Fondazione Prada took care to arrange the room such that it looks as though you’re stepping into one of Godard’s days. Media readers are precariously stacked on an ornately painted wooden table. A coat stand holds a month’s accumulation of outerwear. Pencils and paintbrushes look forgotten on a seat. What results is the opportunity to step inside Godard’s world in a way that goes beyond pressing play on one of his films. Though the auteur is gone, you can still inhabit his work in this intimate corner of Milan.

The problem Albanese will have to solve to win friends in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:34:47 UTC
05:34:47 KST

IN BRIEF
- Australia will face challenges meeting Pacific Island security agreements based on climate change, experts warn.
- Vanuatu has criticised Australia's approval of two coal and gas expansion projects during the Pacific Islands Forum.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's efforts to strengthen Pacific ties and influence the world at the United Nations could be compromised by Australia's failure to meet climate change commitments, critics have warned.
Albanese attended the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) in Palau this week, preparing for an Australian-organised climate meeting to be held in Fiji and Tuvalu next month.
The event will take place ahead of the United Nations' climate change conference, COP31, which will be held in Antalya, Türkiye in November.
The meeting, an outcome of Australia's failed bid to host COP31, will include representatives from Antigua and Barbuda, Cabo Verde, Thailand, Maldives, Timor-Leste, Germany, Mexico and South Korea — and focus on the realities of climate change for the Pacific Islands.
During a press conference in Palau this week, Albanese was questioned about the value of the pre-COP31 event, given the low attendance among non-Pacific Islander leaders.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He accused the journalist of being "so disrespectful" to Pacific leaders present.
"It's about bringing Pacific frontline experience to the centre of global deliberations," he said.
"We need to actually have some respect for the process and respect for our Pacific leaders — and Australia has an absolute interest in engaging with the Pacific."
Albanese's attendance at this year's PIF is the start of a string of international events on his calendar, including the UN General Assembly in New York.
Albanese will address the UNGA on 24 September in a bid to secure a non-permanent place on the UN Security Council in 2029-30.
"A seat on the Security Council would give Australia a stronger voice in the decisions that affect our region," Foreign Minister Penny Wong said.
Climate change key to Pacific security
Wesley Morgan, Australian Climate Council fellow and senior research associate at the UNSW's Institute of Climate Risk and Response, said climate change is the "single greatest threat" to the Pacific Islands.
"When it was first raised at the UN Security Council 20 years ago, Pacific countries said climate change is what guns and bombs are to other nations," Morgan said.
He said the key to Australia becoming the region's "security partner of choice" is proper action on climate change.
In 2022, Solomon Islands signed a security deal with China — an act that got "alarm bells ringing in Canberra", Morgan said.
This was the catalyst for Australia signing bilateral agreements with Tuvalu, Naoero, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji.
These agreements outlined climate change targets for Australia, said Morgan.
He said what's stopping Australia from meeting the agreements is that it is one of the world's biggest exporters of coal and gas — and exports are Australia's biggest source of fossil fuel emissions.
However, the Australian government don't recognise or claim responsibility for export emissions — a decision that conflicts with the world's highest court.
Issuing an advisory opinion in 2025, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) "said explicitly that countries are responsible, not just for their emissions at home, but also for the harm and damage that is linked with their exports of coal, oil and gas," Morgan explained.
He said the ICJ confirmed countries have an "obligation to regulate those industries" and that countries that continue to approve new fossil fuel projects "may be committing internationally wrongful acts".
"The Australian government is yet to really absorb that legal clarification and take it on board. But increasingly, there will be an expectation that Australia does so."
'Our actions don't match our rhetoric'
While Albanese was attending the PIF, the government supported the opening of a new fracking project in the Northern Territory's Beetaloo Basin and approved the expansion of the Saraji mine in Queensland's Bowen Basin.
The events didn't go unnoticed, drawing public criticism from Vanuatu's climate change adaptation and energy minister, Ralph Regenvanu.
"Australia is a major producer of fossil fuels — we all know fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis," he told the PIF.
"The very least a country like Australia could be doing is stopping future expansion, and it's not doing that.
"You need to stop expansion, and you need to start transitioning away."
Morgan said it's not a good look for Australia.
"At the moment, our actions don't match our rhetoric with Pacific leaders," he said.
Simon Bradshaw, Greenpeace Australia Pacific COP31 lead and climate expert, said the PIF was an opportunity to show "real commitment to climate action" and "Pacific partnership".
"These are not the actions of a government aspiring to be a global climate leader and effective middle power in turbulent times," he said.
"They are the actions of a government still beholden to the fossil fuel industry."
However, Albanese remains firm that Pacific leaders "respect" the position Australia has taken on climate change.
"They also understand ... because they're dealing with it as well, that transition can't happen overnight," he said.
Morgan said Australia's failure to meet emissions targets and support for new coal and gas projects will be a challenge at COP31.
But he believes Energy Minister Chris Bowen's role as president of negotiations at COP31 is a sign of "commendable" leadership from Australia.
"At this time, when global cooperation on climate change is under threat and is being challenged, it is very much in Australia's interest to be ensuring countries double down on the goals they have agreed to," he said.

Why the 'great Aussie summer' may become a thing of the past
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
20:34:39 UTC
05:34:39 KST

Last summer, Paris Brooke watched in horror as a bushfire blazed through the national park across the lake from her township of Mallacoota in north-east Victoria.
The town wasn't directly at risk, but she knew what the impact would be.
"The camp park emptied out overnight, leaving businesses that depend on summer tourism stuck with unused supplies and staff, but no more tourists," Brooke tells SBS News.
The exodus was reminiscent of the summer of 2019-20, when Australia's Black Summer bushfires swept through and devastated the beachside town.
Mallacoota was among the hardest-hit areas. Apocalyptic-looking scenes of residents and holidaymakers sheltering in boats off the coast, under a red sky thick with smoke, were broadcast around the world.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
While Brooke hasn't necessarily seen a slowdown in holidaymakers to the town since, she believes stays are shortening and worries the increased likelihood of extreme weather will hit summer trade long-term.
It's why she set up the Wilderness Collective, a community not-for-profit aimed at helping locals build new skills and businesses to reduce reliance on summer tourism.
"People are much more aware of natural disasters such as bushfires or droughts," she says.
On the same day last summer, climate scientist Linden Ashcroft was on the beach in Mallacoota. She recalls her kids playing in the water as embers and burnt leaves fell around them.
"It was pretty heartbreaking and terrifying. Everyone was really creeped out, and the town was covered in smoke," she says.
It left her with a lasting sense of cognitive dissonance — this is not how summer is supposed to feel.
That feeling is now rippling around the country, reaching far beyond places like Mallacoota that are historically prone to bushfires.
"Black Summer 2019–2020 was a real step change; it made people face the reality that summer can't just be carefree anymore," Ashcroft says.
You could call it the end of summer as we know it — or an evolution.
Climate Council director and academic Lesley Hughes says the changing climate is reshaping Australians' notion of summer: instead of looking forward to it, people increasingly feel apprehensive.
"They dread the heatwaves, the bushfires, not being able to do the things they used to. Climate change is stealing the part of the year Australians looked forward to most."
With higher temperatures and more extreme weather events becoming a fixture of the holiday season in parts of the country, could this signal the end of 'great Aussie summer'?
How our summers are changing
Australia is now 1.5C warmer on average than it was a century ago, according to the National Climate Risk Assessment. It's driving more extreme heatwaves and dangerous fire weather.
Monash climate scientist Andrew Watkins, former head of the Bureau of Meteorology's long-range forecast team, says the expected shifts will likely be dramatic.
"Heatwaves will cover larger areas, happen more frequently and grow more intense, with longer fire seasons stretching into autumn and spring. Rainfall will be less frequent but more intense, raising flash flood risk. Tropical cyclones may become less frequent but more severe," he tells SBS News.
Rising humidity is also driving up "wet-bulb temperature" — a combined heat-and-humidity measure that determines how well sweat can cool the body. Watkins says high readings — when sweat stops evaporating because the humidity is too high — put children and the elderly at particular risk.
"The temperature might only be 35, but if the wet-bulb is up to 25, you're going to put your body under a huge amount of stress."
Looking ahead to this summer, the Bureau of Meteorology has forecast a strong El Niño — generally meaning hotter, drier conditions — which it expects will mainly affect parts of Australia's east and south-east, raising the risk of drought and bushfires.
As extreme heat becomes more commonplace in Australia, other countries face similar conditions. Los Angeles was hit by raging wildfires last January, and Europe endured one of its worst summers on record for fire and heat this year.
It's a trend that is unlikely to shift without major and rapid structural changes, shifting global energy use to renewables and divesting from fossil fuels to limit further global warming.
New data published this week by the UN Environment Programme showed the world has lost the fight to limit warming to 1.5C. Even the most optimistic projections now point to warming of at least 1.8C — locking in more extreme weather, ecosystem loss and sea-level rise.
Reorganising the year
As projections worsen, experts are turning their attention to health risks.
Hughes at the Climate Council says the impacts of excess heat on the body can creep up slowly, and are especially dangerous for the elderly, the young, and those with heart or respiratory conditions.
She suggests more public awareness of the risks associated with heat stress is needed, but she's also calling for something more radical: reframing the calendar year to keep more of us inside during the country's hottest months.
Maybe a lot of summer would be better spent indoors, in air-conditioning, working, and leisure time moved to spring and autumn.
"Maybe our biggest school holidays shouldn't be in January," she says, adding "that would be an enormous social change for Australia".
Not everyone can escape the heat during their workday either. Professions such as tradies, farmhands, park rangers, delivery riders and some hospitality and event workers, for example, have no choice but to endure it.
A Spanish study published in 2023 offers another perspective, instead proposing to shift the country's national holidays to align with its hottest weeks to boost productivity and reduce industrial electricity consumption. Researchers found moving Spain's traditional holiday period from August to late July — the point of peak heat damage — would cut heat-driven electricity demand by 3 per cent, lost work hours by 25 per cent, and ozone pollution by 4 per cent.
Whether holidaying or working over summer, the general advice is to find ways to stay cool, and limit outdoor time to early mornings or evenings.
Although now, some Australians are reconsidering how they spend the season altogether.
The rise of the 'coolcation'
Research suggests people are already adapting to climate change without realising it, as evidenced by the rise in 'coolcations' — holidays to cool-climate destinations.
For Australians, this might include escapes to parts of northern Europe instead of southern Europe; visiting the tropics in winter instead of summer; venturing south to New Zealand or Tasmania for a mid-summer break; or snowy escapes to the Arctic, Antarctica or Alpine villages.
Trip.com data shows a 74 per cent year-on-year jump in searches for cooler destinations since the start of 2026, spiking 237 per cent across the June–August northern hemisphere summer. Searches for flights to Iceland rose 85 per cent, as travellers favoured northern Europe over traditionally popular Mediterranean spots. In Asia, cooler destinations such as Inner Mongolia, Yunnan in China and Sapporo in Japan saw similar gains.
Holidaygoers are also increasingly considering extreme weather events when making travel plans. Booking.com's 2026 Travel & Sustainability Report found 74 per cent of travellers now factor extreme weather into where and when they travel, and 31 per cent have cancelled a trip because of it.
In Australia, the Climate Council found 61 per cent of people are concerned about extreme weather disrupting summer holidays and are adapting — shifting from inland bush locations to the coast or travelling in cooler months.
Climate scientist Watkins is a coolcationer and spends his summers camping in Victoria's cooler high country.
"[It's about] beach holidays in spring, camping in autumn, taking more advantage of Easter. Getting up into cooler places over summer is a joy."
Travelling in cooler months isn't just about comfort, of course; it often also means fewer crowds and protecting destinations from over-tourism in mid-summer.
If you're holidaying in summer
However, travelling to far-flung places to access cooler weather may not be viable for some people. Distance and cost can be prohibitive, even for domestic travel.
Simply avoiding regional or bushfire-prone areas isn't necessarily a silver bullet either.
Ashcroft warns that heat risk in major cities can be just as dangerous.
"Urban areas get hotter due to the heat-island effect, so vulnerable people may not be better off in cities."
No matter where you spend the summer months, the advice is familiar by now: watch the forecasts, have a fire or heat plan, know when to leave early if conditions turn catastrophic, and avoid driving through floodwaters or bushfire smoke, which can be as thick as fog. Sometimes that means a detour, or staying put overnight until the danger passes.
Ashcroft thinks the language around summer should change altogether to help people prepare and understand the risks.
"Seasons are baked into how we talk about our year, but they're changing, so the way we talk about them has to change too. The Bureau's new term 'severe weather season' is more honest," she says.
"Being real helps us plan and prepare."
Rethinking summer sport
As our summers become more brutal, outdoor events such as music festivals and sport events may also become more challenging.
Ashcroft questions whether it still makes sense to push elite athletes to compete in extreme heat, conditions that are "not healthy and not safe".
Joanne Bowen is CEO of Cricket for Climate, a player-led movement that aims to build resilience for community clubs and the game. She calls cricket "the canary in the coal mine" for how climate change is disrupting outdoor activities.
Grassroots clubs are already cancelling junior games on hot days, with many lacking the infrastructure and budgets to adequately light night matches.
At the elite level, players have also struggled to perform in the heat, adds Bowen.
"But it's not just about the players; fans in concrete stadiums are exposed as well."
Increasing rainfall during summer is a growing problem too, she adds.
"If there's rain, you simply can't play, and there are commercial consequences for partners and fans."
She expects more games to move to nighttime and says shifting the cricket season to winter or spring is possible, though it would clash with other codes.
Another staple of Australian summer is the Australian Open.
Tennis Australia declined to discuss the long-term viability of tennis as a summer sport or moving the Australian Open from its midsummer slot, but a spokesperson said in a statement the organisation "continues to introduce strategies to protect the safety of players in hot conditions".
These include shading, misting fans, science-based heat guidelines with real-time monitoring, and heat acclimatisation education for players arriving from overseas.
The organisation's response to heat also appears to be shifting. Back in 2014, tournament director Craig Tiley defended playing through 40C conditions, saying "we are, at the end of the day, an outdoor event", even as players required medical attention.
By contrast, this year organisers suspended play after defending champion Jannik Sinner cramped mid-match under 40C conditions, with play resuming under a closed roof.
Planning for future summers
Beyond the challenge of adjusting our summer holiday plans to increasingly extreme weather, a deeper issue persists: how to curb climate change.
The best way to protect Australian summers, experts say, is to stop burning fossil fuels.
"We have to address the root cause of the problem, and Australia has a big responsibility to do that," says the Climate Council's Hughes.
Experts say adaptation can't wait: retrofitting homes with renewable energy, better resourcing emergency services and warning systems, investing in coastal protection, and upgrading infrastructure — from power grids to more public cooling and green spaces — all matter now more than ever.
Climate scientist Watkins wants to see more rigorous climate risk assessments underpin a genuine national adaptation plan, backed by coordination across all levels of government.
"The most important thing is coordinated efforts — talking with communities, business sectors, and the public to find out locally what adaptation is possible," he says.
I think we'll still have fun [in summer]. We'll just need to do things a little differently.
Back in Mallacoota, Brooke’s Wilderness Collective is helping locals to build off-season opportunities.
"We're working hard to broaden the economy, so visitors come throughout the year. Winter is actually the best time to visit; it's less crowded and the weather's beautiful," she says.
"We're starting to see visitors spread across the year, which is great, but we need more of it."
Even as Australians adapt to the new realities of summer, a trade-off is occurring.
For Watkins, adapting also means facing loss.
"There's a kind of grief that doesn't get talked about enough — grief for a place," he says.
"Many of us return to the same spots every summer, hoping our kids will see them the way we first did. But those places are changing. The National Climate Risk Assessment confirms it: huge numbers of plant and animal species are already shifting, with more change ahead.
"That sense of loss is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously."

Poland extends asylum restrictions at Belarus border for another 60 days
Unknown

2026-09-04
20:34:04 UTC
05:34:04 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Poland’s parliament on Friday approved another 60-day suspension of the right to apply for asylum for migrants illegally crossing the country’s border with Belarus, TVP World reported.
A total of 418 lawmakers voted in favor of the extension, while 16 opposed it.
The measure, which will take effect Sept. 18, marks the ninth consecutive renewal.
Poland first suspended the right to claim asylum at the Belarus border in March 2025, following what Polish officials described as an influx of mostly Middle Eastern and African migrants entering the EU through Belarus.
In a motion submitted to parliament, the government said “dangerous incidents have regularly occurred in which aggressive foreign nationals attacked Polish patrols.”
It said migrants had thrown stones, bottles, bricks and other objects at Polish personnel and damaged sections of border barriers.
The government also accused Belarusian state services of participating in attacks on Polish soldiers, police officers and border guards.
It said border guards had prevented attempts supported by Belarusian state services to build and use tunnels beneath the frontier to move groups of foreign nationals into Poland.
Between March 2025 and Aug. 16, Polish authorities rejected 492 asylum applications and accepted 178 from migrants in vulnerable groups, according to government figures.
Meanwhile, attempted illegal crossings have fallen sharply.
Polish Interior Ministry figures showed 235 attempts during the first half of this year, compared with more than 15,500 during the same period in 2025.
Polish and EU authorities have linked the influx to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, while human rights groups have accused Polish authorities of pushing some migrants back to Belarus without allowing them to seek asylum.
Dozens of migrants are believed to have died in the border area since 2021.

More than 900 families displaced in 2 days as fighting intensifies in Yemen’s Taiz

Mohammed Sameai and Mohammad Sio
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
More than 900 families have been displaced in two days as fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis intensified in the western province of Taiz, local authorities said Friday.
Preliminary figures show that 917 families fled their homes Thursday and Friday amid renewed fighting in Maqbanah district and nearby areas, particularly Jabal Habashi, according to the Taiz office of Yemen’s Planning and International Cooperation Ministry.
The office said the escalation had forced residents to evacuate several communities and displacement camps, while residential areas and sites sheltering displaced people had also come under attack.
Families fled parts of Maqbanah, including Ozul Al-Yaman, Al-Abdalah and Al-Ashmalah, as well as Al-Jubb camp. Others were displaced from Al-Rahbah and Al-Rajhi camps in Jabal Habashi.
They moved to safer areas, including parts of Jabal Habashi and Al-Ma’afer districts, the statement said.
Authorities warned that the displacement figure was likely to rise if the fighting continued.
The ministry office said many families had fled with little warning, leaving behind belongings and basic necessities, and were now facing “extremely difficult” humanitarian conditions.
It appealed to local and international relief organizations for emergency shelter, food, drinking water and sanitation services, calling for an “urgent, multisectoral humanitarian intervention” before the crisis expands further.
The displacement comes amid heavy clashes since early Thursday on several fronts in Taiz and neighboring Hodeidah province, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Local media, citing military sources, have reported dozens of government troops and Houthi fighters killed or wounded since the fighting intensified.
Civilians have also been killed and wounded in shelling, but no consolidated official casualty toll has been announced as clashes continue.
The latest violence is part of a series of exchanges that began in July and ended a period of relative calm that had largely prevailed along Yemen’s front lines since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022.
The Houthis have controlled the capital Sanaa and several other cities since September 2014, while the internationally recognized government and allied forces control large areas of southern, eastern and western Yemen.

Tate brothers indicted in Romania over sex crimes involving minors
Romanian authorities have indicted social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate in absentia on charges including human trafficking, sex offenses involving minors, money laundering and witness tampering. The brothers have been held in a US jail since mid-July while fighting a separate British extradition request.
Both have strongly denied wrongdoing.
Andrew Tate, a former professional kickboxer and dual British-US citizen, built a global following promoting wealth, hyper-masculinity and traditional gender roles. His online content has attracted millions of followers while drawing widespread criticism over remarks about women.
Romania’s Directorate for the Investigation of Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) announced on Friday that Andrew had been charged with human trafficking, having sex with a minor, money laundering and influencing witnesses. Tristan is accused of aiding and abetting him.
Prosecutors allege that in 2012 Andrew recruited a 15-year-old girl in the UK by falsely claiming he wanted a romantic relationship with her before taking her to Romania. She was then allegedly forced to produce pornographic content for a webcam business, with the brothers controlling her through threats, emotional blackmail and physical violence.
Tristan allegedly managed proceeds from the operation totaling around $1.25 million. DIICOT is seeking the confiscation of four luxury cars allegedly bought with the money and registered in the names of associates.
Prosecutors have separately accused Andrew of having sex with another 15-year-old girl.
The case has been referred to the Bucharest Tribunal, where preliminary proceedings are expected to take at least two months.
Eugen Vidineac, the brothers’ Romanian lawyer, said the defense would challenge the indictment. Andrew and Tristan, who moved to Romania in 2016, were arrested there in December 2022 in a separate case involving similar allegations. An appeals court later returned that case to prosecutors after finding some evidence inadmissible. The charges were not dismissed, but travel restrictions were lifted in February 2025, allowing the brothers to fly to Florida.
In July, Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service announced additional charges against the Tates, bringing the British case to seven alleged victims and 59 charges combined, including rape, sexual assault and trafficking-related offenses.
The brothers were subsequently arrested in Florida following a British extradition request.
Their lawyer, Joseph McBride, has said Andrew and Tristan will vigorously fight extradition, describing the British case as politically motivated because his clients have repeatedly criticized the UK authorities and political establishment.
