Mudslide-stranded Nepalese border residents in China's Xizang get assistance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:33:00 CST
01:33:00 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Nepalese border residents stranded by a deadly mudslide in Gyirong Town in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region have received assistance and arrangements from the Chinese side for orderly return home or continued stay.
Caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal on Aug. 26, the mudslide swept through Gyirong Port in Xizang, leaving 31 people dead and 531 others missing there as of Friday afternoon. It also disrupted roads leading to the port as well as communications and power supplies on the Chinese side, leaving some Nepalese border residents stranded in the town.
Following the disaster, the Chinese government quickly activated an emergency response mechanism for the resettlement and support of foreign nationals and coordinated efforts to provide daily necessities for stranded Nepalese border residents, address their concerns and facilitate their orderly departure.
At the time of the disaster, Gyaldup Tamang, a stranded Nepalese border resident in Gyirong Town in Gyirong County, was working in a village there, and four of his relatives remained out of contact.
"I was eager to return home, but the damaged roads made it impossible to travel, and I did not know what to do for a while," he said. "Fortunately, the Chinese government offered assistance, helping with exit procedures and arranging transportation. I heard that some Nepalese compatriots have already left through Zhangmu Port."
"We can now complete exit formalities free of charge, and I plan to go through the procedures this afternoon," Gyaldup Tamang told Xinhua on Thursday.
At the Gyirong Port Branch of the Xigaze Municipal Public Security Bureau, many Nepalese border residents were seen queuing to complete exit procedures.
A staff member at the branch said those wishing to leave could complete the formalities by presenting their Nepalese identity cards and China-Nepal border crossing permits. After completing the procedures, they can take government-arranged buses to leave through alternative ports.
For those choosing to stay, local authorities have also made arrangements to meet their basic needs.
A dedicated service site for Nepalese border residents has been established along a street in Gyirong Town, providing free supplies such as instant noodles, milk, beverages and medicines.
According to authorities in Gyirong Town, more than 2,000 items of daily necessities have been distributed to hundreds of Nepalese border residents in the town.

Feature: Afghan entrepreneur takes bus ticket booking online
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
00:32:39 CST
01:32:39 KST

An Afghan woman rides a motorcycle to deliver bus tickets to customers after receiving orders through an online platform in Kabul, Afghanistan, Sept. 2, 2026.(Photo by Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua)
KABUL, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Every morning, Sadaf Afghan arrives at her office in Kabul to receive orders from customers and book bus tickets online, hoping her fledgling business can make travel easier for passengers in Afghanistan.
Her online platform, qasid.af, allows customers to book bus tickets to different destinations without having to visit a bus terminal and pay for them in cash.
"We book tickets for our customers online, make the payment and then deliver the tickets to their doorsteps," Afghan told Xinhua.
The young entrepreneur developed qasid.af about a year ago and launched its online ticket booking and purchasing services five months later with a three-member team.
The business has since expanded to eight employees, including four women, who provide booking and ticket delivery services to customers.
Afghan hopes to further expand the business and open branches in other provinces, creating more job opportunities for Afghans, particularly women.
"Our main goal is to further develop our business and open more offices in the provinces so that we can create job opportunities for both men and women," she said.
Starting a business has not been easy, particularly in a society where many services are still conducted through traditional, face-to-face transactions. But Afghan said the response from customers has been encouraging.
"Launching any business is difficult in the beginning, but we should not give up. In general, people support us," she said.
Afghanistan's transport system remains largely reliant on road travel. With no extensive railway network or metro system, buses are an important means of intercity transportation. Many passengers still have to travel to bus terminals and pay cash for tickets before setting out on often lengthy journeys.
A journey of about 450 km between Afghan cities, for example, can take at least 10 hours, depending on road and traffic conditions.
Afghan believes digital services can make at least part of that experience more convenient.
"We need government support to improve the transport system, provide necessary services and support companies that provide services to travelers," she said.
She also plans to expand qasid.af into air travel, allowing customers to book airline tickets online and have them delivered to their homes.
The company's ambitions are also creating unconventional jobs for young Afghan women.
Mohammadi, 20, is one of the company's female employees. Every day, she rides a motorbike through Kabul to deliver tickets to customers.
"I feel happy to deliver bus tickets to the doorsteps of our clients," she told Xinhua.
Mohammadi said she hopes the company will continue to expand and provide jobs for more people, particularly women.
"It is very good to serve people, and I hope to see more job opportunities created and more people employed," she said.
Having completed the 10th grade, Mohammadi said riding a motorbike and working outside the home have given her a sense of encouragement.
"Riding a motorbike and serving people is encouraging, and I am pleased to see women being encouraged," she said. ■

Iraq proposes new 6+2 Gulf security framework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:30:05 UTC
01:30:05 KST

Breadcrumb
6+2: An Iraqi vision for a new regional security formula
Despite several senior Iraqi officials in Baghdad repeatedly promoting the vision of "joint Gulf security" in recent weeks, there has been no response from outside Iraq.
The vision, known as 6+2 and referring to the six Gulf Cooperation Council states alongside Iraq and Iran, was unveiled by Iraqi government security adviser Qasim Al-Araji last week. The plan calls for a Gulf security system based on "respect for the sovereignty of states".
He said the 6+2 initiative aims to "address the crisis of confidence" between the Arab Gulf states and Iran, without providing further details about its content.
In remarks carried by Iraqi state television, he said: "From this standpoint, Iraq affirms its responsibility to consolidate state sovereignty and the independence of its decisions, place weapons and decisions on war and peace in its hands, prevent its territory from being used to threaten neighbouring countries, and pursue a balanced foreign policy that contributes to de-escalation and the containment of crises."
The Iraqi government has not officially adopted the initiative, nor has it issued a document outlining its provisions.
Political sources in Baghdad said it was proposed last month at a meeting of the ruling Coordination Framework coalition at the beginning of August, attended by Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi, as an Iraqi initiative to establish security understandings with the Gulf states and Iran.
However, a key problem with the initiative may explain the lack of response.
It focuses on the commitment of the eight states bordering the Arabian Gulf not to use their territory to attack other countries. This corresponds with the Iranian narrative repeatedly used after each attack on the Arab Gulf states: that Iran does not target the Gulf states but rather US bases located in their territory and used to attack Iran.
The Gulf states, as well as Jordan, naturally reject this claim, while Tehran has provided no evidence for its allegations.
A senior Iraqi parliamentarian in Baghdad from the Reconstruction and Development bloc, one of the components of the ruling Coordination Framework coalition, said the Iraqi initiative is based on the principle of neutrality in the current war against Iran, which the United States has been waging against it for many months, according to him.
He revealed that the initiative has been accepted by leaders of the ruling coalition but naturally "lacks a guarantor" to make any agreement sustainable and ensure compliance with it, particularly by the Iranians.
The lawmaker, who asked not to be named, added that the Iraqi initiative or vision had received no response from the six Gulf states.
However, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed any initiative aimed at easing the current tensions.
On Wednesday, Al-Araji returned to present the same initiative, saying that "6+2 Gulf security", which includes Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman, alongside Iraq and Iran, is based on the principle of "not using the territory of any state to threaten neighbouring states".
He stressed that his country is capable of "preventing Iraqi territory from being used as a launching point for attacks against neighbouring countries".
Through the initiative, Baghdad aims to once again present Iraq as a bridge for dialogue between Iran and the Gulf states, according to Iraqi security affairs expert Ahmed Al-Nuaimi.
He explained that the initiative was presented through communication channels between Iraq and several Gulf states but did not receive the expected response.
He attributed this to several reasons, most notably that the initiative is based on the principle of states not attacking one another from their own territory.
Gulf states consider this a misleading Iranian narrative designed to cover up repeated attacks against them under the pretext of targeting US bases.
Iranian attacks have hit ports, airports, oil facilities and even civilian sites in the Gulf states, resulting in deaths and injuries, and were not limited to those bases.
Iraq itself has also become a launch point for attacks carried out by armed groups allied with Iran.
However, Al-Nuaimi pointed out that the most important aspect of this vision, which appears to be supported by figures allied with Iran inside Iraq, is that it is a political position directed against the United States.
None of the Gulf states wants to depart from their relatively stable position in this war, which is to remain on the sidelines and avoid being drawn into the war or aligning with either side.
What Iraq has announced so far remains unclear.
No official document containing the initiative's points or principles has been disclosed, and the Foreign Ministry has yet to take any action on it, according to Kurdish Iraqi politician Ali Shankali.
Shankali told The New Arab that Iraq itself still faces problems transporting its oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as repeated attacks on Erbil and Sulaymaniyah carried out by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps from time to time against US interests or Kurdish groups opposed to Tehran.
Iran is also strengthening the position of Iraqi armed factions that refuse to cooperate with the Iraqi state in handing over their weapons, making any initiatives, even if other countries take an interest in them, "unlikely to be guaranteed in implementation".
This is not the first time Iraq has proposed the same initiative.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in late June that his country had proposed holding an eight-party meeting bringing together the Gulf Cooperation Council states, Iraq and Iran to discuss security in the Gulf region.
Hussein said at a joint press conference with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, in Baghdad that "the security of the region should be the responsibility of its states, and different frameworks could be established to protect those states".
He affirmed Iraq's readiness to host such a meeting to discuss the issue, as well as economic relations between the countries of the region.
The Iranian foreign minister welcomed the Iraqi proposal at the press conference, saying, "The issue of security in the Gulf region should be reconsidered, and a new framework should be established that includes all the countries of the region without interference from any country from outside it."
Former Iraqi parliamentarian Mohammed Al-Daraji said that many visions and initiatives had been proposed recently within the Iraqi political scene, but they did not go beyond being matters for domestic discussion and had no bearing on the conflict or the political and security calculations in the region.
Al-Daraji explained that Iraq's ability to play any positive security role in the region would remain "dependent on the government's ability to control armed groups and prevent them from using Iraqi territory to target other countries, such as Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Kuwait".
He said the absence of a Gulf position on the Iraqi vision may be because it had not formally reached them or because they see it as an attempt to make them party to a crisis at a time when they are in fact parties adversely affected by the war in terms of security, economics and politics and were not responsible for it.

Mistrial to be declared in case of Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts mother who killed her 3 children

Mistrial declared in case of Massachusetts mother who killed her 3 children
Jurors fail to agree whether Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible; defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis
A Massachusetts judge declared a mistrial Friday in the case of Lindsay Clancy, who was charged with murdering her three young children, after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.
The jury remained deadlocked after seven days of deliberations following a nearly six-week trial. The central question was not whether Clancy killed the children, which she did not dispute, but whether she was criminally responsible at the time.
Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, strangled five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of the family’s home in Duxbury in January 2023.
She then injured herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life, leaving her paralyzed from the waist down.
Her lawyers sought a verdict of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, arguing that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis and heard a voice telling her to kill the children. Relatives testified that her mental health had deteriorated after the birth of her third child and that she had repeatedly sought medical treatment.
Prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had experienced mental health problems but argued that she understood her actions were wrong. They said she deliberately sent her then-husband out to collect food and medication, having checked how long the errands would take, before killing the children.
The jury foreperson told the court Thursday that one juror acknowledged having doubts but refused to apply instructions on reasonable doubt. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington sought the juror’s removal and disclosed Friday that the holdout was a man, drawing an angry rebuke from Judge William Sullivan, who refused to intervene.
Prosecutors must now decide whether to retry Clancy before a new jury, negotiate a plea agreement or drop the case. She remains charged with murder and is being held at a psychiatric hospital.

86% of enterprises confirmed their critical status — Ministry of Defence
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Defence has completed its review of the status of defence industry enterprises: 86% confirmed it. The rest may submit a complete set of documents to obtain it again.
The Ministry of Defence of Ukraine has completed its review of decisions designating enterprises of the defence industry (defence-industrial complex, DIC) as critically important — to confirm this status, they had to submit documents by 10 August. This was reported by the Ministry of Defence, writes UNN.
Details
It is noted that, as of 1 September of the current year, 86% of the DIC enterprises subject to review confirmed their status as critically important.
The Ministry of Defence noted that the review concerned decisions designating enterprises as critically important that had been adopted before 7 July 2026.
For most enterprises, a simplified procedure was in place — without the need to resubmit the full package of documents.
The following, in particular, could use this procedure:
-  contractors and subcontractors under defence contracts whose defence-related activities account for more than 50% of total production; 
-  residents of Defence City; 
-  certain manufacturers of explosives and ammunition; 
-  enterprises in the defence, aircraft manufacturing and space industries that had previously obtained the status based on a combination of criteria. 
The enterprises on this list submitted documents confirming their current compliance with the criterion on the basis of which the Ministry of Defence had previously designated them as critically important.
Consequently, companies that successfully passed the review retained their status as critically important and the ability to reserve military-liable employees in accordance with the law
At the same time, following the review, 14% of enterprises did not confirm their status as critically important — to obtain it, they may submit a full package of documents to the Ministry of Defence in accordance with the current procedure.
The Ministry of Defence will verify the enterprise's compliance with the established criteria and, following consideration, will adopt an appropriate decision.
We remind you
The number of reserved employees increased by 300,000 over the past year, while an additional 9,000 enterprises were also granted critical status.

====================================================================================================

The capacitor supply chain bottleneck is becoming a bigger AI trade in the market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:24:03 UTC
01:24:03 KST

Trading on commodity cycles within the technology sector is nothing new, and it's often associated with peak moments. Semiconductor ETFs like iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) and VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) date back to the 2000/2001 period. For decades, the quarterly 13F filings of hedge funds have also detailed rapid movements into and out of chip stocks as booms and busts proceeded. AI is creating a new level of interest and playing field for this kind of trading, often through ETFs.
There are roughly two dozen broad-based AI ETFs, but increasingly, there are niche trades targeting components from with the AI economy, such as memory — led by the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) — and more recently, ETFs targeting companies in the photonics market, which focuses on AI data center optical networking innovation. There is also a growing AI thematic bet focused on supply and demand in the capacitor market, components that are crucial to stabilizing the intense power demands in data centers.
It's a trade that Global X — which launched its broad AI ETF, Global X AI & Technology (AIQ), back in 2018 — is planning to launch within a few weeks, according to Pedro Palandrani, Global X head of product research & development, speaking during CNBC's "ETF Edge" podcast earlier this week. The company has a prospectus on file with the SEC for the Global X MLCC & Electronic Components ETF, though it is currently in a quiet period until the ETF launches.
Palandrani says Global X has positioned its thematic investing ETFs within a concept that the investment manager refers to as "conversational alpha."
"I always say these are very relatable concerns," Palandrani told CNBC's Dominic Chu. "Whether the theme is AI or geopolitics and its impact on defense tech, Global X is working with many financial advisors using these ETFs as a way to have conversations with clients on investing opportunities," he said.
Palandrani stressed that this doesn't mean the thematic bets are having a dramatic impact on overall portfolio construction. When it comes to conversational alpha, "they may own two, three, five percent in these thematic portfolios, and that's looking at a 60-40 [60% stock/40% bond] type of portfolio," he said.
But he added, "Most of these client conversations are happening on these thematic categories, how the portfolios are positioned to capitalize on those things that may be headlines grabbers. Investors recognize that very well," he said. "Targeted exposures are top of mind. We will continue to see those targeted exposures within AI," Palandrani said. "Where we see significant opportunity is offering targeted exposure to many of the bottlenecks within AI," he added.
The ETF market focus on multilayer ceramic capacitor manufacturers began last month, with the launch of two portfolios in August: the more pure-play Defiance AI Capacitors Leaders ETF (CAPA) and the broader Tema MLCC & PowerSemi ETF (PSOX).
What makes capacitors critical to the AI data center story
CAPA is a bet on the select group of companies, 10 in all, based in Asia that dominate the capacitor market, including TDK, Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Murata, Kyocera, Yageo, Taiyo Yuden, Maruwa, Walsin, Samwha Capacitor and Nippon Chemi-Con.
"Every AI accelerator, server board, and hyperscale data center depends on capacitors and passive components to condition power, regulate voltage, filter signals, suppress noise, and store energy," Tema stated in its fund overview. It cited data from Murata that "a single AI server built on Nvidia's GB300 platform can require roughly 30,000 multilayer ceramic capacitors, with a full rack consuming hundreds of thousands of units."
Murata, which is the largest MLCC manufacturer, has forecast to investors that MLCC shipments will grow at approximately 30% annually through 2030, tripling 2025 levels. Its stock price has risen over 115% year-to-date.
The Global X MLCC ETF will track the Akros MLCC & Electronic Components Index, which seeks to hold up to 15 companies that are among the largest MLCC manufacturers worldwide or have at least 50% revenue exposure to the component category, according to its prospectus.
Tema's PSOX ETF targets some of those same capacitor makers, plus companies that focus on other aspects of power regulation within the AI market, including U.S.-based Bloom Energy and Monolithic Power Systems. Both thematic trades, "represent emerging AI bottlenecks," Tema states in its fund materials.
Roundhill Investments, whose DRAM ETF has been a breakout star this year with close to $25 billion in assets, is planning to get in on the trade as well, through its CCML ETF, also currently in registration with the SEC.
The MLCC ETFs are off to a much slower start than DRAM and other AI trades in terms of attracting investor interest and asset gathering, with CAPA reporting assets of roughly $3.5 million and PSOX not yet at the $1 million mark. The funds have relatively high expense ratios relative to core equity holdings, though in line with what other thematic ETFs charge, with CAPA's annual expense ratio at 0.75% and PSOX at 0.71%.
Recent press reports on the capacitor market bottleneck have referred to it as "the rice" of the AI buildout story. The CEO for Tokyo-based Taiyo Yuden, whose shares are up over 150% this year, told Bloomberg in June that the company was facing "scary" levels of demand, especially as more advanced chips like Nvidia's Rubin hit the market.
Palandrani said on "ETF Edge" that its approach to thematic ETFs is about identifying a high conviction area, an investable universe of companies that can be wrapped within the ETF structure, and a long-term investment strategy that can allow allow investors to capitalize on secular, strategic areas where it sees opportunities for the next five to 10 years.
With this week also marking the 50th anniversary of the launch of the index fund by Vanguard, ETF experts noted how far fund investing has come, but also how the risk profile has changed, especially within ETFs which first came to market as a new way to gain exposure to low-cost core index holdings but are now the default structure for many trades.
"We are in the midst of thematic tidal wave of ETFs, particularly centered around AI. Issuers are coming out with any form of an AI play possible," said Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas. "These thematic booms tend to come in cycles."
He noted what a big change it is for the market, the "slicing and dicing of these segments" whereas historically ETFs have been about index tracking, broadly diversified vehicles. "You just had to have asset allocation correct and let the market work over time ... limited stock knowledge was needed," he said.
Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management, is cautious on the latest developments. "It's a tale as old as time in asset management, where fund issuers rush to package and sell whatever is capturing investors' attention. Nothing is hotter right now than slicing and dicing the AI trade," he said. "If investors are going to dabble in these products, it's critical they look under the hood to understand exactly what they own and how it fits with the rest of their portfolio," he added.
There are both pros and cons to ETFs such as these newer AI portfolios targeting a small group of stocks, according to Sohn. It is a much sharper tool to gain exposure, he said, but the investor really needs to understand the companies much better on an individual basis than a broad-based index fund holder would. "This is particularly important given a few heavyweight names are pushing this story forward," he added.
For traders who want efficient access to companies powering a certain segment of the AI boom, Sohn says these ETFs can serve a real need: "quick and efficient access to practically any market or theme." That is especially true of a market like MLCCs where the major players are all listed in Asia.
But for many investors, he advises avoiding fund overlap. "If you own one broad AI ETF and overlay it with one of the niche funds, you may have more exposure to certain bellwethers than you need," he said.

Freedom Flotilla announces new mission to Gaza in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:22:43 UTC
01:22:43 KST

Rania Abushamala
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
- Coalition urges supporters to pressure governments to halt weapons shipments to Israel
The Freedom Flotilla Coalition announced a new international maritime mission to the Gaza Strip, with vessels making stops at European ports before a planned attempt to reach the enclave in October.
“We are sailing again because Israel hasn’t stopped its genocide and because Palestine is still not free,” the coalition said in an appeal for international support.
The mission seeks to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza and mobilize public pressure across Europe, the coalition said in a statement published Wednesday.
The voyage is already underway, with the coalition’s Handala II vessel having visited ports in Norway, Sweden and Denmark during June and July.
Another vessel, the Kate, departed from the British city of Bristol in August and subsequently made stops in Ireland, Germany and France, according to the statement.
The vessels are expected to visit ports in Spain, Portugal and Italy before continuing toward Gaza, where the coalition plans to arrive in October.
The mission brings together human rights advocates, trade union activists, elected representatives, journalists, medical professionals and other supporters of Palestinian rights, the coalition said.
The coalition said it would work with local communities to pressure governments to block weapons and energy shipments to Israel, end diplomatic and military cooperation with it and impose sanctions.
“The Freedom Flotilla sails again because our governments continue to fail to uphold their obligations,” said Zohar Chamberlain Regev, a member of the coalition’s steering committee.
“At every port, we will carry the demand that Palestinians be free to live with dignity,” she added.
“In October, we intend to carry that demand and the solidarity of people around the world to Gaza’s shores.”
The coalition urged governments to demand safe and unobstructed passage for the flotilla and to make clear that any attack, seizure or detention of its participants would have consequences.
It also called for immediate and unrestricted access to Gaza and an end to Israeli restrictions on the entry of food, water, medicine and other essential supplies.
Governments should defend freedom of navigation and use diplomatic, economic and legal measures to end the blockade, it added.
“We know that sailing toward Gaza carries serious risks,” said Edward Digilio, an engineer from the US state of Maryland participating in the initiative.
“But silence and inaction carry a much greater cost for Palestinians and the world,” he said, describing the mission as “an expression of shared humanity and a refusal to accept the destruction of an entire people as normal.”
The coalition said Israeli forces had attacked and detained hundreds of flotilla participants during an earlier mission in the spring of 2026. It said volunteers reported severe beatings, broken bones, gunshot wounds, repeated tasering and sexual assault while in Israeli custody.
It also recalled Israel’s May 2010 raid on the Gaza-bound Mavi Marmara, during which 10 activists were killed.

spok bends the geometry of tennis into an optical loop at felipe pantone’s casa axis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:22:16 UTC
01:22:16 KST

Across the tennis court at Felipe Pantone‘s Casa Axis, familiar white lines begin behaving strangely. They follow the expected geometry for a moment, then multiply toward the center, bending through metallic gradients until the entire surface appears to drop away beneath the players. Spanish urban artist Spok Brillor created Hard Court 2 during a 12-day residency at the Valencia creative space, painting an optical version of the court directly into the court itself.
The intervention extends a project that began here last year, when Lucas Benarroch, aka MRKA, painted the first Hard Court across the same playing surface. His version loosened tennis geometry through irregular, hand-drawn lines. Spok takes the opposite visual direction while keeping the court recognizable. Regulation markings become the raw material for an image that seems to recede beneath the ground, with chrome-like passages picking up colors from the surrounding environment.
images courtesy Casa Axis
TENNIS BECOMES THE COMMISSION
Behind the changing surface is C.A.I.O., the Casa Axis International Open, an artist tennis tournament launched in June 2026. Its prize comes with an unusual second assignment: the winner receives responsibility for transforming the court ahead of the following edition. MRKA won the inaugural tournament after having already painted the 2025 court, then handed this year’s intervention to Spok, who had competed alongside him.
That rule gives the tennis match a life beyond its final point. Each edition leaves behind a playable artwork that another artist will eventually paint over, so the surface can shift between competition and installation from year to year. The first Hard Court grew out of the friction between standardized tennis markings and MRKA’s loose gesture. Hard Court 2 works through repetition instead, pulling those same markings inward until the boundaries of the actual court become harder to read.
Spok Brillor transforms the tennis court at Casa Axis with Hard Court 2
SPOK BUILDS A PORTAL FROM PAINT
Coming out of Madrid’s graffiti scene in the 1990s, Spok has since moved across painting, muralism, and installation, often using architectural space, reflections, and imagery informed by science fiction. Here, those interests meet a particularly unforgiving canvas. A tennis court already contains a complete spatial drawing, and Spok works with that drawing rather than covering it, repeating its lines at shrinking scales and shifting their surfaces into polished, almost liquid passages.
From certain viewpoints, the painted court seems to sink several levels below itself. From others, the illusion flattens and the actual playing surface returns to view. Spok has explored this kind of spatial doubling in earlier works, repeating an existing scene within itself to alter how the original place is perceived. At Casa Axis, the idea becomes especially literal: the artwork, the image represented inside it, and the surface used for tennis are all the same court.
the painted intervention repeats the geometry of the existing court inward
CASA AXIS KEEPS THE SURFACE IN PLAY
Casa Axis occupies a 1975 house in L’Eliana, Valencia, where Felipe Pantone established an artistic residency and creative space spanning art, architecture, design, and technology. The tennis court sits within that broader environment of experimentation, though C.A.I.O. has given it a peculiar rhythm of its own. Every tournament now carries the possibility that the place players are standing on will look entirely different the next time they return.
With Hard Court 2, the familiar logic of the sports court survives while its apparent depth becomes unstable. Players still have lines to follow and boundaries to respect, yet beneath those markings Spok has painted another court, followed by another, receding toward an impossible center. C.A.I.O. will return in 2027, which means this painted portal already comes with an expiration date. Whoever takes the next turn will inherit both the surface and the challenge of what Spok has left there.

Malta attorney general set to appeal acquittal in journalist murder trial
Sept 4 - Malta's attorney general is set to appeal the acquittal of a top businessman over the murder of an anti-corruption journalist, seeking a retrial, the Times of Malta and other media reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources.
A jury acquitted businessman Yorgen Fenech in an 8-1 verdict on charges of complicity to murder Daphne Caruana Galizia and criminal association. Caruana Galizia was killed by a car bomb metres from her home in 2017.
The appeal, if filed, would prolong one of Europe's most closely watched murder cases. Five men have been convicted of carrying out the killing or supplying the bomb, but the acquittal of Fenech, who prosecutors said commissioned the murder, has left no one held legally responsible for ordering it.
The attorney general's office has not yet officially declared its intention, and it could not be contacted for comment.
The law allows 15 working days for an appeal on points of law before three judges.
One of Caruana Galizia's sons, Matthew, said in a Facebook post that a push for a retrial “is the right thing".
"All branches of the state including the judiciary must not allow our country to be one in which people get away with murder," he added.
The Court of Criminal Appeal may only consider an appeal from jury trials if it considers there was a "grave irregularity during the proceedings", or if the judgment was clearly the result of a "manifest misinterpretation" or “manifestly wrong application of the law” which could have had a bearing on the verdict.
The grounds upon which the appeal may be filed were not disclosed. Observers said a potential issue concerned what prosecutors were allowed to tell jurors and what they were prevented from telling them. REUTERS

Aesthetics as Engineering Solutions Danjiang Bridge Turns Taiwan’s Resilience into a Landmark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:19:56 UTC
01:19:56 KST

Around the world, many cities are defined by a bridge that can be recognized at a glance: Paris has the Pont Neuf, San Francisco the Golden Gate Bridge, and Sydney the Harbour Bridge. Now Taiwan’s northern coast has a new landmark of its own—Danjiang Bridge, running between the Tamsui and Bali districts of New Taipei City.
After Danjiang Bridge opened to traffic, a special exhibition entitled Engineering Aesthetics of Danjiang Bridge quietly opened to visitors at the Bridge Management Center on the Tamsui side. There are no famous paintings and no cultural relics. The exhibition contains only pylon models, construction drawings, and photographs from the worksite. Yet these seemingly commonplace items tell the story of how a world-class bridge was born—and the story of how Taiwan completed an engineering feat that once seemed virtually impossible.
Layer upon layer of difficulty
Danjiang Bridge is currently the world’s longest-span single-tower asymmetric cable-stayed bridge. Its form is clean and minimal, guided by design principles of fluidity, simplicity, and lightness, but the engineering behind it is anything but simple. Chang Shih-cheng, a senior specialist at the Ministry of Transportation and Communications’ Highway Bureau and curator of Engineering Aesthetics of Danjiang Bridge, talks about how the difficulties behind the bridge began at a civil servant’s desk and continued all the way to the construction site.
More than a decade ago, residents of Tamsui and Bali, on opposite sides of the Tamsui River’s mouth, were looking forward to a new bridge that could take roughly 30% of the traffic burden carried by Guandu Bridge upstream. At the same time, they expected the bridge to preserve the century-old landscape of Tamsui’s celebrated sunset.
The engineering conditions only compounded the challenge. The bridge site sits at the mouth of the Tamsui River, where strong winds blow year-round and can reach Level 17 on Taiwan’s wind scale. Chang describes that as “strong enough to overturn even a truck driving onto the bridge.” The tidal action and saltwater corrosion at the estuary further multiplied the difficulty of construction. In addition, Taiwan’s position at the junction of tectonic plates also means frequent earthquakes that place it among the world’s most seismically active regions.
More difficult still, the underwater base strata on the Bali side are sandy, and the site lies beside Wazihwei Nature Reserve, while possible underwater artefacts from the Spanish and Dutch periods also influenced the decision to place the pylon closer to the Tamsui side (though subsequent surveys found no archaeological remains). Engineering, landscape, ecology, and potential cultural heritage concerns overlapped here, leaving almost no margin for error. Given so many constraints, Chang jokes that based on precedents from the past, the conclusion would have been just two words: “Too hard.” Case closed.
But Taiwan’s highway professionals did not give up. Instead, they looked to the world for answers. Ultimately, Taiwan’s Sinotech Engineering Consultants and Germany-based Leonhardt, Andrä und Partner (LAP) formed the project team and invited the UK’s Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA) to take part in the main bridge’s formal design. The final proposal was for a rare single-tower, asymmetric cable-stayed bridge.
Solving problems through aesthetics
The single-tower design was not merely an aesthetic choice. It was selected to minimize the bridge’s obstruction of Tamsui’s sunset while preserving the maximum integrity of the Bali wetland. To achieve this, the design team stayed in Taiwan for extended periods, calculating where the sun would set in each season in order to find the optimal position for the pylon.
The late Zaha Hadid was often called the “Queen of the Curve,” and the bridge’s A-shaped pylon is formed from fluid, curving surfaces. Chang asks us to look closely: The legs of the A-shaped pylon run parallel to the traffic flow; as the lanes reach the tower base, they naturally part to either side, like a zipper being gently pulled open.
This is not form-making for its own sake, but an engineering solution. When strong winds blow, the airflow moves along the curved surfaces and disperses to either side rather than striking the bridge deck head-on. The entire bridge is therefore better able to meet the powerful winds at the mouth of the Tamsui River.
Meanwhile, the bridge’s streamlined landscape lighting columns each have a different curvature and angle. This is not simply a visual variation; rather, it deliberately disrupts the columns’ natural frequency, reducing wind-induced resonance. Otherwise, when strong winds hit, an entire row of lighting columns could vibrate at the same time—or even break.
At the same time, the lighting columns form a work of art. In the original design competition, the ZHA team titled its proposal “A Dancer’s Quiet Moment at Midnight,” drawing inspiration from the postures of dancers at Taiwan’s Cloud Gate Dance Theatre. The light poles rise gradually from lower to higher and finally meet at the pylon, like a dancer leaping into the air and pausing at the highest point in a moment of prayer.
What is even more intriguing is that the “dancer” faces Guanyin Mountain on the Bali side of the river. Chang says this detail shows how the design team wove local culture into the bridge, allowing a world-class engineering project not only to cross an estuary but also to form an emotional connection with the land beneath it.
Even light and shadow were built into the bridge’s design.
The bridge deck is made of welded steel box girders and is only 4.1 meters thick, reducing weight as much as possible. Seen from a distance, it appears as a light, slender line across the sky.
The design team also treated natural sunlight as a kind of pigment. The pylon’s constantly shifting three-dimensional double-curved surfaces refract light and shadow differently as the angle of the sun changes. From afar, the color of the steel cables nearly blends into the sky, quietly “disappearing” into the skyline. The massive bridge seems to lose its weight, floating lightly over the mouth of the Tamsui River.
In the exhibition, the models, construction photographs, and pylon-evolution display appear to simply present engineering details. What they truly reveal, however, is a way of thinking: not choosing between aesthetics and engineering, but recognizing that “aesthetics solves engineering challenges, and engineering supports the realization of aesthetics,” as Chang puts it.
Taiwan’s resilience, built into a bridge
Danjiang Bridge is not the work of one person. It is an engineering achievement completed by many individuals working together.
Behind it are transnational teamwork, cross-cultural adjustments, the support of migrant workers from overseas, and first-of-their-kind innovations and technologies. It is also the work of small and medium-sized enterprises across many of Taiwan's industries—people who, as the saying goes, “work hard for a time, and take pride for a lifetime.” There are far more stories behind the bridge than can be fully told here.
For many cities, a bridge defines the landscape. For Taiwan, Danjiang Bridge is more than a bridge across an estuary. It is a bridge that symbolizes and gives tangible form to Taiwan’s resilience.

Far-right AfD set for historic eastern win, raising pressure on Merz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:17:31 UTC
01:17:31 KST

Voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt elect a new parliament on Sunday, with the far-right Alternative for Germany well ahead of every other party and Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU) sliding toward one of their weakest results in a region they have governed for decades.
Polls put the AfD above 40%, which would be the party’s strongest showing in any state election. If several smaller parties fall short of the 5% threshold needed to enter the legislature, the far right’s path to an outright majority — and to forming a state government for the first time — could become possible.
According to experts who have long studied political and social change in Germany’s ex-communist east, the AfD’s surge there has been fueled by the migration crisis, the economic fallout of later shocks — including the war in Ukraine — and the failure of Chancellor Merz, the CDU and recent coalition governments to address eastern voters’ concerns.
“Even after nearly 36 years of reunification, the East has not reached West Germany’s prosperity level,” said Jana Hensel, an expert on eastern Germany, adding that enormous economic and social differences remain between the western states and the east.
“We still conduct all the important inner-German debates from a West German perspective. Many East Germans have the feeling of living on the periphery of the country and of not being seen,” she told Anadolu.
That discontent has become most evident in the collapse of support for Merz’s Christian Democrats in Saxony-Anhalt. The CDU has governed the state with changing coalition partners for decades. In 2021, it won 37.1% and formed a government with the Social Democrats and Free Democrats. Five years later, the same party is polling around 23%.
Hensel, who has written several books on eastern Germany, said Sunday’s election is not only about state and local politics. Anger at Merz’s economic policy in Berlin and at the government’s course on Ukraine has fed the AfD’s gains, she said.
“In East Germany, there is a widespread feeling that people do not feel seen. And of course this state election is also a ‘no’ to Friedrich Merz,” she said. “It’s also a vote against the federal government’s policies. It’s a vote against Friedrich Merz’s reform package,” she added, pointing to the chancellor’s unpopular plans on tax, pensions and healthcare.
Antipathy toward Merz in Saxony-Anhalt has been strong enough that CDU lead candidate and Premier Sven Schulze spent the campaign distancing himself from Berlin, while the chancellor largely stayed away from major public rallies and voter-facing events.
The AfD has gained momentum in Saxony-Anhalt behind Ulrich Siegmund, a popular far-right politician who has reached beyond the party’s traditional base.
The 35-year-old has run a highly visible campaign, with a strong social media operation and close contact with voters. So confident of victory, he has already published a government program and a 100-day plan built around tougher immigration rules.
Siegmund has pledged to expel people without legal status “from the first minute,” expand deportation detention from a handful of sites to hundreds and require asylum seekers to work or lose benefits.
Steffen Mau, a professor of sociology at Humboldt University in Berlin, noted that the message is resonating in a state with weaker growth than much of Germany, higher unemployment and an older, shrinking population.
“The population overall is shrinking, but migration is increasing,” Mau told Anadolu. “So very often shrinking societies fear migration, fear newcomers.” That pattern, he added, “is something that we can observe not only there, but also in other East German parts.”
While the AfD climbs on an anti-immigration platform, mainstream parties warn that a far-right victory would sour the political climate, deepen polarization and further embolden neo-Nazis and other right-wing extremist groups.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch as a confirmed far-right extremist organization. Citing that assessment, the CDU and the other mainstream parties have said throughout the campaign that they will not cooperate with the AfD or enter a coalition with it after Sunday’s vote, regardless of the result.
As the AfD has campaigned hard in Saxony-Anhalt, the war in Ukraine has been its other main line of attack on Merz. During the election campaign, the party has said Germany should end military and financial support for Kyiv, lift energy sanctions on Moscow and return to cheap Russian gas.
Experts say the war has laid bare the gap in priorities between west and east. In much of western Germany, cutting Russian energy and arming Ukraine were widely seen as a strategic necessity. In parts of the east, those same policies were often treated as decisions imposed from outside, with ordinary households left to pay the price in higher energy bills.
“Nothing has benefited the AfD as strongly as Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine. Since then it has grown again,” Hensel said. The party, she continued, “grew in 2015 during the migration crisis and now again since the start of Russia’s war of aggression. That is the decisive reason.” East and West, she added, “look at this conflict differently.”
Hensel said Merz’s government had not answered those eastern doubts and that, unlike under former Chancellor Angela Merkel, the lack of diplomatic efforts has further strengthened the AfD’s hand on this topic.
As the latest polls show the AfD still rising and the CDU heading for one of its worst results, many analysts expect a large far-right win and a weak night for the conservatives on Sunday to reopen debate over Merz’s standing inside his own party.
“I think it's quite significant, we will have a shift in the political landscape, an enormous success, most possibly for the right-wing extremist AfD,” Mau said. “And this will have repercussions on the federal government in Berlin. It will put Chancellor Merz very much under pressure.”
A poll by public broadcaster ARD this week found 83% of eligible voters nationwide dissatisfied with Merz’s performance, the lowest satisfaction rating the survey has recorded for a sitting chancellor.
Hensel said the result in Saxony-Anhalt would likely shake politics in Berlin and could have consequences for Merz, triggering a debate within his own party.
“What happens in Berlin in the coming days, nobody can say at the moment. I don’t think the coalition government will collapse,” she said. “But whether Friedrich Merz will continue to be chancellor of the Federal Republic — one can at least put a question mark after that.”
A leadership fight in the Christian Democrats after the election would not by itself dissolve the Bundestag or trigger a snap election. If party pressure forces Merz out, parliament could elect a new chancellor without a national vote.

Russia’s War Is Closing Its Own Skies as Airport Shutdowns Hit 993 in One Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:16:34 UTC
01:16:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s War Is Closing Its Own Skies as Airport Shutdowns Hit 993 in One Month
Russia’s civilian aviation network suffered record disruption in August as Ukrainian drone operations repeatedly forced airports to suspend flights, with nearly 1,000 temporary closures recorded in a single month even before President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly declared Russian airspace increasingly unsafe.
According to The Wall Street Journal, citing aviation-security firm Osprey Flight Solutions, Russian airports were temporarily shut 993 times during August—more than a third above the July figure, WSJ reported on September 3.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
On an average day, drone threats forced temporary restrictions at 32 airports across Russia, including major aviation hubs around Moscow and St. Petersburg.
The disruption over the summer has already surpassed the total recorded during all of last year.
From June through August, Russia experienced 2,182 temporary airport shutdowns. By comparison, 1,923 such cases were recorded throughout the entirety of 2025.
At the same time, Ukrainian drones are entering Russian-controlled airspace in unprecedented numbers.
Osprey estimated that around 16,000 Ukrainian drones crossed into Russian airspace in August, much of which Moscow continues to keep open to civilian aircraft.
Around 11,000 drones were recorded in June and more than 13,000 in July. Earlier in 2026, monthly totals generally remained between 4,000 and 5,000, apart from May, when the figure rose to 7,544.
The rising number of UAVs, combined with Russian air defenses attempting to intercept them and widespread GPS interference, is increasingly complicating civilian aviation.
Ukraine fully closed its own airspace to commercial traffic when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Moscow, by contrast, has kept most of Russia’s airspace open, restricting civilian flights primarily in regions closer to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy warned international airlines and insurers on September 1 that the risks of continuing to operate in Russian airspace were mounting.
“Although the Russian authorities do not report this as they should, the Russian sky will de facto be closed: the war unleashed by Russia is closing its sky,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that Ukraine does not target civilian aviation.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such—not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” the Ukrainian President stated.
Ukraine has also formally raised the issue with the International Civil Aviation Organization, arguing that Russia’s decision to keep civilian aircraft operating amid increasing military activity creates unnecessary risks.
Russian officials insist they will prevent major disruption.
“We are constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have solutions for all of this. We will not allow any significant disruption to civil aviation,” Russian Transport Minister Andrei Nikitin said.
The operational figures, however, are moving in the opposite direction.
In the first three days of September alone, Russian airlines canceled an average of 86 flights per day, according to Flightradar24.
August exceeded that level on only two individual days—August 10, when 104 flights were canceled, and August 18, when 93 were called off.
Earlier, Turkey’s largest private airline, Pegasus Airlines, turned several Moscow-bound aircraft around mid-flight and canceled dozens of services to Russia overnight, amid drone-related disruptions at Russian airports and warnings from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the growing risks of operating in Russian airspace.

Ukraine’s FPV Drones Burn Rare Russian 2S43 Malva, One of Moscow’s Newest Howitzers, Video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:16:03 UTC
01:16:03 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s FPV Drones Burn Rare Russian 2S43 Malva, One of Moscow’s Newest Howitzers, Video
Ukrainian FPV drone operators destroyed a Russian 2S43 Malva, one of Moscow’s relatively rare new wheeled self-propelled howitzers, the 22nd Separate Mechanized Brigade reported on September 4.
Ukrainian reconnaissance first located the Russian artillery system before FPV crews were directed toward the target. Several drones subsequently struck the Malva, destroying the vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The 2S43 Malva is a 152mm self-propelled howitzer mounted on an 8×8 wheeled chassis. Russia began serial deliveries of the system to its military in late 2023, introducing it as a more mobile alternative to heavier tracked artillery.
At around 32 metric tons, the Malva can reach speeds of approximately 50 mph and travel up to roughly 620 miles without refueling. It carries a five-person crew and up to 30 artillery rounds.
Its primary weapon is the 152mm 2A64 gun, the same type used by Russia’s tracked 2S19 Msta-S self-propelled howitzer. With standard ammunition, the gun has an effective range of roughly 15 miles.
The wheeled chassis allows the Malva to move between firing positions more quickly than many traditional tracked artillery systems, an increasingly important capability on a battlefield where drones can locate artillery shortly after it opens fire.
But the system remains relatively scarce. Open-source estimates indicate that only a few dozen Malvas have entered Russian service, making each confirmed loss particularly notable as Moscow continues introducing the relatively new platform.
Ukrainian units have previously targeted Malvas with drones, gradually adding the system to the growing list of modern Russian artillery vulnerable to FPV strikes.
The 22nd Brigade marked the latest loss with a play on the howitzer’s floral name.
“The ‘Malvas’ by the house will bloom no more,” the brigade said.
Previously, Ukrainian FPV drone operators from the MARA Unmanned Systems Battalion destroyed what the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade described as possibly one of the last Russian infantry fighting vehicles remaining in its area of responsibility on the Lyman front.

2026 Ig Nobels honor cockroach milk, interspecies kissing, taunting venomous snakes, and more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:15:06 UTC
01:15:06 KST

How nutritious is cockroach milk? At last, this burning question is getting the recognition it so sorely deserves: the team answering it has received one of the 2026 Ig Nobel Prizes.
The annual awards, which recognize the most absurd research science can offer, were handed out at a ceremony in Zurich on Thursday. And yes, the winners in chemistry—Leonard Chavas, now at DECTRIS Japan, and Subramanian Ramaswamy, now at Purdue University—really did calorie count the milk proteins cockroaches make to nourish their young. (Their results, based on advanced x-ray crystallography, indicate cockroach milk is more than three times as energy-dense as ordinary dairy.)
The insect enthusiasts were in good company: other winners included University of Oxford scientists who devised a proper definition of “kissing” in order to argue that human ancestors smooched Neanderthals, a team that bravely (or stupidly) taunted venomous snakes to study why they bite and researchers who confirmed what we all intuitively know: people who drive expensive cars tend to be jerks.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A posthumous award in medicine was given to the late Japanese physiologist Tokuji Unno for his landmark 1977 study on the aerodynamics of nose blowing. The schnoz was a theme: another award went to a study that showed parents like their babies’ scents—but find their teenagers’ odors repulsive.
Speaking of foul-smelling things, where would humanity be without the now Ig Nobel–winning knowledge of what happens to 1,000 pairs of underpants buried for months at sites around the globe?
Past prizewinners have run the gamut of science that, at first glance, appears to be entirely unessential. There was the physician who analyzed the growth rate of his fingernails for 35 years and the geologist who looked into why his colleagues lick rocks. Or how about the research duo that examined how bedsheets get wrinkled—or the team that perfected the arcane art of collecting whale boogers via remote-controlled helicopters? And let’s not forget the stalwart scientists behind the world-shattering revelation that tortoises don’t notice other animals yawning.
While, on the surface, the Ig Nobels might seem like a silly good time, there is a point to the zaniness: the awards’ twofold purpose is to make people laugh and then think. Scientific advancements don’t proceed in linear fashion; they usually zig and zag before reaching any point of significance for everyday people’s lives. Take, for instance, research honored in 2012 in which scientists used a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) machine to find dubious signs of “brain activity” in a stone-dead Atlantic salmon. That seemingly laughable result ultimately led neuroscientists to rethink how they analyze their data.
Because of concern for the safety of international winners, this was the first time the awards bash occurred outside the U.S., but American fans of absurd science won’t miss out on the fun entirely. A smaller ceremony will be held in Cambridge, Mass., on September 24.

Israel’s Gaza expulsion plans, Nepal’s loss and damage test, and Syria’s $7 billion deal: The Cheat Sheet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:15:04 UTC
01:15:04 KST

Share & more
Our editors’ weekly take on humanitarian news, trends, and developments from around the globe.
On our radar
Israeli ministers push plan to expel Palestinians from Gaza
Two Israeli government ministers have said that Israel is seeking to forcibly expel Palestinians from the Gaza Strip en masse – which would be a war crime under international law. On 2 September, Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel was seeking Donald Trump’s permission to expel Palestinians from Gaza, adding there was “no real solution for Gaza without migration” and that the Israeli government was “organised and ready to get them out”. On 3 September, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir followed up by saying that Israel has a plan to forcibly expel all 2.1 million Palestinians from Gaza over the next six years, starting with 250,000 people in the first year. Ben-Gvir said there were countries willing to take in expelled Palestinians, but did not specify which ones. The comments come in the lead-up to tightly contested Israeli elections next month. However, the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza is something Israeli leaders and government agencies have consistently mooted since 7 October 2023. According to reporting, Israel’s Intelligence Ministry proposed plans for the removal of Palestinians from Gaza as early as 13 October 2023. The vast majority of Palestinians are barred from entering the nearly 70% of Gaza currently under direct Israeli military occupation. Around 2.1 million Palestinians are crammed into the remaining territory, over which Israel also exerts significant control, including continuing to restrict aid access and the blocking of any reconstruction efforts.
Nepal flood puts loss and damage funding to the test
Nepal’s catastrophic Himalayan flood is rapidly becoming a test case for climate justice. On 26 August, a collapse of glacier, rock, and ice near the Nepal-China border sent a wall of material down the Bhoteloshi-Trishuli river system, killing more than 1,250 people in Nepal and leaving more than 4,200 people missing. Kathmandu formally asked the UN’s Loss and Damage Fund for an unspecified amount of emergency financing, arguing that the destruction exceeded its response capacity. On 3 September, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said the government had sought an immediate $20 million from the fund, adding that this assistance alone was “definitely not adequate”. The appeal is unusually urgent: The fund has yet to make its first country payout, and its next board meeting is not until December. Khanal has also called on the US, China, and India – the world’s top greenhouse gas emitters – to contribute “climate compensation”. Officials have estimated Nepal’s direct losses at $2.56 billion, with recovery costs at $4-$7 billion. For more on how early warning systems were overwhelmed and on what can be done to prevent similar disasters in the future, read our in-depth analysis.
Somalia’s political fight is spilling onto the battlefield
Somalia’s insecurity is worsening. Federal forces this week beat off an attack on Baidoa, the largest city in South West State, by militia loyal to ousted governor Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. The government accused Laftagareen’s fighters of collaborating with al-Shabab insurgents in the assault. Türkiye has thrown its weight behind the President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s government. A Turkish drone was reportedly used in a strike on a pro-Laftagareen general, while Ankara’s F-16 fighter jets have also been in the air, reflecting a relationship that has evolved from “Islamic humanitarianism” to hardnosed strategic interest. Several federal states and regions oppose Mohamud, accusing him of centralising power, pushing electoral reforms to extend his rule, and ousting uncooperative regional leaders. Laftagareen suffered that fate in March, triggering repeated attacks on Baidoa by his militia. Meanwhile, the drawdown – and looming funding crisis – of the African Union's peacekeeping force is intensifying the power struggle between Mogadishu and the states. No unified security architecture exists, creating fertile ground for further fragmentation.
Algeria’s rare intervention betrays fears of a fracturing Sahel
A surprising outcome of the failed coup against Niger’s military junta on 29 August was the arrival, a day later, of an Algerian air detachment, including four SU-30 fighter jets. The powerful deployment was a clear signal that Algeria was breaking from its non-interventionist traditions and wanted its troubled southern neighbours in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger – to take note. Algeria was not involved in the quashing of the putsch against General Abdourahamane Tchiani by disgruntled soldiers angered by command failings in the war against jihadist insurgents. That win was down to the presidential guard, backed by Russia’s Africa Corps. But Algeria does fear state collapse, triggered by Islamist insurgencies that have their roots in its own violence of the 1990s. Algeria’s new-found interest happens to coincide with the start of construction of a Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline that will stretch from Nigeria to the Mediterranean coast. While Algeria offers a strategic alternative to Russia’s military intervention in the AES, military backing alone will not resolve the political grievances that fuel armed opposition and leave Sahelian juntas vulnerable to coups.
Tech and rights collide as new Human Rights Council session begins
A new session of the Human Rights Council opens 7 September in Geneva, with a wide swathe of escalating crises in the foreground and the UN’s budget crunch overhead. New updates or sessions on genocide prevention, an updated database on businesses in Israeli settlements in Palestine, and examinations of rights in Sudan and Afghanistan, are among the many pressing issues on the schedule. Tech is colliding with human rights and that’s reflected on the agenda: There are sessions on technology-facilitated gender-based violence, protecting human rights defenders in the digital era, how mercenaries use tech, and how artificial intelligence affects cultural and development rights. As on any multilateral stage these days, money troubles are never far away. Rights experts mandated by the council will be reporting less often to the General Assembly, weakening oversight and political attention, the International Service for Human Rights warned. Meanwhile, the advocacy NGO is urging more scrutiny of a country where rights and the rule of law are eroding: the United States.
Weekend read
And finally…
The pressure to tell a story of suffering
In this relatively short New York Times essay, author David Treuer deftly weaves in so many themes that are likely of interest to Cheat Sheet readers. He writes of being Indian (his word of choice for Native American) and moving from the Leech Lake Ojibwe Reservation to the hallowed halls of Princeton University, and initially feeling driven to tell false tales of suffering because that’s what people expected of someone like him, not understanding that someone like him could be relatively happy, or complicated, or even mediocre. And the realisation that he had also been consuming lies about Princeton vs. his home, which were really about civilised vs. savage. Treuer’s piece offers plenty of food for thought about the expectations and narratives we place on marginalised groups – and, ultimately, on ourselves.

Iran shifting military doctrine toward preemptive attack: Army spokesman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:07:59 UTC

Ahmet Dursun, Baybars Can, and Rania Abushamala
04 September 2026•Update: 04 September 2026
Iran has been gradually shifting its military doctrine toward preemptive attack since the June 2025 war, an army spokesman said Friday.
“When we face an American threat, we defend ourselves, and international law allows us to defend ourselves preemptively,” Mohammad Akraminia said during a program broadcast by Iran’s state television.
Akraminia said Iranian forces targeted US bases stretching from Jordan to the United Arab Emirates in response to American attacks.
Iran also destroyed air defense systems at US bases across the region, he claimed, warning that Tehran would respond “faster and more forcefully” if it faced another Israeli attack.
“Some of these bases housed radar facilities and air defense systems, which were destroyed,” he said.
“With the destruction of these systems, targeting the occupied territories and the Zionist regime’s bases in the region has become much easier than in the past,” he added.
Commenting on Israeli threats against Iran, Akraminia said Israel was currently preoccupied with elections and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was making domestically focused statements for electoral purposes.
He stressed that any Israeli attack would be met with strikes carried out “more easily, more quickly and more forcefully.”
On June 13-24, 2025, Israel, with US backing, carried out a military campaign against Iran targeting military infrastructure, missile launch sites and nuclear facilities, while also assassinating senior military commanders and nuclear scientists. Iran responded by launching more than 550 ballistic missiles and hundreds of drones at Israeli military and intelligence sites. The 12-day war ended with a ceasefire on June 24.
Regional tensions have escalated since US-Israeli attacks on Iran began on Feb. 28 this year, triggering Tehran's retaliatory missile and drone attacks against Israel and US interests in countries across the region. Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 18 concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled amid disagreements over security arrangements in the strait.

Iran-Russia alliance grows despite US pressure
TEHRAN — Russia’s robust and uncompromising support for Iran in the face of US military adventurism and all-out economic warfare has made it abundantly clear that the strategic partnership between Tehran and Moscow will never be swayed, deterred, or disrupted by outside pressure.
Rather than achieving its intended goal of isolating Tehran, Washington’s aggressive, coercive policies and warmongering have produced the exact opposite effect, acting as a powerful catalyst that has brought Iran and Russia closer together than ever before.
Moscow has repeatedly and forcefully denounced the unprovoked US war on Iran, while flatly dismissing Washington’s economic pressure as an illegitimate tool of Western hegemony. The United States, meanwhile, has sought to aggressively tout the supposed impact of its unilateral sanctions in an obvious bid to distract global public opinion from the strategic failure of its joint military campaign with Israel against Iran, which began six months ago.
In an effort to tighten its economic siege, the administration of President Donald Trump has pressured other sovereign nations to unilaterally sever their legitimate trade and financial relations with Iran under the banner of what the White House has termed “Operation Economic Outcast.” In characteristic hyperbole, Washington went so far as to compare this sweeping sanctions blitz to the historic Allied invasion of Normandy in World War II, theatrically nicknaming it an “economic D-Day.”
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared that the European Union had formally joined Washington’s campaign to completely sever Iran from the global financial architecture. Furthermore, in an interview on Fox News on Wednesday, Bessent blatantly demanded that Russia “stay away” from Iran and abandon its ties with Tehran—a provocative demand that was promptly and decisively rejected by Moscow.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov affirmed that Russia will never give up its strategic relations with its long-standing partners to appease Washington. Peskov declared that it is entirely unrealistic for the United States to believe it can monopolize international relations or dictate terms to independent global powers, emphasizing that Russia has its own dependable partners and friends and will vigorously maintain, protect, and expand these friendly and partnership relations regardless of Western hostility.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also explicitly and unequivocally expressed Russia’s profound support for Iran during his high-profile meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
“As I have repeatedly said before, Russia is standing in full solidarity with the people of Iran. We admire your courage and resilience in your fight for your national interests,” Putin told Pezeshkian during their crucial meeting held on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan’s capital of Bishkek. He further noted that the friendly relations between Russia and Iran are developing steadily and dynamically across all areas, adhering strictly to the letter and the overarching spirit of the historic Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.
Russia and Iran have significantly and systematically expanded their multifaceted cooperation in recent years, deepening their bonds across a wide and comprehensive range of vital areas, including bilateral trade, energy integration, strategic transportation corridors such as the International North–South Transport Corridor, and advanced defense cooperation. In January 2025, the two countries officially signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement, providing a rock-solid, institutionalized framework for further strengthening bilateral cooperation, neutralizing illegal Western sanctions, and consolidating their joint resistance against unilateralism across multiple strategic sectors.
Moscow’s principled and unyielding stance comes even as CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly attempted to intimidate the Kremlin during an unannounced, high-stakes trip to Moscow on Tuesday. Ratcliffe reportedly issued direct warnings demanding that Russia immediately scale down its support for Iran, backing the threat with Washington’s earlier vows to significantly expand extraterritorial secondary sanctions against sovereign countries that refuse to cut their economic ties with Tehran.
Yet, amid mounting Western threats, ultimatums, and economic blackmails, Russia’s position leaves no room for doubt that Moscow regards its strategic partnership with Iran as a permanent, non-negotiable, and long-term priority in the emerging multipolar world order. Rather than bowing to Western pressure or succumbing to Washington’s coercive tactics, Moscow and Tehran are digging in their heels, actively turning mounting Western hostility into an enduring catalyst for deeper, irreversible strategic cooperation. Washington’s desperate efforts to drive a wedge between the two nations have completely backfired, pushing both countries ever closer together on the geopolitical and economic chessboard.
The powerful statements delivered by Putin and Peskov carry immense strategic weight in the wider context of the two-day SCO summit that concluded on Tuesday. SCO leaders—including President Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif—collectively signed the “Bishkek Declaration,” which explicitly and unequivocally condemned the joint US and Israeli war of aggression against Iran.
In the joint declaration, the leaders of the Eurasian powers denounced the military aggression as a flagrant violation of the fundamental principles and norms of international law, state sovereignty, and the United Nations Charter, warning that such reckless unilateral actions create grave, unprecedented risks to international peace, regional security, and global stability.
The SCO heads of state also officially expressed their sincere and deepest condolences on the assassination of Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, who was martyred on the first day of the joint US-Israeli war on February 28. In his SCO meeting with Pezeshkian, Putin specifically asked the Iranian president to convey his warmest regards and words of sincere, unwavering support to Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, who was elected Leader of the Islamic Revolution following the assassination of his father.
Putin’s message of support to Iran’s new Leader is significant in this context. It suggests that Moscow’s backing for Tehran is rooted not in short-term political calculations, but in a broader strategic relationship that Russia is determined to maintain.
