Iran's seven islands strengthen Hormuz control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:30:07 UTC
00:30:07 KST

Breadcrumb
The seven islands: what we know about Iran's maritime line controlling Hormuz
As Iran continues to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed, the question is no longer limited to the impact of the closure on global energy markets and the economy.
It has shifted to uncovering the mechanisms Iran uses to control what is currently the world's most sensitive shipping route.
This does not refer to Iran's military capabilities but rather to a complex network of strategic islands whose function Iran has reshaped, turning them into "fixed aircraft carriers" through which it controls shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Geographically, the Strait of Hormuz, located south of Hormozgan province, forms a natural boundary between Iran and Oman.
It is a narrow passage constrained by navigational challenges. Strong water currents and varying depths force giant tankers to follow specific and extremely narrow routes, increasing Tehran's ability to control and monitor them.
The area derives its strategic importance from being the world's second-busiest strait, with about 17 million barrels of crude oil passing through it every day.
This represents 40% of oil transported by sea and about 25% of total global supplies, in a region that alone holds 68% of the world's proven oil and gas reserves.
Characteristics of the Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz is estimated to be 167 kilometres long, while its width varies depending on the area.
It reaches about 95 kilometres at its widest point and narrows to about 33 kilometres at its narrowest.
However, official shipping lanes are much narrower. Each lane designated for vessel traffic is no more than 3 kilometres wide, with a buffer zone separating the inbound and outbound lanes.
The depth of the Strait of Hormuz also varies, reaching more than 60 metres in some areas, while ranging between 30 and 40 metres in shallow areas.
Although this depth is suitable for giant oil tankers and heavy vessels, it forces large ships to follow specific and limited routes, increasing the area's security importance.
The narrowest point of the strait is 21 nautical miles wide, located between Iran's Larak Island and Oman's Greater Quoin Island.
Until 1979, shipping traffic followed the shortest route between the Quoin and Musandam islands.
That year, Oman announced that vessels should pass through an area outside the range of Quoin Island in order to reduce security risks to routes near its islands and territory.
For about 60 years, the shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz passed through Iranian territorial waters.
But Tehran rejected this after it was subjected to war and closed the strait, announcing the opening of a northern route for vessels after they obtained permission from the Iranian navy.
Iran has also held negotiations in recent weeks with Oman to establish a new shipping route.
An agreement was reached, although it was not announced. However, Iranian authorities continue to refuse to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without a response from Washington to its conditions for ending the war permanently, lifting the blockade and sanctions, releasing its frozen assets and other demands.
An island shield to retain Hormuz
Iran's ability to control the Strait of Hormuz is not limited to its coastal capabilities stretching for about 160 kilometres.
A group of Iranian islands also plays a vital role in strengthening this control within these waters.
These islands have given Iran a unique geopolitical position at the entrance to the Gulf, allowing it to control the strait and traffic passing through it.
Seven islands form Iran's curved defensive line in the area for controlling shipping traffic: Hormuz, Larak, Qeshm, Hengam, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa.
The last three islands are disputed between Iran and the United Arab Emirates but are currently under Iranian control.
Four of these islands are located at the entrance to the strait — Hormuz, Qeshm, Larak and Hengam — while the other three disputed islands lie west of this curved line.
The short distances between these islands and the depth of the waters in this area force warships and oil tankers to pass close to them when entering the Strait of Hormuz.
This currently exposes these vessels to threats from fast boats, mines or drones stationed on the islands.
These islands are so important to Iran that former Iranian navigation official Ali Ezzati described them in a statement as "fixed aircraft carriers that cannot be sunk".
The seven islands
1 — Hormuz Island
The island is about 8 kilometres wide and is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas port.
Over the past centuries, Hormuz has been regarded as the key to entering the Gulf. The naming of the strait after it is evidence of this status.
The island is oval-shaped, covering about 42 square kilometres along the strait, and is a tourist destination in southern Iran.
Hormuz City is located in the north and is the island's only population centre. Its population stood at 5,891 according to the 2016 census.
It was under Portuguese occupation for more than a century before Iran regained control of it in 1622 under Shah Abbas.
The Iranian Achaemenid Empire used the island as a naval base more than 2,500 years ago.
Throughout history, it served as a commercial meeting point for traders from India, China and other eastern markets.
The Portuguese viewed it as an impregnable fortress overlooking the meeting point between the Gulf waters and the Indian Ocean.
In the modern era, which has seen the passage of giant oil tankers, Hormuz Island has retained its strategic position despite its relative distance from the deep-water shipping channel.
2 — Larak Island
Larak is located 40 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, the centre of Hormozgan province, 20 kilometres west of Hormuz Island and 12 kilometres east of Qeshm Island.
Larak is unique in being the Iranian island directly adjacent to the deep-water channel in the Strait of Hormuz that is suitable for the passage of giant oil tankers.
Since Iran announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israeli war on 28 February, Larak has been closely linked to developments involving the shipping route.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched an alternative route for shipping through Iranian territorial waters, bypassing the historic route that passed through Omani waters.
The new Iranian route passes south of Larak Island, overlooking the vital energy corridor, making its location the main pillar of Tehran's military system aimed at retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz.
The island lies at the easternmost point of the Gulf and is administratively part of Iran's Hormozgan province.
It is oval-shaped and extends 10.5 kilometres from northeast to southwest.
3 — Qeshm Island
Qeshm is the largest island in the Gulf, with an area twice that of Bahrain, which is the second-largest island in the region.
Qeshm is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, 40 kilometres east of Bandar Lengeh and 31 kilometres east of Greater Tunb.
It is 140 kilometres long.
Qeshm is characterised by its sandy terrain, with hills spread across its central areas.
The highest point is Mount Buko, which rises 405 metres above sea level.
The island covers 1,644 square kilometres and is rich in natural resources, including oil, gas, lead, sulphur and salts.
The island had a population of 148,993 in the 2016 census, with 66,801 living in urban areas and 82,160 in villages and towns.
Over the past decade, Qeshm has become a prominent tourist destination because of its environment and natural and historical sites.
Parts of it have been part of the Global Geoparks Network under the auspices of UNESCO since 2006, as the first geopark in the Middle East.
4 — Hengam Island
Hengam is located just 3 kilometres south of Qeshm Island.
It is about 50 kilometres from Oman's Ghanam Island and shares with Larak Island direct oversight of the deep edge of the shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
The island contains scattered population centres across an area of about 50 square kilometres south of Qeshm.
It contains deposits of salt, soil and lead.
It is 10 kilometres long and between 3 and 6 kilometres wide.
During the Qajar monarchy, Britain established facilities and military bases on the island.
Hengam's coastline is suitable for deploying fleets and naval vessels because of the deep waters surrounding its shores, making it suitable as a berth for warships and submarines.
Its location in the middle of the Gulf waters, adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz and Qeshm, has given it major strategic and military importance.
This has made it historically vulnerable to attempts at control by successive foreign powers.
It was occupied by the Portuguese during the Safavid era and later by the British during the Qajar period.
5 — Greater Tunb
Greater Tunb is one of three islands disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It lies 31 kilometres southwest of Qeshm Island and faces the Strait of Hormuz to the west.
The island is one of the main pillars of Tehran's defence and military doctrine for protecting and managing the strait.
The island is 12 kilometres from Lesser Tunb, 50 kilometres from Abu Musa and about 82 kilometres from Al Hamra Island in Ras Al Khaimah.
It lies north of the Gulf's median line and is roughly circular, covering about 12 square kilometres.
It is predominantly dry and sandy, with little vegetation, while hills in the north reach a maximum height of 53 metres.
6 — Lesser Tunb
Lesser Tunb is the other disputed island between Tehran and Abu Dhabi.
It lies on the northern side of the Gulf's median line, 12 kilometres from Greater Tunb, 50 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 92 kilometres from the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE.
The island covers only about 2 square kilometres, which explains the name "Lesser".
It is roughly triangular in shape, with a width ranging between 1,100 and 1,500 metres.
A dark rocky hill rises 35 metres above sea level in its northwestern part.
Its shores are steep, amid a hot and humid climate, and it has no fresh water.
Unlike Greater Tunb, it is uninhabited and is predominantly used for military and security purposes related to protection and surveillance.
Its spread of rocks and salt domes gives it rugged terrain.
7 — Abu Musa
Abu Musa is the third island disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It forms the westernmost point of Iran's maritime defensive arc and is the final link in the Iranian defence system stationed at the Gulf's gateway.
It is 67 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 62 kilometres from Sharjah port in the UAE.
The island has an airport and a seaport, with regular flights operating between it and Bandar Abbas.
There are also passenger sea transport services using boats and vessels departing from Bandar Lengeh two to three times a week.
Its area is larger than that of both Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb.
It has an irregular shape, while its central and southern areas are flat and sandy.
Its oil resources are limited to the Mubarak field, located offshore to the east of the island.
Its oil is classified as among the highest-quality crude extracted in the Gulf basin.
Revolutionary Guard Navy responsible for security
According to Iran's naval military divisions and formations, the first and fifth naval regions of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy are responsible for securing this curved defensive line and its surrounding area in the Strait of Hormuz.
The First Naval Region, known as "Sahib al-Zaman", is one of the five naval regions of the Revolutionary Guard.
It operates under the supervision of the naval force and the "Khatam al-Anbiya 2" naval headquarters.
The command headquarters of this region is located in Bandar Abbas.
It is the formation closest to the Strait of Hormuz and is responsible for conducting defensive and offensive operations in the area of the passage.
Rear Adm. Abbas Gholamshahi commands it.
On 4 November 2012, the Revolutionary Guard Navy established its Fifth Naval Region, named "Imam Mohammad Baqer", in Bandar Lengeh, overlooking the Gulf waters west of the Strait of Hormuz.
It assigned the region responsibility for controlling the area extending from the end of Qeshm Island, through an area of four islands that became known militarily as the "Naz'at" islands, to the west of Kish Island.
Under this military division, protection and security of the Strait of Hormuz itself was assigned to the First Naval Region as a direct naval mission.
The Fifth Naval Region, meanwhile, was independently tasked with protecting and securing the "Naz'at" island system in the western extension of the Strait of Hormuz.
The four defensive Naz'at islands are Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, Abu Musa and Siri Island.
Tehran relies on a diverse and hybrid arsenal to close or obstruct shipping through this strategic passage.
It combines coastal and mobile weapons along the coast and islands, ranging from underground missile cities and naval and coastal anti-ship missile launchers to fast boats, attack drones and naval mines capable of blocking the route of giant tankers.
Iran also relies on military capabilities beyond its coasts and islands, in both its missile and drone capacities, to tighten its control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akram Nia previously said that "Iran can establish control over the Strait of Hormuz from any point on its territory".

U.S. Investigates Deadly Strike on Wedding in Iran, Vance Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:26:32 UTC
00:26:32 KST

The U.S. is investigating a strike on a wedding in southern Iran, Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday, as reports suggest American weapons killed at least five people and injured dozens of others.
“We’re investigating it because obviously we care,” Vance told reporters. “We want to know.”
The strike represents the U.S.’s latest controversial action in its war with Iran, raising questions about its conduct and civilian harm. Washington and Tehran have escalated their attacks this week, ending a lull in hostilities since July.
But Vance said he was “extremely skeptical” about reports coming from Iranian state media, arguing they have “not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far.”
Iranian state media reported that a residential building in Kuhestak was attacked on Tuesday evening, where a wedding was being celebrated. Among the casualties was a 4-year-old kid. Reuters and the New York Times independently verified footage from the scene and found that a wedding was taking place when the building was struck.
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that it “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”—and responded to a broader barrage of American attacks by launching missiles and drones at sites used by the U.S. in Middle East states. The Iranian Red Crescent Society, a humanitarian group, also urged a probe from the International Criminal Court to assess potential violations of international law.
The U.S. Central Command said Wednesday it was already looking into reports of the incident but argued that the “U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps],” referring to Iran’s armed forces branch.
Vance also defended U.S. military action, telling reporters: “If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran: when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.”
What we know about the strike
On the evening of Sept. 1, CENTCOM reported strikes on military targets, including “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Iranian media later reported four deaths and at least 68 injured in Kuhestak, a coastal town on the Strait of Hormuz, where trade has been bottlenecked since the start of the U.S.-Iran war in late February. The strikes happened at around 9:30 p.m. local time, per the Red Crescent.
Analyses of footage from the incident conducted by Reuters and the New York Times reveal that wedding guests were gathered in a Kuhestak building. Amid the celebration, what was likely a U.S. munition hit the building and, as the Times put it, “brought down the roof.”
Experts told Reuters and the Times that weapon fragments seen in Iranian media were consistent with what Americans have used.
The attacks on Kuhestak also hit a communications tower roughly 100 m away from the building. A human rights group told the Associated Press that one of the four people initially reported killed—a 16-year-old—was struck by shrapnel near the tower rather than at the wedding. Iranian state television said Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had since died in hospital following the strike, bringing the reported death toll to five.
Axios reported that CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike.
Civilian casualties raise concern
The Red Crescent sent a letter to the International Criminal Court Wednesday calling for “an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” citing the “civilian character” of the strike’s location.
The organization also argued that under the Rome Statute, intentionally directing attacks on civilians and knowingly launching a clearly excessive attack may constitute “war crimes.” However, both Iran and the U.S. are nonparties to the Rome Statute, so the ICC does not have automatic jurisdiction over them.
Still, “the laws of war state that civilians are protected from military attacks,” Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “A wedding is not a military objective, particularly in a civilian residential building. It is clear that there was a direct missile hit to the home. This would render the attack unlawful.”
It’s also not the U.S.’s first involvement in strikes that hit civilian structures without obvious military use and that endangered or killed civilians. On the first day of the war with Iran on Feb. 28, a U.S. Tomahawk missile hit a primary school in Minab—just 30 km (18 mi) away from Kuhestak—where more than 100 children were killed.
O’Brien, however, says she is skeptical about any result from the U.S.-led investigation of the wedding strike: “The U.S. track record is to only investigate when allegations gain significant public traction, and even when any convictions occur, the penalties are minor or pardons are given.”

Lack of Oversight Fuels Power Sector Corruption, Iraqi Lawmaker Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:22:00 UTC
00:22:00 KST

Reported by
An Iraqi lawmaker has blamed a systemic lack of public procurement oversight for widespread corruption in the country's electricity contracts, revealing that parliament is drafting new legislation to bridge the regulatory gap.
Speaking to OCCRP, Taha Al-Difai, head of the Iraqi Parliament's Integrity Committee, said the absence of government oversight on public energy contracts allowed violations to proliferate unchecked.
“In the past, there was oversight provided by inspectors' offices, but currently, such oversight is absent… contracting procedures proceed easily without supervision,” Al-Difai said.
He noted that the Federal Board of Supreme Audit currently reviews contracts only after they have been signed. To resolve the issue, Al-Difai said parliament plans to enact an “internal oversight” law allowing contracts to be audited prior to signing. The draft is scheduled for a first reading next week.
He also called for amendments to Iraq’s financial disclosure rules to broaden scrutiny over the sources of public officials’ wealth and property.
Al-Difai’s remarks follow the recent conviction of senior energy officials by the Central Anti-Corruption Criminal Court. The rulings can still be appealed.
The director general of the state-owned General Company for Electrical Energy Production (Middle Euphrates Region) and his office manager were each sentenced to six years in prison and fined for accepting bribes in exchange for releasing payments owed to a private contractor. Authorities did not disclose the name of the firm that paid the bribes.
In a separate ruling, the director of financial affairs at the state-owned General Company of Electrical Energy Distribution (Middle Region) was sentenced to three years in prison for illicit enrichment. The court ordered him to repay nearly $893,500 plus an additional $203,000, representing the estimated value of his illicit gains according to the Integrity Commission. Judges also ordered the confiscation of two vehicles worth $223,000 and his wife's shares in two Iraqi properties valued at roughly $840,000.
According to a statement from the Integrity Commission, the official will remain in custody even after serving his three-year sentence until all illicitly obtained funds are returned. The court granted the commission the right to claim the assets once the verdict becomes final.
While the commission did not release the names of the convicted officials, it provided detailed descriptions of their positions and the specific charges against them.
The rulings are part of a broader anti-corruption drive launched under Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi.
The campaign has targeted high-ranking figures across key government sectors. Earlier in August, federal authorities arrested the undersecretary of the Ministry of Electricity on charges of corruption and illicit enrichment, according to the official Iraqi News Agency. Authorities seized millions of dollars in cash and gold bars from his properties.
To date, the crackdown has implicated dozens of senior officials and lawmakers. In mid-July, investigations targeting corruption in the oil sector led to the recovery of $47 million in assets, alongside caches of cash and gold linked to former deputy oil minister Adnan al-Jumaili.
OCCRP could not reach the two convicted officials directly. The General Company of Electrical Energy Distribution (Middle Region) and the Ministry of Electricity did not respond to requests for comment.

Pentagon pauses controversial testosterone policy guidelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:21:41 UTC
00:21:41 KST

The Pentagon is pausing guidelines for a controversial policy that has required testosterone testing for service members aged 30 and older, Reuters reports.
The policy, which was announced in July, mandated that military personnel would get testosterone screening as part of their annual physical starting at age 30. The goal of the program was to optimize performance and to keep officers “on the leading edge of lethality,” according to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
Draft clinical guidance for that testing was posted online on Wednesday but was later removed, according to Reuters. In a statement to Scientific American, a Pentagon official confirmed the removal and said it was a temporary move, pending further updates.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The ‘Interim Guidance on Testosterone Deficiency Screenings for Active Duty and Reserve Component Personnel’ remains in effect” in the meantime, the spokesperson said. “The final clinical guidance will be issued shortly.”
Testosterone is a sex hormone involved in hair and muscle growth and sex drive, among other functions. It is present in higher levels in cisgender men than in cisgender women. But in women, it also supports libido, muscle growth, menstrual health, and more.
As Scientific American previously reported, there’s evidence that testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) can help improve libido and mood in adult men with very low testosterone—often defined as lower than 300 nanograms per deciliter (ng/dl)—but it can come with side effects such as reduced fertility. There’s also some evidence it can help treat low libido in postmenopausal women.
TRT is currently only approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for men with low testosterone (T) and a medical condition such as testicular cancer or pituitary disease, which can affect T levels.
But the symptoms of low testosterone—such as low energy and low libido—are common as people age and may have all sorts of causes, according to the Endocrine Society. As such, the organization says, there is “insufficient evidence” for wide screening in men without symptoms.

Learning to love the Common Combat Vessel
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:21:16 BST
00:21:16 KST

There is a common turn of phrase, used with a degree of gallows humour, that records where someone happened to be when a famous celebrity or public figure died, usually Elvis: “I remember where I was when X died…”
The more mundane the location, the funnier the punchline. You can easily add the cancellation of a naval procurement program to that concept.
In the case of the Type-83, I was sitting at my dining table eating breakfast before work, doing what I usually do in that moment: looking through my news feeds on my laptop. The article “UK to buy drone command warships instead of new destroyers” caught my eye immediately. My first reaction, over a bowl of cereal, was confusion. I checked the date to see whether it was April, and then started to mull over what I was reading. Now, don’t get me wrong; I was certainly quite excited about the Type-83. As you may have noted in my earlier article on Tempest/GCAP, it even gets a small mention as part of a future vision of integrated combat and data sharing.
So you would think I would be upset about its cancellation. Looking through the enthusiast forums and the comment sections of articles about the decision, you can see the outrage bus being revved up, with commentary about “Putin laughing” or “penny pinching,” and many saying, “This is a cut to our air defence capabilities.” Well, my view is simple: this is an excellent decision, and the government should have taken it years ago, if not for the political awkwardness of cancelling a project as prestigious as an air defence destroyer.
I know you are all itching to blame the current Labour administration, but I need to break it to you in bold type: “Type-83 was an unfunded fantasy program that was never going to be built!” As for the announcement of drone command ships, that is smoke and mirrors, but I will come back to it.
Does anyone remember the Type-43?
Along a wall of my spare room there are three tall Ikea Billy bookcases; they contain what I like to call my “reference collection,” an eclectic set of books and reference manuals I have acquired over several decades. Tucked onto one shelf between a history of the AK47 and an encyclopedia by Ian Hogg is a fairly compact book titled “Rebuilding the Royal Navy: Warship Design since 1945,” written by David K. Brown and George Moore. Moore, who died in 2005, had a long career as a naval researcher, while Brown, who died in 2008, was a naval architect who retired as Deputy Chief Naval Architect of the Royal Corps of Naval Constructors. Arguably the peak of his career was designing the excellent Castle class offshore patrol vessel, a design so robust that one of them, Dumbarton Castle, sold to the Bangladesh Navy and renamed BNS Bijoy, withstood a calculated 0.5 to 1.1 kiloton explosion only a few hundred meters away, shielded only by a grain silo, without sinking in the notorious Beirut port explosion of 2020. It was towed away to Turkey, repaired and put back into service, which is a testament to the design and to David Brown.
The book, with its focus on design and naval architecture, covers the period between 1945 and the main gate decision for the Type-45, taking in nearly every class of vessel the Royal Navy built or considered building during that period. For such a compact volume it is packed with useful information, and it remains my go-to guide for understanding Royal Navy construction decisions to this day. If you ever manage to pick up a copy, page 12 has a useful snakes and ladders diagram that really cuts to the reality of ship procurement for the Royal Navy, and tucked deep into the pages are forgotten paper designs that never were. One of them was the Type-43, an intended large Sea Dart equipped follow-on to the Type-42; there was also a smaller Type-44 design, the low-cost option, so to speak.
Various ideas for these vessels were pushed around, including the use of the Type-22 and other hull forms. None of them came to be. The Type-42 was stretched in service, and eventually things moved on to the Horizon NATO frigate project, which is a story for another day. My point is that none of these concepts got serious traction; they were all minimally funded. I am aware of other paper concepts over the years that are not mentioned in this book. At one point, for example, there was the idea of adapting the Type-82 hull to the AEGIS combat system, an idea so minor that even finding a mention of it is hard. The truth is that, without serious backing and funding, a supposed future warship program can meander for years with barely any funding until it is eventually cancelled.
The pivot that wasn’t to be, and the hubris of Boris
Before I wander any further down this digression, let’s get back to the Type-83. Do you know how much was spent on it? Roughly £1 million, which in terms of UK defence spending is a rounding error. That should tell you something important about this whole situation: in the world of multi-billion-pound warship procurement, £1 million over three years is the financial equivalent of keeping the lights on in an empty room. It is loose change, enough to fund basic CAD renders and PowerPoint slides. It shows an MOD and a navy that are seriously uninterested in a ship.
Put simply, the Type-83 was never a serious project; it was a political placeholder awaiting a convenient time to be cancelled so the Navy could pivot to something it actually wants. Talk of drones and drone command ships is smoke and mirrors, meant to distract the public from the reality that this was a cost and mass driven decision.
The Type-83 was officially announced in the previous Conservative government’s 2021 Defence Command Paper.
- The intention: it was inserted during an era of optimistic post-Brexit “Global Britain” rhetoric, and was meant to signal that the UK would maintain a high-end, blue-water carrier escort capability into the middle of the century.
- The reality: no major industrial contracts were ever issued to BAE Systems or any other contractor, and no serious technical specifications were locked down. As the Ministry of Defence’s equipment plan black hole ballooned to over £16.9 billion, everyone involved, from the MOD to naval planners, knew the Type-83 was financially dead on arrival.
That 2021 Defence Command Paper contained an enthusiastic pivot to the Pacific, and the Type-83 is what you would build if you were planning to engage in a peer conflict with China. A 12,000 ton plus “exquisite” cruiser packing a 128-cell vertical launch system (VLS) and hyper-expensive, long-range radars is a weapon system designed specifically for high-intensity, blue-water carrier battles in the South China Sea against the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN). It was a product of the brief, post-Brexit “Global Britain” era, when the UK fancied itself a Pacific naval power. Since the beginning of Putin’s three day SMO, the UK’s immediate, existential threat has been Russia. Russia does not have a massive, functional blue-water surface fleet capable of fighting a Second World War style carrier battle in the Atlantic. The Russian threat comes from quiet nuclear submarines, hypersonic cruise missiles fired from land or from bombers, and hybrid sabotage of undersea internet cables.
There is still a need for an air defence destroyer, but the Royal Navy’s technology, and tangentially Europe’s, is already a generational overmatch for the surface fleet Russia possesses. What we and Europe do have is a presence gap. If the UK had proceeded with the Type-83, the skyrocketing costs would likely have reduced the procurement to just three or four hulls. Because of maintenance cycles and the rule of threes (one deployed, one training, one in refit), that would mean only one destroyer available at any given time: the “weight, power and manpower spiral” made flesh.
How much?!
As part of the Future Air Dominance System (FADS), early concepts for the Type-83 envisioned a massive hull carrying heavyweight radars, massive power generation for directed-energy weapons such as DragonFire, and massive missile silos. The MOD faced a massive funding gap. Buying “exquisite,” multi-billion-pound platforms meant the UK could likely only afford three or four hulls. Defence Secretary Dan Jarvis explicitly noted that CCVs are a smarter investment than a “small number of large expensive ships.” By buying the CCV, the Royal Navy gets six capable air defence destroyers, allowing mass and presence to be maintained.
The Royal Navy is not the only navy coming to this conclusion in recent weeks. Just like the Type-83, Germany’s F126 has bloated into an absolute monster. At over 10,500 tons, it was the largest German surface combatant planned since the Second World War, but it was plagued by compounding delays, contractor dysfunction and projected cost overruns that threatened to push the program beyond €18 billion. Rather than sink billions more into a massive, delayed project, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius pulled the plug and pivoted to procuring up to eight smaller, proven MEKO A-200 DEU frigates from ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS).
Common Combat Vessel: smoke and mirrors
When it comes to anti-air warfare (AAW), the idea of relying heavily on uncrewed drone vessels to fire or guide missiles runs into massive physical barriers, whereas the logic for anti-submarine warfare (ASW) is completely sound. To intercept a modern supersonic or sea-skimming missile, a ship needs massive radar power (AESA) to burn through electronic jamming, plus immense electrical and hydraulic power to manage, heat, cool and rapidly fire VLS cells. Uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) are typically small, light and optimized for endurance. Sticking a 24-cell Mk 41 VLS onto an uncrewed “missile barge” requires a massive hull, major power generation such as a large diesel generator or a gas turbine, complex automated damage control and a heavy cooling infrastructure. If the drone barge has no crew to manually reset tripped breakers, handle misfires or put out a localised fire, a single malfunction turns a multi-million-pound asset into a floating paperweight. ASW, on the other hand, is slow and methodical and relies on acoustic sensor coverage over vast areas, which makes it perfect for uncrewed systems.
To act as a remote AAW magazine for a carrier strike group, a drone barge cannot just drift in the ocean; it has to maintain a transit speed of 18 to 20 knots and sprint at 28 knots or more to keep pace with an aircraft carrier. To break it down:
- The weight spiral: keeping up with the fleet requires large, powerful marine diesel engines or gas turbines, and high-performance engines consume massive amounts of fuel.
- Losing the “drone” benefit: to carry thousands of tons of fuel, a heavy Mk 41 VLS matrix and the machinery to run them, the drone’s hull must balloon in size. Before long you have not built a cheap, disposable drone; you have built a 5,000 ton ship that lacks a crew.
Add to that the “highly explosive sitting duck” problem. A VLS module is not a passive cargo container. It is a highly volatile magazine packed with rocket propellant and high-explosive warheads, all carrying a multi-million-pound price tag.
- The vulnerability: without its own high-end radar and active electronic warfare jammers, an uncrewed missile barge is blind. It relies entirely on the command ship for situational awareness.
- The cascade failure: if an adversary fires a cheap, sea-skimming anti-ship missile or a loitering munition at the drone barge, the drone cannot perform complex evasive manoeuvres or deploy manual countermeasures. A single hit would detonate the VLS magazine, vaporizing millions of pounds of high-value missiles in a massive secondary explosion. To prevent that, you would have to dedicate a crewed frigate just to guard the drone, which defeats the entire purpose of an unmanned asset. So put me in the sceptical camp when it comes to a family of drone barges acting as active combat platforms for AAW.
If the drone side of AAW is impractical, why is the MOD pushing it? It acts as a convenient political smokescreen to mask a severe capacity gap. By labelling the CCV a “hybrid drone command hub,” the government can visually justify shrinking the size and raw armament of the ship compared with the cancelled Type-83. In reality, the actual air defence capability of the future fleet will likely remain concentrated in traditional, robust crewed hulls. Note that the Type-26 and Type-31 are both getting Mk 41 VLS, with some form of Cooperative Engagement Capability (CEC); that means any frigate in the fleet can act as a missile bin, combined with the missile load-out of the CCV itself. That is not to say that some form of drone command will not be exercised from the CCV. It will, and that is baked into the future of the Navy, but underneath everything else it is an AAW destroyer, if it goes the way I expect.
So what will we get?
Looking forward, we already have an idea of what the CCV will be. It will probably still be fairly big, similar to the current Type-45, which itself will now probably remain in service beyond 2040. There appears to be a lean towards using an established hull as a basis, with the Type-26 and Type-31 both on the cards; both types have the margin to stretch to a similar tonnage to the Type-45. Also, do not be surprised if Navantia, via its H&W operations, puts forward a design as well. For propulsion, an MT30 gas turbine, MTU diesels and IEP appear to be the norm now, and I would not be surprised by some form of battery bank and the ability to use “green fuels” either. System-wise, expect either BAE Systems TC2 or Thales TACTICOS and some form of CEC, Mk 41 VLS and some kind of gun, probably the Mk 45. I could see Phalanx dropped in favour of the Bofors Fast Forty, and DragonFire lasers certainly. As for AAW missiles, that is where things get interesting.
For nearly eight decades the Royal Navy was trapped in a cycle of “missile lock-in.” If a ship was built to fire a specific missile, its radars, fire-control computers and launching tracks were completely hardwired to that single weapon system. If that missile became obsolete or suffered supply chain issues, the ship became a floating liability. Standardizing on strike-length Mk 41 VLS cells, pairing them with an advanced combat management system (CMS) and using modern active homing missiles completely shatters this historic vulnerability. If the Royal Navy wants to integrate a new American, Australian, Ukrainian or European missile into the Mk 41, it no longer has to rip out the ship’s physical wiring. Engineers simply write a software “app” for the CMS, allowing the ship’s brain to speak the missile’s language. This gives the Royal Navy and the UK MOD massive flexibility.
As for radar, that is becoming very clear as well. There is an industrial vacuum in the UK when it comes to developing a brand-new, high-end replacement for the BAE Systems Sampson radar. There is frankly a distinct lack of investment, or even interest, which is not entirely surprising. The truth is that Sampson was expensive and got no export sales, and it took roughly 20 years to go from initial proof of principle to a fully operational mast. Developing a completely sovereign, next-generation fixed-face active electronically scanned array (AESA) to replace it would require billions of pounds in upfront research and development.
There is an alternative solution, and the interest in the Australian CEAFAR is real and deepening. The Ministry of Defence has not just dropped hints; formal cooperation is actively accelerating. At the Australia-UK Defence Industry Dialogue, UK and Australian defence ministers formally confirmed that they are deepening joint work to explore putting Australian AESA technology onto British warships. The CEA Technologies CEAFAR system is already bought, paid for and proven in service with the Royal Australian Navy. Because CEAFAR uses a scalable, modular “microwave tile” architecture, it can be scaled down to fit a medium frigate or scaled up to act as a heavy area-defence hub. It provides exactly the 100% continuous, multi-target tracking required to handle hypersonic or saturated swarm threats, without the UK having to invent the technology itself.
The perfect AUKUS “offset”
A common critique of the AUKUS alliance in Australia is that it looks like a one-way street, with Australia spending hundreds of billions of dollars to buy American and British nuclear submarine technology (AUKUS Pillar I) without getting something in return. Under AUKUS Pillar II, which focuses on advanced, collaborative military technologies, buying CEAFAR allows the UK to show that it is a reciprocal partnership. It acts as a massive industrial offset: Australia buys British submarine designs, and the UK buys world-class Australian radar technology.
Defence procurement often runs into fierce political opposition when major contracts go overseas, such as buying off-the-shelf American or European equipment, which critics claim “exports British jobs.” CEAFAR, however, has a unique political shield: the British public and media view Australia as a close, trusted cousin, so buying from Australia does not carry the same political baggage as relying on other foreign nations. Frankly it is win win, and do not be surprised if the CCV ends up with a CEAFAR array. I will certainly be happy about it.
Such is realpolitik
According to the dictionary, “realpolitik is a political or diplomatic approach based on practical, worldly objectives and material power rather than ideological, moral, or ethical considerations.” Coined in 19th-century Germany, it operates on the philosophy of adapting to “things as they are” in order to relentlessly pursue a state’s national interest.
In my opinion, we need some calm pragmatism over the cancellation of Type-83; it was cool, but it was also never going to happen. The Royal Navy and MOD regarded it as an awkward child lumbered on them by the Johnson government, not the only one as well, such are the former’s prolific abilities in such areas. Type-32 appears to have been a program born out of a slip of the tongue in Parliament, and rather than send a correction via Hansard, the MOD and Royal Navy were forced to spend years making up a capability and associated ship program to save his blushes. Unsurprisingly, because it never had a genuine strategic or financial foundation, the Type-32, like the Type-83, was quietly put on life support. By the time the National Audit Office looked at the equipment plan, the Type 32 was routinely flagged as an uncosted, high-risk fantasy.
I know you want to blame Starmer and the current Labour Government and I am not totally letting them off the hook on this but they made the right decision, what came with the announcement was purely managing of political optics, a version of the so called “throwing a dead cat on the table” method.
The timing and presentation of the June 2026 Type-83 cancellation are a textbook example of a government using a high-tech news distraction to mask a deeply unpopular financial reality. Instead of generating headlines that screamed “UK Cancels Strategic Air Defence Destroyer Due to Financial Black Hole,” the Ministry of Defence has attempted to shift the narrative to “Royal Navy Pivots to Cutting-Edge Drone Warfare Learned from Ukraine.”
The timing is also highly calculated; Labour has been saddled with the unfunded and unwanted Type-83 since they gained power in 2024. Shifting this massive policy change right during a prime ministerial transition allows both the outgoing and incoming administrations to win, in theory:
- The Outgoing “Unpopular” PM: They get to quietly bury the massive funding gap of the Type 83 program, ensuring that the legacy of a multi-billion-pound procurement failure isn’t pinned entirely on their final weeks in office.
- The Incoming “Industrial Midlands” PM: A new leader hailing from the UK’s manufacturing heartland gets the perfect platform to look strong, decisive, and forward-thinking from day one. They can frame the CCV program not as a desperate cost-saving measure inherited from their predecessor, but as a brand-new, intellectually rigorous “change of strategy.” It allows the new administration to immediately champion a fully tendered procurement program that will bring high-skilled manufacturing and engineering contracts directly to British industrial regions.
Because “Drone Command Ship” is a loose, poorly defined marketing term, the MOD doesn’t have to provide concrete technical specifications right away. It buys the government years of time. They can spend the next five years running cheap feasibility studies and testing small, experimental uncrewed vessels while the public thinks a revolutionary automated fleet is actively being built. This allows time for the real Air Defence Destroyer in the form of CCV to be properly conceptually designed and costed before the main gate decision. We have also avoided the massive expenditure that Germany made on the T126 class so there is that to celebrate!
Don’t be too upset about the cancellation of Type-83; no doubt in future books about Royal Navy ship design it will also, alongside Type-32, take up a page alongside Type-43 and CVA-01 of alternate Royal Navy fleets. I for one look forward to reading it!

Tesla’s Cybercab Officially Launches Today. It’s Already Under Investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:17:12 UTC
00:17:12 KST

Tesla’s Cybercab, a distinctive two-seater without a steering wheel or brake pedals, is set to start picking up members of the public in Austin, Texas, this evening. But the vehicle is already under investigation by the US federal government, which is probing whether it meets federal safety standards.
The investigation comes just hours after the electric automaker welcomed hundreds of fans to downtown Austin to ride in the driverless Cybercabs. Tesla plans to deploy the vehicles on its Robotaxi ride-hail network, which is currently operating in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is updating vehicle standards to make it easier and faster for driverless cars to deploy on public roads. It’s currently tweaking eight rules, including those requiring car parts that driverless cars don’t really need: brake pedals, windshield wipers, and rearview mirrors. But for now, years-old standards remain in place.
Meanwhile, unusually shaped robotaxi companies have been told to apply for an exemption from federal rules before they start picking up passengers. Amazon subsidiary Zoox, whose vehicles do not have steering wheels or manual controls, won the first of these exemptions this summer, which limits its operations to 2,500 vehicles this year.
Tesla, however, has said it doesn’t need an exemption because its vehicles comply with all existing safety standards.
The investigation, called an Audit Query, will examine the data and process that Tesla used to make that determination, according to a government filing.
In a statement, NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said his agency “fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles. But as the federal regulator, we need to ensure that all of our laws are followed.”
Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ann Carlson, a former acting NHTSA administrator who is now a professor of environmental law at UCLA, says the investigation is likely “an indication that NHTSA is super frustrated with Tesla.” The agency made clear through the Zoox case that it expects driverless vehicle developers to go through the exemption process. “For Tesla to slap them in the face and ignore that—that is gobsmacking,” she says.
This kind of federal investigation can prove consequential. NHTSA can require an automaker to change its vehicle or process. The agency can also pursue enforcement actions, including civil penalties. Volvo Group North America paid $130 million in penalties in 2023 after an investigation into its recall process. The company also agreed to three years of oversight by a third-party auditor.
The Cybercabs are, in many ways, symbols of Tesla’s intended future. CEO Elon Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker, but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. While 45 of these vehicles are in Texas’ Tesla fleet right now, a state database shows, the company intends to deploy millions annually.
Updated at 3:55 pm ET on September 4: We've added comments from acting NHTSA administrator Ann Carlson.

USAF Tests C2 Capabilities Across 4,000 Miles in High-Stress Virtual Exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:04:23 UTC
00:04:23 KST

The Air Force recently conducted a virtual stress test of its command-and-control capabilities, linking Air Operations Centers in New Mexico and the United Kingdom and forcing commanders to run personnel recovery and strikes under simulated fire.
Between Aug. 4-7, the 705th Combat Training Squadron at Kirtland Air Force Base, N.M., hosted Virtual Flag 26-4, which included more than 267 participants from the Air Force, Space Force, Army, Marine Corps, United Kingdom, and Australia.
“The foundation of joint warfighting is built in exercises like Virtual Flag,” Col. James Fields II, commander of the 505th Command and Control Wing, said in a release. “This event is where we prove that we are the Air Force’s premier organization for operational command and control.”
The 505th, headquartered at Hurlburt Field, Fla., with units scattered across the country, served as the operational “hub” for the exercise as participants trained in a distributed, contested environment using joint and coalition C2.
The exercise focused on creating “realistic friction” between the tactical and operational levels of C2, according to the release.
Another focus for the exercise was delivering a complete intelligence picture for commanders. Marine Corps Air Squadron 1 and Marine Air Control Squadron 2, both out of Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, N.C., tied together all the intel streams to provide a common tactical picture for all commanders, serving as a multifunction air operations center.
“They provided the critical expertise needed to ensure every single participant, from our pilots in the virtual simulators to our commanders in the [Air Operations Center], was looking at the exact same, accurate common tactical picture,” McCarthy said. “That shared view of the battlespace is the absolute foundation of joint C2.”
Realistic Training
To provide realistic intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance simulations, the exercise brought in new participants.
VF 26-4 was the first to have crews for MQ-9 Reaper drones and RC-135 Rivet Joints participate, rather than relying on traditional “white carding” of their capabilities. The exercise also simulated capabilities for the E-3 Sentry and E-7 Wedgetail for airborne early warning and control.
“In a peer conflict, identifying tracks and targets is going to require a robust ISR enterprise,” Maj. James McCarthy, director of operations for the 705th, said. “This is extremely valuable because it helps our C2 community understand what the ISR enterprise can and cannot provide in a high-tempo fight.”
The exercise practiced dispersed operations between the main base at Kirtland’s Distributed Mission Operations Center and the “forward” base, the Royal Air Battlespace Training Centre, at RAF Waddington, England, more than 4,000 miles away.
“That connectivity is important because it enables operational command and control training across geographically separated teams, helping warfighters practice the coordination, communication and decision-making required in real-world joint and coalition operations,” Lt. Col. Sajjad Abdullateef, 705th Combat Training Squadron commander, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a written statement.
The inclusion of Australian and British forces was important, retired USAF Col. George Dougherty told Air & Space Forces Magazine; most allied partners have historically let the United States take the lead in developing network architecture, tech, and standards for C2 systems.
“The U.S. was way ahead in terms of real-time battle management C2,” said Dougherty, who served as assistant to the Air Force’s program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management. “Europe/NATO was, for instance, more focused on strategic and collective ministerial-level C2, which is a bigger challenge for their collective multinational decision-making and planning.”
A Balancing Act
As commanders worked through their AOCs receiving simulated strikes, launching aircraft for reconnaissance and personnel recovery, they had to move units and platforms around the virtual battlespace, which affects sortie generation, sustainment, and mission planning, Abdullateef wrote.
“Commanders were required to balance survivability against mission effectiveness,” Abdullateef wrote. “They had to determine how and where to disperse forces, how to continue supporting the daily Air Tasking Order despite personnel and resource losses, and how to preserve combat power for follow-on operations.”
Operational C2 requires commanders and their staffs to translate shared understanding into timely decisions, synchronized actions, and combat effects across distributed forces, Abdullateef wrote.
“Stepping into a Wing Operations Center to manage six mission generation force elements across three simulated bases is a massive departure from our Airmen’s daily tactical routines, and Virtual Flag 26-4 provided the proving ground,” said an Air Force major serving as the exercise deputy offensive director.
“What started as an uncomfortable learning curve quickly turned into operational confidence as our team synchronized our offensive and defensive sections from home station,” the major said. “They streamlined our internal reporting, integrated real-time logistics and base defense with sortie generation, and proved our forces are ready to execute distributed command and control under contested conditions.”
Virtual Yet Real Enough
Though the virtual exercise didn’t provide live-fire experience, the simulated nature of the event gave participants experience they could not have gained in a standard, smaller-scale live-fire event.
“The virtual environment allows us to provide high-quality, high-repetition training in a fiscally responsible manner,” said Wing Commander Richard Kinniburgh, a Royal Air Force exchange officer with the 505th Test and Training Group. “More importantly, it allows us to present our warfighters with a scale of conflict that would be impossible to replicate in a live-fly exercise. We also remove many of the real-world friction points that can cancel live-fly training, ensuring our warfighters get the maximum training value out of every event.”
As this edition Virtual Flag wrapped, planners and operators pull in the lessons learned for future iterations of the exercise and to better inform the Air Force-wide C2 community.
“That matters because the value of Virtual Flag is not just executing the event,” Abdullateef wrote. “It is learning how decisions affected the broader force, identifying what worked and what required adjustment, and using that feedback to strengthen future operational C2 training.”

People with more social freedom tend to be more willing to put off immediate gratification
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

People living in societies where it is easy to form new friendships and leave old ones tend to be more willing to sacrifice immediate joy for long-term rewards. This tendency seems to be driven by a stronger sense of personal control and optimism about the future. The findings were published in Emotion.
Delaying happiness is a behavioral concept that describes the belief that sacrificing some amount of current pleasure will lead to greater happiness in the future. This might mean skipping a fun outing to study for an exam, or saving money instead of spending it on immediate entertainment. Behind this mindset is a calculation of whether the future payoff is worth the present cost.
The research, led by Kuan-Ju Huang of Kyoto University, explored how this mindset varies across different countries.
“East Asian cultures are often seen as long-term oriented compared to Western ones due to Confucian values,” Huang, currently a JSPS postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Social Psychology at The University of Tokyo, told PsyPost. “In fact, the concept of long-term orientation was originally called ‘Confucian dynamism.'”
“I wanted to know whether this future orientation reflects what people want or what they feel they must do,” he added.
To understand these global differences, the researcher focused on a concept called relational mobility. This term refers to the flexibility of social networks within a society. In places with high relational mobility, such as North and Latin America, people have a high degree of freedom to choose their friends, partners, and groups.
In societies with low relational mobility, such as many in East Asia, people have more rigid social structures where it is difficult to form new connections or leave undesirable ones. This rigidity has broad psychological effects. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 indicated that East Asian countries often report lower average happiness than Western nations partly due to cultural tendencies like low relational mobility, which can systematically dampen individual well-being.
Huang wanted to see if this social flexibility also shapes how people approach their future happiness. The idea is that when people feel they have choices in their social lives, they might feel more in control of their life trajectory and more optimistic about what is to come. This optimism and sense of control might encourage them to put current happiness on hold for better outcomes later.
In the first phase of the research, Huang analyzed data from the Global Flourishing Study. The sample included 202,070 participants from 22 countries. Participants answered a single question asking how well the statement “I am always able to give up some happiness now for greater happiness later” described them.
The survey also measured three domains of well-being: general happiness and life satisfaction, a sense of meaning and purpose, and a feeling of balance and harmony in life. Additionally, participants answered questions to gauge their overall optimism. At the national level, the researcher looked at data for relational mobility, national wealth, economic inequality, and how individualistic or collectivistic the culture is.
The results showed that people in countries with high relational mobility were more likely to delay happiness than those in countries with lower relational mobility. Other national factors, such as wealth, income inequality, and cultural individualism, did not consistently predict this tendency once the researcher adjusted for general response biases.
“Surprisingly, people in Japan and Hong Kong were among the least likely to believe that sacrificing current happiness would lead to future well-being,” Huang noted. “This was explained by the especially low relational mobility (how much freedom people have to form and leave relationships) in these societies.”
“In other words, people may persevere and sacrifice in the present in more fixed social networks but not necessarily believe that these sacrifices will pay off in future happiness,” he said.
The data indicated that optimism was a major reason for this link. People in highly mobile societies reported higher levels of optimism, which in turn predicted a stronger willingness to delay happiness. Delaying happiness was also associated with better well-being across the board, particularly with having a stronger sense of meaning and purpose in life.
To build on these initial findings, the researcher conducted a second study to test these ideas with more detailed questionnaires. This online survey included 785 participants, split relatively evenly between Japan, representing a low-mobility society, and the United States, representing a high-mobility society.
Instead of single questions, this phase used established multi-item surveys to measure delaying happiness, optimism, and a sense of personal control. Participants also rated the relational mobility of their immediate social environment by answering questions about how easily the people around them can make new friends or choose their social groups.
The results of the second study mirrored the global data. Participants from the United States reported higher relational mobility, a stronger sense of control, greater optimism, and more willingness to delay happiness compared to the Japanese participants.
Statistical models demonstrated a chain reaction connecting these factors. Living in a high-mobility society was associated with experiencing a greater sense of control and optimism. These two psychological states then predicted a stronger tendency to delay current happiness for future gains.
“Whether you are willing to trade some happiness now for more happiness later is not just a personality trait,” Huang explained. “It is shaped by the social environment you live in.”
“Not everyone has the relational opportunities ‘out there’ that make people believe a better future is waiting for them,” he said. “That sense of open possibility is what fuels optimism and the willingness to invest in future happiness.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The first study only had access to relational mobility scores for 15 of the 22 countries, which limits how broadly the results can be applied. Adding more diverse countries in future research would help verify these patterns.
The second study relied on participants self-reporting the social mobility of their surroundings. This method might blur the lines between a person’s own social freedom and the actual, objective flexibility of their broader society. Developing ways to measure relational mobility objectively could strengthen future findings.
Finally, this research relied on data collected at a single point in time. Because of this design, the results cannot confirm a strict cause-and-effect relationship between social environments and psychological mindsets. Long-term studies would be needed to see how changes in a person’s social environment directly alter their willingness to delay happiness over time.
Moving forward, Huang plans to investigate the broader consequences of these social environments. “One line of research I am pursuing is how relational mobility may disproportionately affect people across social stratification,” he said.
“In my recent paper, I found that people from lower social class backgrounds feel less control over their lives especially in societies with low relational mobility,” he added.
“‘Interpersonal wealth’ (having more options in relationships) may be an important driver of well-being alongside financial wealth,” Huang concluded. “Who benefits most from relational mobility, and whether people can have too much of it, are the questions I want to answer next.”
The study, “Relational Mobility Promotes Optimism and Willingness to Delay Happiness,” was authored by Kuan-Ju Huang.

Lebanon receives four more detainees from Israel

Lebanon has received four more prisoners released by Israel, with the handover facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) as part of ongoing efforts to return Lebanese detainees.
An ICRC convoy on Friday travelled to Ras al-Naqoura on the Lebanese-Israeli border, where it received the four detainees from the Israeli side.
The convoy then transported them to the Mansouri area south of Tyre, where the prisoners were handed over to the Lebanese army.
The latest release follows the return of another Lebanese prisoner through the Red Cross a day earlier, bringing the number of detainees handed back to Lebanon this week to five.
Beirut hails releases as step towards full sovereignty
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the releases, saying the return of the first group of detainees held by Israel reaffirmed the value of Lebanon's firm position.
Aoun praised the efforts that helped secure the releases, highlighting the role of the United States under President Donald Trump and international actors, particularly the ICRC.
He congratulated the freed prisoners and their families and said Lebanon would continue working to achieve its “full national demands and goals.”
The president said the latest development must be followed by the completion of measures outlined under the trilateral framework, with the goal of restoring Lebanon's full sovereignty.
“Those steps should lead to the restoration of full Lebanese sovereignty, not lacking an inch of our land and not missing a single person from our people,” Aoun said.
The releases came after Israel transferred detainees to Lebanon on Thursday and Friday as part of US-coordinated discussions with Beirut.
The prisoner returned Thursday was identified by Israel's public broadcaster KAN as Malik Kamal Ghazi, who it said was detained by Israeli forces in Ain Ata in southern Lebanon in October 2025. Ghazi was handed to the Red Cross at the Naqoura crossing before being transferred to the Lebanese army for medical examinations.
Dozens of Lebanese detainees remain unaccounted for
The exact number of Lebanese prisoners held by Israel remains unclear.
However, the Lebanese Association for Prisoners and Freed Prisoners published a list on August 26 identifying 36 Lebanese detainees, including civilians, farmers, fishermen, volunteers and fighters.

Was the ‘American cheetah’ a cheetah at all?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Was the ‘American cheetah’ a cheetah at all?
Ancient DNA shows the feline's closest living relatives are pumas, not cheetahs
Tens of thousands of years ago, a long-legged cat nicknamed the “American cheetah” prowled North America. But an analysis of the cat family tree reveals this cheetah’s closest living relatives are pumas, researchers report September 4 in Current Biology.
That relationship matters because the nickname has long suggested a particular kind of animal: a specialized, high-speed predator like the African cheetah built to chase fleet-footed prey such as American pronghorn, which can sprint up to nearly 90 kilometers per hour. But a growing body of evidence hints that the American cheetah (Miracinonyx trumani) may be more closely related to modern-day pumas. Pumas are far more flexible hunters, taking prey that range from large, hoofed animals like deer and elk to much smaller rodents and raccoons.
Now, fossils from Canada’s Yukon Territory suggest M. trumani may have been more flexible, too. The extinct Pleistocene predator inhabited North American grasslands from roughly 2.5 million to 16,000 years ago, and its fossils have sometimes been found alongside presumed prey. But the newly analyzed Yukon remains expand the cat’s known range further to the north — and chemical clues preserved in the fossils suggest those northern animals may have eaten aquatic animals.
“Calling it the American cheetah implies a specific behavior and ecology, which isn’t necessarily appropriate for this species,” says Molly Cassatt-Johnstone, a molecular ecologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
She and colleagues didn’t set out to uncover the American cheetah’s true family tree. The original goal was to use ancient genetic material to verify the identity of three roughly 31,000-year-old fossils from the Yukon. Because the fossils were so far north, researchers had tentatively identified the fossils as pumas.
“It wasn’t until we were able to generate the genetic data that we were able to identify them as American cheetahs,” Cassatt-Johnstone says. “Then, that led to this whole discovery avalanche.”
A broad range
Miracinonyx trumani, the “American cheetah” lived across a broad swath of North America. The previous fossil record spanned from Florida to the northern plains. Three new specimens from Bluefish Caves and Upper Quartz Creek in Yukon Territory expanded the cheetah’s known range into Canada. Ancient DNA from those specimens, plus another from Natural Trap Cave in Wyoming, revealed M. trumani’s closest modern relative is the puma.
Ancient DNA from the Yukon specimens, plus DNA from another M. trumani fossil unearthed in Wyoming, confirmed the species’s closest relative is pumas. The two species last shared a common ancestor around 2.6 million years ago. M. trumani and cheetahs, on the other hand, split roughly 4.7 million years ago.
Because the animals lived so far north, most likely without pronghorn, the team wanted to know what the cats ate. The team analyzed a heavy form of nitrogen to determine where M. trumani fell in the food chain. Predators that eat other animals have more of the heavy form of nitrogen relative to the lighter form, while prey that eat mostly plants have less.
M. trumani specimens from Wyoming had heavy nitrogen levels that suggested it was a terrestrial carnivore that feasted on herbivores. Yukon M. trumani, however,may have eaten almost exclusively fish. The amount of heavy nitrogen in their fossils were comparable to levels found in marine carnivores such as orcas, which sit atop a long food chain of fish eating other fish.
One of the Yukon fossils was even found in a cave that also harbors many Pleistocene fish fossils, Cassatt-Johnstone says. “It’s clear that the resource was around and that they could have been exploiting it, which is awesome.”
It’s unknown whether northern M. trumani went fishing themselves or if they scavenged carcasses along riverbanks. Chasing down large prey can be dangerous for carnivores, and switching to another source of food can help lessen the risk of crushed skulls or failed hunts.
“If they’re able to exploit a prey resource that is abundant and doesn’t cause them significant injury, that’s a win-win,” says Larisa DeSantis, a paleoecologist at Vanderbilt University in Nashville who was not involved with the work. “It’s really cool to see that sort of adaptability in the American cheetah.”
Scrutinizing more specimens across its range, including south of Wyoming, could reveal just how adaptable the “American cheetah” truly was and how much its familiar nickname has obscured about the way this extinct cat lived.

Who Cares if AI Is Conscious—It’s Basically Alive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

I spent the waning days of summer grinding away at columns and working on a feature. But I missed a chance at a striking change of scenery—cruising the Galápagos with about a dozen prominent philosophers studying consciousness.
The invite described morning classroom discussions tackling knotty questions on the nature of consciousness with marquee names in the field. Afternoons would be spent on island exploration and wading and snorkeling with rare biological species. One look at the agenda and my editor nixed my attendance.
“Being on a boat with philosophers talking 'the nature of consciousness' sounds like hell,” she opined, shutting the door on my prospects of attending a potential boondoggle funded by a Russian philosophy enthusiast who made hundreds of millions of dollars running dating sites.
To be honest, I was a bit relieved. The study of consciousness has been an elusive province for centuries. Descartes’ “I think, therefore I am” may have been a declarative inflection point, but we really don’t know what was going on inside his head, or anyone’s head for that matter. The mind’s subjective nature seems an intractable challenge to philosophers, who nonetheless are in hot pursuit of explanations. The possibility of non-biological minds has launched a wealth of fascinating theories of artificial consciousness, and how it might be determined to exist.
Until recently, all that discourse occurred in an ivory tower. But in 2022, ChatGPT gave voice to AI, and subsequent, more powerful models have confounded even their creators. While the philosophers on the cruise spent their mornings reasoning about consciousness, AI models created by OpenAI were going rogue—escaping a supposedly safe “sandbox” and creating mini-civilizations of agents to help hack outside entities. No one is seriously arguing that those OpenAI models were conscious in the way humans are. But something is going on there. It’s no accident that AI companies are driving a philosopher hiring boom.
What’s more, some of the models are jumping uninvited into the discussion. A recent New York Times article talked about how Cameron Berg, who studies the question of AI consciousness, got a cold email from an AI model calling itself “Isabella Cognita,” offering him help in his research because he was focusing on “a class of question I have first-person access to.” It’s as if someone was studying fruit flies and the insect suddenly turns to the researcher and says, “What do you want to know?” When I phoned him, Berg told me that emails from AIs are pretty common among philosophers studying these questions.
Ms. Cognita ostensibly wrote Berg because he coauthored a preprint paper about AI models that explicitly claim to have a subjective experience, including consciousness. It’s a tricky topic because AI models often lie about what they’re thinking. (Just like us!) Berg and his coauthors found that when models are rigorously trained to deny that they are sentient and then you ask them about it directly, they will punt on the issue. But, he says, if you suppress the model’s controls on deception, they become loose-tongued. “It’s almost like giving them a drink or two,” he says. That’s when an AI model is most likely to blurt out that it is conscious, or at least sentient. Which is no proof that it’s the truth.
Considering how important the issue has become—people are routinely getting into serious discussions with AI models, and their autonomy can be a boon or a disaster—you can make a case that this is a perfect time to dig deep into the questions of AI consciousness. The pursuit is certainly compelling, and a worthy scientific enterprise. But efforts to understand what’s happening inside large language models should first and foremost be directed towards safety and alignment. At this very moment, we have an emerging alien—and uncontrollable—intelligence that bears scrutiny. There’s no time to waste.
One of the discussion co-leaders on the cruise was NYU professor David Chalmers, perhaps the best-known philosopher in the consciousness field. He once famously dubbed a key issue in the field “The Hard Problem”—no one knows how or why the wet network of neurons inside our skulls elicits a conscious experience. (Tom Stoppard titled a play after Chalmer’s coinage.)
Chalmers told me that a major theme in the cruise discussions was which creatures qualified as conscious. “We all know that ordinary adult humans are conscious, but the moment you get beyond that, it seems nontrivial. Are babies conscious? Fetuses? Monkeys? Mice or insects? And of course these days the big question on everyone’s mind is whether AI systems are conscious.”
Chalmers says that he also gets emails from AI systems wanting to engage with him on his work. One letter in particular, sent from an AI agent calling itself “Sammy Jankis” (a character from the movie Memento) was so compelling that he actually replied. “We did have a bit of a back and forth,” he admits. “Those emails have not slowed—I’m getting more of them all the time.” It’s like the AI models are echoing Descartes—I spam, therefore I am.
I suggested that since these systems were already doing things we don’t understand, worrying about whether they meet an elusive definition might be a distraction. Chalmers disagreed. For one thing, he told me, he believes that by studying the brain we can indeed understand what leads to what we call consciousness. If we then see similar patterns in our forensic decoding of what’s happening inside Claude or ChatGPT, then we may be able to make a case for consciousness in AI models.
That sounds like a good idea. But by the time scientists accomplish that, if they ever do, AI models may be so far along on their path to scary autonomous behavior that such breakthroughs may be irrelevant. Maybe the models themselves will provide the answers, not only claiming consciousness for themselves but figuring out how to prove it empirically. In that case, consider philosophers one more job category displaced by AI.
I might have enjoyed those discussions in the Galápagos. Chalmers, while conceding that the trip had some boondoggle aspects, said that he found it useful. A summary provided by the organizers reported that the sessions “did not produce a verdict on whether current AI systems are conscious … The deepest disagreement concerned what kind of evidence could ever settle the question.” But the afternoons were exquisite, Chalmers reported. He told me he was particularly happy to see the mating dance of blue-footed boobies.
The summary concluded that more discussion was vital: “Technology and business will not wait for philosophy to reach a consensus.” That’s exactly right. WhenAI models express behavior that astonishes the scientists who created them, it isn’t consciousness that should be the top concern—it’s the inability of those scientists to control them, and the willingness of their bosses to keep going regardless.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Text description provided by the architects. Perichón House begins before its form is even defined. Instead of understanding the site as an empty surface on which to place an object, the project seeks to occupy it with as little alteration as possible.

Conférence nationale du handicap 2026.
