Why did Xi choose to visit Egypt amid the US-Iran tensions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:21:59 UTC
22:21:59 KST

Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Cairo as China and Egypt marked 70 years of diplomatic ties, shortly before a possible meeting with US President Donald Trump in late September.
The visit came amid renewed regional tensions, with US forces attacking IRGC targets and Tehran retaliating by attacking American bases across the Middle East.
Egypt, which has been largely silent on US-Iran tensions, condemned recent Iran attacks on Arab states.
During the visit, Xi and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called for a “comprehensive agreement” to end the war with Iran and signed more than 20 agreements. They included a deal allowing Beijing to complete the third phase of a joint industrial zone at the Suez Canal, expanding China’s economic presence along one of the world’s most important trade routes.
Cairo and Beijing have a significant economic relationship, with bilateral trade reaching close to $21 billion, as the two countries have linked Egypt’s Vision 2030 with China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
“There is a clear economic interest on both sides, especially given the current circumstances in the region,” Altay Atli, an expert on Chinese politics and a senior scholar at Sabanci University’s Istanbul Policy Center, tells TRT World.
He highlighted both states’ growing concerns that the war in Iran has stalled global trade because of tensions in the Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz straits.
Egypt, whose economy depends heavily on Suez Canal trade, has been concerned that pro-Iranian Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb have disrupted shipping across the Red Sea, reducing revenues.
Burdened by deep structural debt, the Egyptian economy has long been vulnerable to regional conflicts like the current Iran-US war.
China, a major consumer of Gulf oil, has also been concerned about the Iran conflict, as blockades across the region’s two key straits have disrupted global energy shipments.
“While the anniversary provided the occasion for the visit, the deeper issue is a shared interest in regional stability,” Atli tells TRT World, referring to possible Egyptian-Chinese cooperation to ensure regional stability across the Middle East.
Why Egypt matters
Despite Houthi attacks in the Red Sea, Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz has pushed more oil tanker traffic towards the Suez Canal, making the waterway even more strategically important at a time when China is increasing its investment there, according to Atli.
Egypt could also help China deepen its engagement not only with Arab states but also across Africa, given Cairo’s involvement in several regional conflicts, including those in Palestine, Sudan and Libya.
“In that sense, Egypt offers China geography, markets, and political legitimacy at precisely the moment Beijing wants a larger Middle Eastern role,” Dania Thafer, the executive director of Gulf International Forum, a Washington, DC-based research institute, tells TRT World.
Atli also highlights Egypt, the most populous Arab state with good relations with both China and the US, as “a potential point of convergence” between Washington and Beijing.
“Egypt is continuing to diversify its partnerships, bringing in Chinese investment and cooperation without giving up its relationship with the United States. And China, for its part, seems quite comfortable being one partner, but a very important one, among several, rather than trying to pull Egypt exclusively into its camp,” says Atli.
While Egypt has substantial economic ties with China, it remains the second-largest recipient of US military aid, receiving roughly $1.3 billion annually, while pursuing a foreign policy of “strategic balance.”
“For Xi, engaging such a close US partner allows China to demonstrate that deeper relations with Beijing do not require governments to formally abandon Washington,” says Thafer.
This balancing act between the two great powers may also be one reason for Xi’s visit to Cairo ahead of his possible late September meeting with Trump.
China wants to guide Cairo “to lead from the center” because Beijing supports “an architecture that develops in concentric circles,” says Dan Steinbock, a geopolitical analyst and international economist.
“Egypt could serve as the maritime anchor of this new architecture, preempting interference in regional choke points,” Steinbock tells TRT World.
That potential role also carries a message for Washington.
Kadir Temiz, director of ORSAM, an Ankara-based Turkish think tank, believes that “Xi’s Egypt visit might also be a coded message to the Trump administration that if the US can not secure regional stability, China and its Middle Eastern partners can offer an alternative order based on regional autonomy.”
‘Regional autonomy’
The meeting also came at a time of what Atli describes as “a broader regional trend”, with several Middle Eastern countries exploring a shift away from reliance on the US security umbrella toward a more regional security architecture, as reflected in the recent Mecca Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
“Xi’s four-point proposal with its emphasis on greater regional ‘strategic autonomy’ fits into that trend. Notably, China did not name either Iran or the United States in this proposal,” says Atli.
He refers to the Chinese leader’s call for Middle Eastern countries to be “the masters of their own affairs”, oppose external interference and pursue regional dialogue on peace and security.
“Xi’s proposal is based on the idea of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security. That echoes the basic thinking behind the Mecca Agreement, which is that countries in the region should rely less on outside security guarantees and do more among themselves,” Atli says.
But Atli also stresses that the Mecca Agreement and Xi’s Cairo proposal are “very different things”, noting that the former is a defence pact with concrete commitments, while the latter rests on a much broader diplomatic and economic framework.
“China is trying to position itself as a complementary player in this emerging regional environment, rather than trying to create or join an arrangement like Mecca.”
Cairo was also part of a quadrilateral format developed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan in the wake of US-Iran tensions, which sought a third way to address regional conflicts.
While Egypt did not join the Mecca Agreement, Ankara expects Cairo could eventually join the defence pact.
“During his visit, Xi explicitly called for Middle Eastern nations to explore a new, independent security architecture and oppose external interference. By echoing the philosophy of the new Mecca alliance, China actively backs indigenous security arrangements run by regional leaders rather than external powers,” Steinbock says.
Thafer also sees parallels between the two approaches, saying that “Xi's Cairo message fits remarkably well with the political logic behind Mecca”.
But she notes that China is not “offering to become the region’s new security guarantor” by endorsing greater regional security autonomy.
“The Egypt-China communiqué does not mention the Mecca Pact or commit China to collective defence,” she says.
“Put differently, China appears interested in helping legitimise a new regional security architecture without underwriting it in the way the US historically has. That distinction is crucial.”
The Mecca Agreement signatories have publicly said the pact is not directed against any particular country and instead aims to develop a regional security arrangement. Most recently, the foreign ministers of the three countries announced the establishment of a Strategic Political and Defence Committee, signalling the agreement's growing institutionalisation.
“It is significant that, prior to his visit to the US, Xi articulated an approach emphasising the importance of regional powers taking ownership of their situation,” Temiz tells TRT World.
“His argument—that countries should take their own initiatives rather than relying on external forces to define the Middle East's security architecture—aligns interestingly with the rhetoric developed by the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani trio.”
Hongda Fan, a Chinese professor and director of the China–Middle East Center at Shaoxing University, also believes Beijing is closely following the heightened tensions in the oil-rich region, adding further significance to Xi's Cairo visit.
“Beijing is certainly paying close attention to cooperation among the major Middle Eastern powers,” Fan tells TRT World.
Beijing has repeatedly expressed support for Middle Eastern countries to “determine their own destiny” and deepen cooperation among themselves, Fan says.
In particular, Beijing encourages “the formation of a security framework by major regional powers that can bring stability and peace to the region,” he adds.
“This aligns with China's interests. A more stable Middle East is more beneficial to China. After all, the realisation of China's strategic goals in the Middle East depends on the cooperation, support, and coordination of the region's major powers.”

What a Record Hunting and Fishing Expansion Means for America’s Wildlife Refuges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

The Department of the Interior implemented a massive expansion of fishing and hunting access in the United States, opening 1,488 opportunities across 32 states. With the rule in effect as of Monday, more than 92 million acres, or 95% of National Wildlife Refuge System land, are now available for the practices.
Expanded hunting and fishing are now allowed in areas where the practices were never before legal, including Rocky Flats National Wildlife Refuge in Colorado and Stewart Lake National Wildlife Refuge in North Dakota.
The rule also permits hunting and fishing for additional species and expands some seasons at locations where those activities were already allowed.
“America’s hunters and anglers now have something significant to look forward to in the fall,” said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum in the press release announcing the rule Aug. 13. “We are also promoting good government by reducing the regulatory burden and working with states to facilitate these outdoor activities.”
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) oversees more than 570 national wildlife refuges that were “established to serve a statutory purpose that targets the conservation of native species dependent on its lands and water,” according to the agency’s website.
Christopher Williams, a professor of wildlife ecology at the University of Delaware, says the refuges were initially created to protect wildlife and then later helped to combat “extreme market hunting,” or unregulated hunting of animals. They became safe habitats and breeding sanctuaries for endangered species under the 1966 Endangered Species Preservation Act.
Now, hunting and other forms of recreation are permitted across a majority of those refuges when “compatible with each station’s purpose and mission under federal law,” per FWS.
The very definition of a refuge seems to have “slowly morphed into an entity that was meant to provide an opportunity for hunting access,” Williams says.
The new rule raises a question of compatibility: How can the refuges fulfill their conservation mandate amid the nation’s largest-ever expansion of hunting and fishing?
Does hunting undermine the purpose of a wildlife refuge?
The FWS said this week’s expansion is about “maximizing access where compatible with conservation goals.”
It also said that the new rule will help revitalize rural economies, as hunters and anglers contribute more than $144 billion annually to the U.S. economy.
“These activities support jobs, fund conservation efforts, and sustain outdoor traditions that connect communities to the land and to each other,” the August announcement read.
Sporting groups touted the “historic expansion” and its potential ability to help retain hunters and fishers at these refuges, which may rely on them for curbing overabundant and invasive species.
Williams says it makes sense that conservation groups support the expansion, since hunters and anglers play an “enormously important role in American wildlife conservation.”
“And with long-term concerns about declining hunting participation, providing meaningful access remains an important part of recruitment, retention, and reactivation efforts,” he says.
“BHA applauds all efforts to responsibly expand and improve public access for hunters and anglers and appreciates the Administration’s recognition of the important role sportsmen and women play in the conservation and stewardship of public lands and waters,” Backcountry Hunters & Anglers said in a statement when the expansion was proposed in May.
This was not the first time the Trump Administration proposed such an expansion. A version of the rule from 2020 opened some 859 opportunities across 2.3 million acres. The increase in scope from his first term is about 73%.
The new rule also makes more than 1,000 modifications to existing federal regulations that previously guided access to the refuges, including simplifications and deletions. The Trump Administration has said the sweeping revisions aim to make it easier to understand and enforce guidelines from state to state. But some conservationists have concerns about how the abrupt elimination of that many regulatory mandates, all at once, will affect the refuges.
Robert Fischman, professor of environmental law at Indiana University Maurer School of Law, says that such a dramatic overhaul is worth noting. “I mean, 1,000 rules sounds pretty important,” he tells TIME.
The new rule reverses restrictions on lead ammunition
One significant change that comes with the new rule is a reversal on lead ammunition and tackle.
Following a lawsuit in 2021, the government said it would phase out the potentially harmful materials and require hunters and anglers to switch to non-toxic alternatives.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued FWS after it proposed an expansion on hunting opportunities during Trump’s first term. The lawsuit argued that the expansion could jeopardize protected species, which are susceptible to ingesting the lead ammunition and tackle. It also claimed that there would be residual harm to the greater ecosystem, as lead ammunition and tackle can contaminate fields and waterways.
The lawsuit was settled under the Biden Administration in 2022, with FWS saying it would phase out the use of lead ammunition and tackle at several refuges across the country.
Aaron Bloom, a senior attorney with nonprofit Earthjustice's Biodiversity Defense Program, said the phase-out was supposed to go into effect across eight refuges in September 2026. But with the new rule, the phase-outs will no longer take effect.
In response to the reversal, Bloom says Earthjustice will be looking at litigation—as will other environmentalist groups.
These phase-outs would have “protected both wildlife and human health, hunters and their families, from the adverse impacts of lead poisoning,” Bloom tells TIME. “There's absolutely no reason we should be allowing them in our wildlife refuges.”
Recent staffing cuts raise concerns about oversight
FWS staffing decreased by approximately 18% between April 2024 and May 2025, according to agency records obtained by the Center for Biological Diversity. The decline can be attributed in part to the “workforce optimization initiative” implemented by the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of 2025.
Fischman and Williams both express concern about the staffing cuts and how they will impact oversight amid expanded hunting and fishing access.
“What I'm hearing from people who are on the ground is you have whole national wildlife refuges that no longer have any staff there full-time,” Fischman says. “You have a refuge manager running around from one refuge to another, riding circuit to try to keep things together.”
Fischman questions whether there are enough staff left to “really understand” and document the impacts of the new rule. He says that streamlining refuge-specific regulations makes enforcement easier and may partially compensate for staffing reductions; however, he is skeptical that states have enough staff to patrol the affected refuges and ensure that hunters and anglers are complying with the regulations that do still apply.
“It’s dependent on there being people there to maintain trails, to monitor impacts on species, to enforce the law,” he says. “It could be that the rulemaking seems pretty logical [to the Administration], but on the ground can't be practically implemented in a way that is consistent with public safety and compatible with both the system mission and the refuge purposes.”
According to Williams, it's all a balancing act. He points out the need to preserve conservation efforts while boosting the economies of rural communities and reversing a long-term decline in hunting participation in the U.S.
“On one hand, are you reaching a point where you might be doing some harm of not having adequate sanctuary for wildlife? Or maybe you are making a net improvement to increase retention and recruitment of hunters, which provides a financial benefit?” he wonders. “The answer is probably yes on both sides of the house.”

ICCIMA, IRU examine routes for facilitating money transfer
TEHRAN- The President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture (ICCIMA) during a webinar meeting with the new Secretary-General of the International Road Transport Union (IRU), examined routes for facilitating money transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU.
According to IRNA, quoting the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Samad Hassanzadeh on Wednesday held a webinar meeting to discuss ways to facilitate fund transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU.
At the outset of the online meeting, the President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines, and Agriculture congratulated the new IRU Secretary-General on assuming his role, stating: "We are very pleased that a scientific and economically cultured figure has accepted this responsibility."

He referred to efforts to find channels for facilitating money transfers in light of international sanctions, and addressing the Iran Chamber President, said: "I thank you for acting proactively and responsibly to find methods for money transfers."
Habib Turki outlined three routes for facilitating money transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU and said: "With the channels we have evaluated so far, we are very hopeful that the problem of fund transfers between the Iran Chamber and the IRU will be resolved."
Increasing Iran's credit with the IRU, accelerating the process of sending carnets to Iran, and selecting new agents were among the key topics discussed in this online meeting.

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
16:09:44 EEST
22:09:44 KST

Canada’s labor market is losing momentum — how much did employment decline, and did the “dispute” with the US have an impact?
Kyiv • UNN
In August, Canada lost 41,700 jobs, while unemployment remained at 6.4%. New US tariffs threaten further slowdown.
In August, Canada's economy lost 41,700 jobs, signaling a sharp slowdown in hiring after an exceptionally active summer period; meanwhile, the unemployment rate remained unchanged at 6.4%, reports UNN, citing Reuters.
Details
The August report provides one of the last "clean" pictures of the state of Canada's labor market before the effects of new 50% tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump begin to affect the economy.
These tariffs affect a relatively small share of Canadian exports, but they target vulnerable industries — including wood product manufacturing — increasing the risk that the recent growth in labor-market activity could practically evaporate.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters had forecast an increase of approximately 15,000 jobs (following a significant increase of 75,100 in July). The forecast for the unemployment rate matched the actual figure.
The Canadian dollar fell 0.51% to 1.3860 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar (or 72.15 U.S. cents). The yield on two-year government bonds rose after the labor-market data were published, increasing by 1.3 basis points to 2.469%.
According to Statistics Canada, the main reduction in employment occurred in the full-time sector (down 35,900 positions), while the number of part-time jobs decreased by 5,800.
Recent hiring figures were inflated by temporary factors, such as hiring staff to conduct the census and work related to the FIFA World Cup; together, these factors generated an increase of 181,000 jobs from April to July.
The growth in recent months was also explained by the fact that the economy as a whole demonstrated considerable resilience to U.S. trade restrictions that have been in effect for more than 18 months, and mass layoffs have so far been avoided.
However, the entry into force of the new U.S. tariffs and Canada's retaliatory measures (starting early next week) is expected to slow this growth somewhat. Four out of five members of the labor force are employed in the services sector, including health care, education, transportation, and finance; this sector bore the brunt of the employment decline in August.
According to Statistics Canada (StatsCan), 51,500 jobs were eliminated in this sector in August; the greatest losses occurred in industries such as business and support services (including building services), as well as wholesale and retail trade.
The unemployment rate remained at its lowest level in two years, despite the economy facing a wave of tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.
Slower labor-force growth, caused by stricter immigration rules and an aging workforce, also contributed to improved unemployment figures in recent months.
The labor force, which stood at 22.632 million people, declined for the first time since February.
The youth unemployment rate rose by 0.3 percentage points in August, reaching 12.9%, interrupting the downward trend observed from April through July.
Average hourly wages for permanent employees — an important indicator of inflationary pressures — fell to 2% in August (from 3% a month earlier), reaching their lowest level in more than seven years (excluding the pandemic period).

Philippines' Vice President Sara Duterte Faces Arrest Over Alleged Grave Threat to President Marcos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:09:39 UTC
22:09:39 KST

A Philippine court on Friday ordered the arrest of Vice President Sara Duterte over alleged grave threats to her former ally, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., his wife, and a former House Speaker.
The warrant against Duterte, 48, set the bail at 120,000 pesos ($1,900) for each of the three counts against her.
“Regardless of the question on jurisdiction, she has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies,” Duterte’s lawyer said in a statement.
Duterte has been charged with threatening the lives of Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and his cousin, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The case stems from a November 2024 virtual press conference where the Vice President revealed an apparent assassination plot against Marcos, his wife, and Romualdez.
“I already talked to someone—I told him, If I’m killed, kill [Marcos], Liza Araneta, and Martin Romualdez,” she said in Filipino, “No joke, no joke. I already gave orders. If I die, I told them, ‘Don’t stop until they’re dead.’ And then he said, ‘Yes.’”
The threat is also one of the allegations included in the impeachment complaint against Duterte, on top of alleged misuse of public funds as Vice President and during her stint as Education Secretary. Duterte has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
The Vice President is currently standing trial at the Philippine Senate, serving as an impeachment court, following her second impeachment in May. If convicted in the impeachment court, she could be removed from office and barred from running in the 2028 national elections, where she said she plans to contest the presidency.
Philippine law typically allows candidates to run for public office even if they face pending criminal charges.
Duterte controversies and public standing
Duterte is the daughter of former President Rodrigo Duterte, who is awaiting trial before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, for the thousands of deaths attributed to his violent anti-drug campaign.
The Duterte family still enjoys broad public support in the Philippines, despite the controversies. Recent surveys show Sara Duterte herself is the top preferred candidate by Filipinos to succeed Marcos, whom she had a falling out with. Marcos, who took office in 2022, is limited to a lone six-year term.
The presidential office said in a statement that it “respects the decision of the court” to issue an arrest warrant.
Jean Encinas-Franco, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines, tells TIME that “the law has finally caught up with the Vice President,” but questioned the timing of the arrest warrant’s release. Franco said Duterte’s arrest warrant could successfully repel criticisms that Marcos is a “weak” leader as the impeachment proceedings have dragged on.
However, Franco says it remains unclear which political camp—if any—will benefit from the latest political development. “We don't know what will happen because it's still 1-½ years [until the elections] and that's a lifetime in Philippine politics.”

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-04
13:07:45 UTC
22:07:45 KST

From naval blockade to land corridors: Iran's strategic pivot
TEHRAN- Iran's maritime trade has faced serious disruption due to geopolitical tensions and sanctions, but this challenge has unexpectedly accelerated the development of land-based transit routes. What initially appeared as a strategic vulnerability—over-reliance on the Strait of Hormuz—is now forcing a fundamental shift in the country's trade infrastructure. The result could transform Iran from a sea-dependent economy into a regional transit hub connecting East, West, North, and South.
The recent naval pressures, intensified after failed military confrontations, have exposed a long-standing weakness: Iran's trade was disproportionately channeled through a single maritime choke point. Rather than simply imposing costs, however, this constraint has made the diversification of trade routes an urgent necessity. In response, Iran is actively developing four major land corridors that could redefine its economic geography.
First, the East-West Railway Corridor links China to Iran via Central Asia, passing through Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This 10,400-kilometer route can cut shipping times from 30 days by sea to just 15 days by rail, significantly reducing costs and risks. Second, the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), through Pakistan's Gwadar port and Iran's Rimdan border, offers an eastern bypass of the Strait of Hormuz. Third, the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) connects Iran to Russia and India, providing access to northern and southern markets. Fourth, the Shalamcheh-Basra railway—only 32 kilometers short of completion—can open Iran to Iraq, Turkey, and the Mediterranean.
According to Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of Iran's National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, the government has actively expanded trade cooperation with neighbors like Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkey, Pakistan, and Oman. He emphasized that these corridors have prevented shortages of essential goods during the crisis, ensuring price hikes rather than outright scarcity.
The activation of the Iran-Pakistan transit corridor is particularly significant. With instability on Pakistan-Afghanistan border routes, Islamabad now looks to Iran for access to Central Asian markets. Iran's Mirjaveh and Rimdan terminals are central to this exchange, with a bilateral trade target of $10 billion. Rimdan has been developed since 2020, with passenger facilities and infrastructure upgrades underway.
These corridors must not remain temporary fixes. If completed and sustained, they can offer lasting competitive advantages, attract investment from China, India, and Russia, and reduce Iran's vulnerability to maritime disruptions. What began as a forced response to containment can become a permanent pillar of Iran's economic strategy. The lesson is clear: a country with Iran's geography cannot be blockaded when it turns its land borders into bridges rather than barriers.

Fitch upgrades Portugal's rating to A+ and says outlook is "stable"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:07:50 UTC
22:07:50 KST

On Friday, the financial agency raised Portugal's debt rating from "A" to "A+", with a "stable" outlook, the agency said in a published note.
Ratings agency Fitch has upgraded Portugal's sovereign debt rating from "A" to "A+", with a "stable outlook", the company said in a notice published on its website (source in Portuguese), keeping pace with the recent wave of confidence shown by other ratings agencies and investors in the country, according to Portugal's Agency for Investment and Foreign Trade (AICEP). According to the Portuguese government, "all financial ratings agencies" assign Portugal an "A" rating.
In August, Standard & Poor's (S&P) (source in Portuguese) confirmed its unsolicited sovereign credit ratings for Portugal of "A+/A-1" for long- and short-term foreign and local currency debt, and maintained the positive outlook. Morningstar DBRS also confirmed, in July 2025 (source in Portuguese), the Republic of Portugal's rating at "A" (high), with a "stable outlook".
Fitch Ratings' announcement on Friday is based on the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, in particular the projected reduction in debt and more robust economic growth than in other countries, underpinned by a "strong political commitment to fiscal prudence".
"The upgrade reflects the strengthening of Portugal's public finances, including a projected path of declining public debt and budget balances that are considerably stronger than those of comparable countries, supported by a strong political commitment to fiscal prudence," Fitch says.
According to the agency, Portugal's ratings are supported by governance indicators above the median for countries rated "A", as well as institutional strengths linked to membership of the European Union and the euro area. These factors are, however, offset by still-high levels of accumulated public and external debt.
Fitch adds that the "prudence" of policies, repeatedly better-than-expected budget performance and persistent current-account surpluses have strengthened the resilience of the Portuguese economy and its ability to "absorb shocks".
The agency expects public debt to fall from 89.7% of GDP in 2025 to 87.0% in 2026 and 82.9% in 2028, supported by the maintenance of primary surpluses and moderate nominal growth. Even so, the ratio is expected to remain above the forecast median of 59.5% of GDP for countries rated "A".
On Thursday, the Minister of State and Finance, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, said that the fall in the debt-to-GDP ratio "is the result of the work of families and businesses in recent years (source in Portuguese)", stressing that this process "cannot be interrupted and that it is necessary to maintain the pace of public debt reduction". Joaquim Sarmento added that it is necessary "to sharply reduce bureaucracy, which stifles companies and citizens and limits and delays private investment, especially foreign direct investment", which will have "a strong impact on our country's potential GDP", he said.
On X, the finance minister hailed the "excellent news for Portugal, which regains an A+ rating for the first time since March 2011".
This morning, the President of the Republic also welcomed the agency's rating decision. "This is excellent news for the country and an important external recognition of Portugal's performance, the result of a medium- and long-term evolution, sustained by the efforts of the Portuguese people and by a responsible orientation maintained under different governments," António José Seguro writes on the Presidency website (source in Portuguese). "A better rating will improve financing conditions for the state, businesses and families, support investment and job creation and allow more public resources to be directed towards people's needs," the president hopes.
"When the year 2026 comes to be read in retrospect, this will surely be one of its most relevant economic news stories," Seguro adds.
Increase in defence spending puts public finances under pressure
Fitch estimates that the budget surplus will fall from 0.7% of GDP in 2025 to 0.1% in 2026, affected by emergency support and reconstruction spending related to storms, by the tax-cut and housing measures set out in the 2026 State Budget, by peak investment linked to the loan component of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP) and by higher spending on wages and pensions.
These effects are expected to be partially offset by higher social contributions, linked to continued employment growth, and by a significant dividend distribution from Caixa Geral de Depósitos, according to the agency.
For 2027 and 2028, Fitch forecasts an average deficit of around 0.4% of GDP. The agency anticipates that demographic ageing and lower migration "will increase spending and put pressure on social contributions", although it notes that the Social Security Financial Stabilisation Fund, with assets equivalent to 13.9% of GDP at the end of 2025, "provides a substantial safety margin".
The cost of housing is also a concern, although the rapid rise in house prices has not yet translated into "significant short-term macro-financial risks"; it may "increase vulnerabilities in the property market and is aggravating pressures on affordability", the agency stresses.
In the first quarter of 2026, residential property prices were about 99% above the level recorded in the fourth quarter of 2019, compared with 31% in the euro area.
Low housing supply and strong demand, linked to high immigration, suggest that pressures in the property market are mainly "structural, limiting the likelihood of a sharp correction in the short term", says Fitch, which suggests that "a solid banking sector should help contain the financial risks related to the property market" and the resulting build-up of household debt.
Another factor to bear in mind is NATO's target of reaching 5% of GDP in defence spending by 2035, which Fitch expects will "add pressure to public finances in the medium term". Even so, the international ratings agency considers that the track record of budgetary policy, relatively stable over successive changes of government, mitigates the risks associated with greater political uncertainty.

Israeli journalist Gideon Levy says attacks by Israeli occupiers in West Bank amount to ethnic cleansing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:59:51 UTC
21:59:51 KST

Israeli journalist and writer Gideon Levy said escalating attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are part of a systematic campaign backed by the Israeli army and government to displace Palestinians.
“You see, there is a whole thinking behind it. Sure, that’s an attempt for an ethnic cleansing of the West Bank, and it is systematic, and it is backed by the Israeli authorities, no doubt,” Levy told Anadolu in an interview.
The number of attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank rose from 1,291 in 2023 to 1,449 in 2024 and 1,835 in 2025. A further 761 attacks were recorded in the first four months of 2026.
More than 90% of cases opened by Israeli police against occupiers are closed without indictments, while conviction rates remain at about 3%, contributing to what critics describe as de facto impunity.
Levy told Anadolu that the attacks are aimed at gradually pushing Palestinians out of the West Bank, beginning with shepherds and small communities before expanding to villages and buildings.
“It’s very clear, I mean, it’s systematic, it is backed by the army and the government, and it has a very clear goal to try to push the Palestinians away from the West Bank.
“Now, they cannot push away three million people, so they try to do it with the weakest points, with, first of all, they started with the shepherds, with small communities, then they go to villages, so they start to take the first row of buildings.”
 
Israeli army accused of collaborating with occupiers
Levy said the Israeli army and government support the campaign and that soldiers sometimes cooperate directly with occupiers.
“It is a plan, there is a plan, there is a program, it is very systematic, and it has very clear goals. It’s much more than this, the army takes part in part of the pogroms. It’s not that they try to avoid and don’t succeed, they have no intention to avoid it.”
“On the contrary, in many cases, you see soldiers collaborating with the settlers. But in any case, the army is not doing anything to protect the only role in the West Bank is to protect the settlers, no matter what the settlers are doing. And the Palestinians remain totally helpless.”
Levy said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich plays a particularly important role in supporting the settlement movement through government funding and that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also bears responsibility.
“It’s extremely influential. And together with a few other ministers, they enable all this project. First of all, in really sending them enormous sums of money.”
“I mean, the budgets that go to them are unbelievable. And there’s no one to stop them, because the government supports it.
“So all together, sure, Smotrivich has a very important role, but you cannot release from accountability Netanyahu, who enables all this, because Netanyahu could have stopped it.”
Levy attributed the lack of accountability for attacks by Israeli occupiers to what he described as an apartheid system.
“The settlers will not happen to them nothing. First of all, to answer you why, because it is an apartheid system. As simple as this, Jews and Palestinians are not equal in the West Bank in accountability.”
 
No major policy change expected after elections
Levy said international criticism has failed to deter Israel, noting that the country has not faced what he considers effective sanctions.
“It’s all condemnations and talking, but the world didn’t take any real serious measures against Israel. Your country did, Türkiye did, obviously, but the West, I mean, the EU, the US, they didn’t take any measures against Israel. So Israelis are not afraid of it at all.”
He said the upcoming elections are also influencing developments in the West Bank, while Netanyahu is seeking to escalate tensions on several fronts.
“Why only the West Bank? Why not Gaza? Why not Lebanon? Why not Iran? I mean, he’s trying, and this government is trying to heat up all the fronts.”
Levy said the government is seeking to seize as much territory as possible before the elections because it believes it could lose power.
“In the West Bank, it is another aspect, and this is also the fact that they feel that they might lose the elections, and therefore they try to achieve as much as possible until the elections, because all those territories, all those fields that they can take over, one million dunam already, they will never be returned to the Palestinians.
“They try to catch as much as they can until the election, and to build as many new outposts as they can, because they understand that after the elections it will be much harder, because there will be a new government. So there is a direct connection between this and the elections.”
Levy said he does not expect a major change in Israeli policy even if Netanyahu’s government is replaced.
“Unfortunately, the good news is that this government will end its role. It will step down, but I don’t think that there will be a major change, neither toward the Palestinians, nor toward Gaza, nor toward southern Lebanon.”
“None of them criticized the genocide in Gaza. None of them seems to be very troubled by what’s happening in the West Bank. I think in the West Bank, they will stop a little bit the settlers, yes, but strategically, the Palestinian state, any kind of solution, end of occupation, end of apartheid, all those things don’t interest them at all, and they will continue the same policy, which is, as you rightly say, it’s Israel’s policy.”
“It’s not the policy of one government or another,” he concluded.

In a first, 9 Isro staff bodies seek 'written clarity' on private sector shift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
12:50:58 UTC
21:50:58 KST

The joint representation has been signed by the Isro Staff Association, SAC Employees Welfare Association and others.
BENGALURU: For the first time since the government began opening India’s space sector to private industry six years ago, nine employee bodies at Isro centres representing thousands of staff under the Department of Space (DoS), have formally raised concerns over the direction and basis of the transition. They have sought written clarification from chairman, space commission, who also serves as secretary, DoS and chairman, Isro.“Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned Isro. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces Isro to a residual R&D boutique while the realisation of the nation’s launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands,” the representation dated Sept 4 and accessed by TOI, reads.Terming technology developed by Isro a national asset, they said its transfer must be transparent, accountable, and consistent with strategic, safety and employment considerations. “...Serving employees have an earned right to be informed, consulted and protected. Natural justice and good administration require that policy of this magnitude be explained to the workforce by the Department itself.”The joint representation has been signed by the Isro Staff Association, SHAR Employees Association, Isac Employees Association, Isro Staff Association-LPSC, Isro Staff Association-BBU, NRSA Employees Union, Space Employees Association-BBU, Isro Staff Association-IPRC and SAC Employees Welfare Association.
Pointing to a recent public statement reportedly made by IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka on Isro eventually “not manufacturing any launch vehicles”, they asked if his statement “represents an approved decision of the Govt of India, Space Commission or DoS… If approved, the date, authority and text of the policy decision may kindly be indicated.”“What will be the future mandated role of Isro — specifically, whether design, development, realisation, integration, testing and launch of PSLV, LVM-3, SSLV and successor vehicles will continue as Isro functions or will cease. Whether any decision has been taken to exclude PSUs from the proposed transfer of PSLV/LVM-3 production, and the justification for such exclusion,” they asked.They also sought in writing the institutional arrangement under which publicly created technology, test facilities, launch complexes and know-how — built with taxpayer funds and the labour of generations of Isro employees — are being transferred or opened to private operation, and the role of NSIL vis-a-vis IN-SPACe in such transfers.“Isro was built as a national scientific institution with public funds, public purpose and a public workforce. Launch-vehicle design, realisation, integration, testing and launch operations are not merely ‘manufacturing contracts’. They are the core competence, institutional memory and strategic capability of the organisation,” the representation reads.They said they have reasonable fear that a progressive withdrawal of Isro from launch-vehicle and satellite realisation will tamper experiments after research, shrink in-house work, freeze or reduce sanctioned strength, and close promotion and skill-development avenues in technical, scientific, administrative, stores, purchase, quality, safety and industrial cadres.“Existing employees may be rendered surplus, or redeployed, or left without meaningful work while the same tasks are performed by private contractors using publicly developed technology…Regular recruitment to Group A, B and C posts — already constrained by vacancies and attrition — will further decline, denying opportunity to meritorious youth who look to Isro as a public career of honour, not as a private contractor's workforce,” the letter reads.
Congratulating Isro on the success of the GSLV-F17/EOS-05 mission, the letter read: “...We once again proved that we can rise from ashes and fly like a phoenix.”“We submit this in a constructive and democratic spirit. Our loyalty to Isro and to the national space programme isn’t in question. Precisely because of that loyalty, we consider it our duty to seek clarity before uncertainty hardens into irreversible policy,” they said, adding that they will plan further course of action once the written reply is received.

Interview: Father's wartime diary demonstrates best, worst of human nature: Lisbon Maru survivor's son
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:11:45 CST
22:11:45 KST

by Yu Aicen, Zhang Feng
LONDON, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- "From the island a never-to-be-forgotten sight met our eyes, for as far as the eye could see, the ocean was dotted with men and wreckage..."
These are the words of Andrew Salmon, a British Royal Artillery sergeant who was rescued by Chinese fishermen in the Lisbon Maru incident. There is an unusual calmness in his account as he recalls an ordeal that brought him face to face with death.
It was Andrew's wish to have his account published. He wanted to tell the story of his harrowing experience and how he survived with the help of Chinese fishermen. But that wish was never fulfilled before his death in 2000. More than two decades later, his son, Kenneth Salmon, took up the task and finally saw the manuscript published this year under the title "Surviving the Lisbon Maru."
"I had always felt a little bit guilty about not taking my father's manuscript and doing something with it," Kenneth said in a recent interview with Xinhua, describing how he felt before taking on the project. "I knew that it was his, if you like, his dying wish that the book would be published."
Andrew's manuscript largely corroborates what is already known about the calamitous incident. In October 1942, the Japanese-requisitioned Lisbon Maru, carrying more than 1,800 British prisoners of war (POWs), was torpedoed by a U.S. submarine near Dongji, Zhoushan, in eastern China. As the ship sank, local Chinese fishermen came to the rescue. Historical records show that 198 Chinese fishermen helped 384 POWs reach safety.
After escaping the sinking ship, Andrew spent about two hours in the water before joining another survivor, "Ginger" Howell, on a piece of floating wreckage. They were eventually rescued after Ginger, who spoke Shanghainese, hailed a fisherman in a sampan.
"The fisherman picked us up and took us to the opposite side of the island where there was a tiny beach on which he dropped us, fortunately, as the side nearest the Lisbon Maru was steep and rocky," Andrew wrote.
He went on to describe the survivors' first night after the incident on an uninhabited island, where they "huddled together for warmth." They were later taken by a fisherman to "a larger island," where they were given food and clothing, which they "welcomed gratefully," before being recaptured by Japanese soldiers.
"He was lucky that he got out..." Kenneth said. "And he was lucky that he was taken ashore, and the Chinese fishing community gave him food, drink, and shelter, and, of course, warmth, which was very important."
But many others were not so fortunate. A total of 843 POWs died in the incident. Some went down with the ship, while others drowned or were killed by Japanese soldiers during the desperate escape.
The decision to finally complete his father's unfinished book took shape in 2024, when Kenneth was inspired by the release of the documentary film "The Sinking of the Lisbon Maru" and encouraged by people around him.
"When my father retired, it was his desire to do something tangible to memorialize people who were involved in the Lisbon Maru, not only the prisoners of war, but also the Chinese fishermen who rescued them."
He, in his term, "eventually gave in to that pressure," and started to work on the unfinished manuscripts. They include not only Andrew's writing, but also first-hand accounts from the fellow survivors that he was in touch with.
Kenneth completed the book using his father's unfinished manuscript, which in turn drew on Andrew's wartime diary. He believes his father carried the diary with him when he escaped from the Lisbon Maru, allowing its pages to survive against all odds, just as their author did.
Kenneth also wrote parts of the book himself, filling in gaps and adding his own account of two visits to Dongji, in 2024 and 2025, to pay tribute to the waters that witnessed his father's most traumatic experience.
"I had prepared a wreath of poppies with my father's photo in the center, which I threw into the sea," read in one of the several chapters by Kenneth, describing his journey to Dongji in 2024. "That particular wreath had adorned my father's coffin in 2000 and it seemed an appropriate offering."
"These first-hand accounts by survivors provide a deeply personal perspective on the tragedy," Kenneth said. "They show that wars are fought by ordinary people and this story demonstrates both the very best, and the very worst, of human nature in the reality of war." ■

Feature: Syrian displaced girl stitches yarn into hope in E. Lebanon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
21:11:34 CST
22:11:34 KST

BEIRUT, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For 13-year-old Syrian girl Bissan Hikma al-Halabi, crochet began as a way to pass the time in displacement in Lebanon.
But it became so much more: an outlet for her creativity, a source of satisfaction and a path toward a small business that provides a source of income for her family.
In a side room of her family's home in Joub Jannine, a town in eastern Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, balls of brightly colored yarn, scissors, needles and stuffing materials surround the wooden table where she works on her latest creations.
With a crochet hook in one hand and yarn running through the other, al-Halabi carefully turns loops of thread into dolls, bags and other pieces.
"After I finish my schoolwork, I pick up the hook and yarn and start crocheting. Crochet is not just a hobby for me, it has become part of my life," said al-Halabi.
Al-Halabi was born and raised in Lebanon. Her family had fled the al-Amara neighborhood of the Syrian capital Damascus and lived in Lebanon since 2012.
Three years ago, she began learning crochet from her mother, who is skilled in the craft. "The difficult economic situation faced by my family was my main motivation for learning it, as I wanted to help my mother," she recalled.
Al-Halabi began with simple pieces, learning the basic stitches before moving on to more complicated designs. Some pieces take several hours to complete, while larger or more intricate designs can require several days of work.
"I started with simple things and gradually moved on to more varied designs, making bags, accessories, toys and dolls, children's clothes, bedroom items and decorations," she said.
She also takes care to give each piece its own character, from choosing the colors and determining the shape and size to adding the final details.
"If I don't like one of the stitches, I undo it and make it again," she said, describing the patience and concentration required to complete her work.
So far, al-Halabi has made around 100 crochet pieces, spanning 17 different types. Her products are priced between 10 and 25 U.S. dollars, depending on their size and level of detail.
This summer, she took part in five fairs in towns across the Bekaa Valley, alongside other artisans. At the fairs, hundreds of visitors were drawn to the tent displaying her handmade pieces, helping her earn more than 1,500 U.S. dollars in net profits.
"My participation was well received by visitors, particularly mothers who showed interest in handicrafts," she said. "The dolls and toys I made also attracted children."
What started as a pastime has also opened up new possibilities for her future.
She said that she wants to expand her production, market her creations, participate in more exhibitions, to eventually turn her craft into a small business that could provide more income for her family.
Her participation in exhibitions has also brought her work wider attention and encouragement.
Shawki Dallal, head of the Rashaya Fine Arts Workshop, said the organization was pleased to support and showcase al-Halabi's work, describing crochet as a craft that combines creativity, precision and patience.
Dallal said the girl is among the Syrian children living in Lebanon who deserve opportunities to develop their abilities.
"It is a humanitarian message that gives hope to a child who creates beauty with her own hands," he said. ■

====================================================================================================

Watching violent online pornography is linked to poorer sexual health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:00:47 UTC
22:00:47 KST

Young adults who watch violent online pornography tend to report worse sexual well-being, lower empathy, and more acceptance of violence against women than those who watch nonviolent content. These patterns, which look different for men and women, suggest that the specific types of sexual media people consume might shape their interpersonal relationships and physical experiences. The research was published in the journal Behavioral Sciences.
The World Health Organization defines sexual health as a broad state of physical, emotional, and social well-being. This definition goes beyond the mere absence of disease to include psychosocial skills that help people form healthy relationships. Two of these foundational skills are empathy, which involves understanding and sharing the feelings of another person, and sexual assertiveness.
Sexual assertiveness refers to a person’s ability to communicate their desires, initiate wanted encounters, and refuse unwanted sexual activity. Higher levels of this skill protect against sexual coercion and encourage safer sexual practices. Empathy also plays a role in sexual health by fostering mutual satisfaction and reducing the likelihood of aggressive behaviors.
While people consume large amounts of online pornography, research on how different types of explicit media relate to sexual well-being remains mixed. Prior studies often grouped all pornography together, masking how specific content might correlate with different outcomes. Psychological models of media consumption suggest that the consequences of watching pornography depend heavily on the specific context and material viewed.
In recent years, highly accessible online platforms have exposed young viewers to increasingly extreme content during their formative years. To address the knowledge gap regarding specific content, public health researcher Belén Sanz-Barbero from Spain’s National School of Public Health and her colleagues investigated how different forms of violent pornography associate with various dimensions of sexual health.
The researchers organized a large online survey of 3,607 young adults living in Spain between the ages of 18 and 35. For their primary analysis, they isolated a subgroup of 1,985 individuals who reported being sexually active and having watched pornography in the past year. This final group included 1,249 men and 736 women.
The participants answered detailed questionnaires regarding their pornography viewing habits and sexual experiences. To avoid social desirability bias, the tendency for survey respondents to answer questions in a way that will be viewed favorably by others, the researchers avoided using extreme words like rape. Instead, they provided subtle descriptions of sexual encounters and asked participants to rate how often they watched those specific scenarios.
The researchers then categorized the participants based on the most extreme type of pornography they regularly consumed. The three categories were pornography with no explicit violence, pornography featuring degrading or humiliating acts without physical violence, and pornography featuring physical violence. Degrading content included scenes featuring insults, threats, or domination practices that did not inflict physical pain.
Physically violent content included depictions of nonconsensual acts, the use of force, or painful submission practices. The survey instrument also measured the participants’ empathy, sexual assertiveness, and acceptance of violence against women. Additional sections of the questionnaire asked respondents about their sexual satisfaction, their ability to reach orgasm, and whether they had been recently diagnosed with any sexually transmitted infections.
The researchers found that consuming violent pornography was widespread among the study participants. More than 63 percent of the men and nearly 51 percent of the women reported watching pornography that contained physical violence. Men who watched these physically violent videos scored lower on psychological tests measuring empathy and sexual assertiveness compared to men who watched nonviolent pornography.
Both men and women who watched physically violent pornography demonstrated a higher acceptance of violence against women. Men who watched degrading or humiliating content also showed this increased acceptance. The researchers noticed distinct differences between men and women regarding physical sexual function and interpersonal satisfaction.
Men who watched physically violent content were more likely to report enjoying and having fun during sexual activities than those watching nonviolent videos. At the same time, these men were more likely to report feeling discomfort during real world sexual encounters. They also experienced greater difficulty getting or maintaining an erection and were much more likely to use sexual enhancement drugs.
Past studies have shown that the prevalence of erectile dysfunction in men under 40 has increased in recent decades. The researchers proposed that unrealistic sexual fantasies created by violent pornography might cause feelings of distress or moral incongruence when they are not fulfilled in real life. This distress could ultimately interfere with physical sexual function and satisfaction.
For women, watching physically violent pornography was associated with a higher likelihood of struggling to reach orgasm when with a partner. However, these women did not report this same difficulty when experiencing sexual activity alone. The researchers proposed that unrealistic expectations created by violent media might make it harder for viewers to communicate their boundaries or achieve satisfaction with real partners.
The survey also tracked recent diagnoses of sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea, human papillomavirus, and chlamydia. Individuals of both sexes who watched violent pornography reported higher rates of these recent infections. However, the differences were not statistically significant after the researchers adjusted the data for other demographic variables.
Because this research relied on a survey administered at a single point in time, it cannot prove that watching violent pornography causes these negative sexual health outcomes. The relationship might work in the opposite direction. For example, individuals who already struggle with low empathy or sexual dysfunction might seek out more extreme or violent material to achieve sexual arousal.
The psychological theory of empathy suggests that media consumers often identify with one specific actor in a scene, leading to an empathetic disconnection from the other people involved. It is possible that men with naturally lower empathy are drawn to media that allows them to disconnect from the experiences of women. Women might possess a greater emotional resilience to the effects of violent pornography due to different patterns of empathetic identification.
The survey also depended on participants accurately and honestly reporting their viewing habits. Even with built-in statistical adjustments for social desirability, people might naturally underreport socially unacceptable behaviors and overreport positive traits. The researchers also noted that their sample focused heavily on sexually active individuals, which might limit how well the findings apply to broader populations.
Future longitudinal studies tracking viewers over several years will help determine whether exposure to violent pornography directly alters psychosocial development. Until then, public health interventions targeting young adults could focus on building communication skills and critical thinking regarding the sexual scripts modeled in digital media. Recognizing violent pornography as an emerging factor in sexual health could help educators promote safer and more respectful relationships.
The findings offer a new perspective on how digital media habits align with physical and emotional well-being. The study, “Violent Content in Online Pornography Is Associated with Sexual Health of Women and Men,” was authored by Belén Sanz-Barbero, Vanesa Pérez-Martínez, Ana Rico, Laura Otero-García, Marta Fernández-López, Ariadna Cerdán-Torregrosa, and Carmen Vives-Cases.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered a 72-hour halt to strikes on Kyiv, the Kremlin said Saturday, as U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow seeking to revive stalled efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Peskov said the decision was linked to preparations for Witkoff and Kushner’s planned visit to Kyiv on Sunday, which Ukrainian officials have confirmed.

The visit comes as Russia and Ukraine intensify aerial attacks, more than four years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kyiv would suspend airstrikes during the envoys’ visit and called on Russia to do the same, raising hopes for at least a temporary reduction in hostilities as diplomatic efforts resume.
Washington’s push to end the fighting, now in its fifth year, has lost momentum as U.S. attention has been focused for the past six months on its war with Iran. The last known visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, was in January, when they met Putin at the Kremlin. They have never previously visited Kyiv.
The envoys were met at the airport in Moscow by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, Tass reported. Dmitriev shared photos of himself meeting the U.S. delegation as they disembarked, alongside the caption, “Welcome to Moscow, Peacemakers.”
With peace efforts stalled, Russia has intensified its attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with relentless bombardments recently stretching into daylight hours as Ukraine faces shortages of air defense systems.
On Friday, a Russian drone hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv, the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, which is one of the agencies involved in carrying out deep-strike operations inside Russia.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes have hit Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce hubs, seeking to undermine the Kremlin’s war effort and economy while making ordinary citizens feel the consequences of the war.
The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, while the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.
In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports and linked the attack to the planned U.S. visit.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” he said.
“We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.”
Russian attacks killed five people and wounded five more at an industrial facility in Ukraine’s southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. He described those killed as employees at the site.
“A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives,” he said.
A 62-year-old man was wounded and several homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.
In a statement Saturday, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as “major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine’s military production.”
A further two people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s Kyiv region, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. In the Boryspil district, a fire sparked by a strike partially destroyed a nine-story residential building.
Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping center in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said. A 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were hurt.
Emergency crews responding to the incident were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency service said.
Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine’s air force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft, around half of them jet-powered, as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the air force.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks wounded three people, including a 14-year-old girl, in Russia’s border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
In a statement, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

His remarks came after two senior Israeli ministers publicly discussed plans that would involve Palestinians leaving Gaza.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said Thursday that he wanted to see about 250,000 Palestinians leave Gaza during the first year, followed by the departure of the rest of the population over the next six years.
Defense Minister Israel Katz said a day earlier that Israel was prepared to facilitate the departure of Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land, but was waiting for the United States as discussions continued over where those Palestinians could go.
Katz also claimed, without providing evidence, that about 80% of Gaza's residents wanted to leave but were being prevented from doing so by Hamas.
Huckabee said the administration of President Donald Trump supports Palestinians having the option to leave Gaza if they choose, but rejected any suggestion that they should be forced out.
“There is an open-mindedness if people wish to leave, that they should have the right to leave,” Huckabee said, describing it as a “disgrace” to “incarcerate” Palestinians inside Gaza.
“Nobody is suggesting there would be forced displacement,” he added. “The Israelis are not, the Americans are not. I know of no one who supports that.”
Under international humanitarian law, the forced displacement of civilians from occupied territory is prohibited and can constitute a war crime.
The issue is particularly sensitive after Israel's military campaign in Gaza, launched following the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, displaced virtually the entire population at least once, according to international organizations.
Trump himself caused international alarm earlier in his second term when he proposed relocating Palestinians from Gaza and redeveloping the devastated coastal territory as a luxury resort. The proposal drew widespread opposition, including from Arab governments such as Egypt, which borders Gaza, before the administration softened its position.
Huckabee's comments on Gaza came during a visit to Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian town in the West Bank where a large share of the roughly 4,000 residents hold U.S. citizenship.
The ambassador visited the home of Samir Hazmeh, a Palestinian-American whose property has repeatedly been targeted by Israeli settlers. Huckabee said he wanted to hear the community's “legitimate grievances” and stressed that Israel has a responsibility to protect Palestinian civilians.
“One of the messages that we have been sending and we will continue to send is that people in these communities have a right to live with a level of security and safety, and that the government has a responsibility to make sure that that happens,” he said.
As Huckabee met with residents inside Hazmeh's home, a settler from a nearby outpost approached the area on a quad bike.
Israel has controlled the West Bank since capturing the territory in the 1967 Mideast war. Violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinians has persisted for decades, while rights groups and Palestinian residents have frequently accused Israeli authorities of failing to hold perpetrators accountable.
Huckabee stopped short of directly criticizing the Israeli government but said Washington expected those responsible for attacks to face punishment.
“Our clear message is that crime is crime, terror is terror,” he said. “When people do it they should have an expectation that they will have severe consequences.”
Huckabee said confronting settler violence was also in Israel's interest because the actions of a relatively small number of extremists risk damaging the country's international reputation.
“Their reputation does not do well when it appears that this tiny little group of marauders are somehow representative of the larger population,” he said. “I don't believe that it is.”
“There may be a few hundred who are responsible, but that's a few hundred too many,” he added.
Huckabee spent about two hours meeting Palestinian-American residents at Hazmeh's home before joining them for a traditional meal of maqluba, a rice and meat dish prepared by cooking the ingredients in a pot and then flipping it upside down before serving.
Hazmeh said settlers had smashed the home's windows twice, attempted to force open its gates and tried to set the property on fire. He said he installed barbed wire around the house and displayed an American flag in hopes that it would offer some protection.
Yasser Alqam, another Palestinian-American who met with Huckabee, said he owns land about 100 meters away but has been unable to return after repeated attacks by settlers.
Alqam said he believes the United States has enough leverage to pressure Israel to arrest settlers known to authorities.
“The United States already has the ability to put pressure on Israel to at least arrest those settlers who are known to the authorities,” he said.
He also expressed surprise that Trump had lifted sanctions imposed by the previous administration of President Joe Biden on Israeli settlers accused of extremist violence.
Alqam's wife, Jinan, told Huckabee she hoped the U.S. ambassador could help protect Palestinian families trying to reach their land to harvest olives.
She said she wanted his help so residents could “reach our land and pick the olives” during the upcoming harvest.
The visit came as Netanyahu's government has accelerated approvals for new Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The settlements are considered illegal under international law, a position rejected by Israel.
More than 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank alongside roughly 3 million Palestinians.
The issue has become increasingly contentious as Netanyahu has relied on far-right political figures in his governing coalition, including ministers who have openly advocated policies that could lead to the removal of Palestinians.
Huckabee, an evangelical Christian pastor and former Arkansas governor who has long been a strong supporter of Israel and its settler movement, invoked his religious beliefs when discussing attacks against Palestinians.
“I think the Scripture is pretty clear,” he said. “Thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not kill, and thou shalt not even covet.”
His comments also follow a rare public confrontation over settler actions last month, when Huckabee intervened after settler extremists blocked basic supplies from reaching another Palestinian-American resident in the West Bank town of Qusra. Netanyahu subsequently condemned the settlers involved.

Pakistani Prime Minister Congratulates Meloni on Record-Long Tenure
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
14:38:09 CEST
21:38:09 KST

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif congratulated Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on becoming the prime minister who “has remained in office continuously for the longest period in the history of the Italian Republic since World War II”: according to a statement released by the Italian Embassy in Islamabad.
                                    
                                       
				    In a message posted on his X profile, Sharif wrote: “My heartfelt congratulations to Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni for becoming the longest-serving prime minister without interruption in Italy’s post-World War II history. With her capable leadership, she has contributed significantly to Italy’s progress and its growing stature on the world stage.” 
   The Pakistani prime minister added that he looks forward to continuing to work with Meloni to further strengthen relations between Pakistan and Italy in a variety of areas, and extended his best wishes for future success.

Italian Sports Day Around the World: The Third Friendship Run in Zagreb
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-05
13:08:43 CEST
20:08:43 KST

The third edition of the Friendship Run took place today in Zagreb; the event was organized by the Italian Embassy to celebrate Italian Sports Day Around the World, promoted by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Among the event’s partners were the Italian Cultural Institute, FederEsuli, the Italian Union, the Croatian Ministry of Tourism and Sports, the City of Zagreb, the Croatian Academic Sports Federation, and Barilla.
                                    
                                       
				   “The Friendship Run is part of a broader framework of sports diplomacy activities promoted by the Italian Embassy in Zagreb throughout 2026. On September 14, an exhibition will open at the Italian Cultural Institute in Zagreb dedicated to Italy’s greatest sailor, Agostino Straulino—an Olympic and world champion born in Lussinpiccolo. A second leg of the Friendship Run is also scheduled for September 19 as part of the Pula Marathon,” stated Paolo Trichilo, the Italian Ambassador to Croatia.
                                    
                                       
				   In his remarks, he noted that Italy is known for its fine cuisine, high fashion, excellent design, and advanced technology, but also as a major sporting power. In addition to its great athletes and a strong sports industry, Italy is also a host to major international sporting events—two of which took place this year: the Milan-Cortina Winter Olympics and the Mediterranean Games in Taranto. Furthermore, the race achieved its goal of strengthening the friendship between Italy and Croatia, two countries that share the same universal values of sport.
                                    
                                       
				   The competition awarded prizes to the top three finishers in both the women’s and men’s categories, as well as to the youngest and oldest participants. In addition, the three fastest male and three fastest female students received a gift from the Croatian Academic Sports Federation. Two prominent Croatian athletes were present at the awards ceremony: Ana Sršen, a multiple medalist and holder of several world records in Paralympic swimming, and Filip Pravdica, who had just returned from the 20th Mediterranean Games in Taranto with a silver medal in the long jump.
